paragraphs.text: Homily on the First Psalm by our Father among the Saints, Basil, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. 1. All Scripture is inspired by God and useful. The Spirit composed it so that all of us, as if in a common hospital for souls, might each choose the remedy for our own ailment. [?]

[?] and instilling a sober way of thinking about pleasure. The Holy Spirit saw that the human race is hard to lead toward virtue, and that because we lean toward pleasure we neglect the upright life. So what does he do? He blended the delight of melody with the teachings, so that through the sweetness and smoothness of what we hear we might take in, without noticing, the benefit of the words. He does as wise physicians do: when they give the sick bitter medicines to drink, they often smear the cup with honey. That is why these harmonious melodies of the psalms were devised for us: so that those who are children in age, or simply young in character, may seem to be singing while in truth they are training their souls. For hardly anyone among the many and careless ever went away with a command of an apostle or a prophet fixed in his memory; but the words of the psalms they sing at home and carry about in the marketplace. And sometimes a man who has turned quite savage with anger, once the psalm begins to work its charm on him, goes away at once with the wildness of his soul lulled to sleep by the melody. 2. A psalm is calm for souls and an arbiter of peace. It quiets the turmoil and surging of our thoughts. It softens the soul's anger and brings its unruliness to self-control. A psalm draws people together in friendship, unites those who are divided, and reconciles enemies. For who can still regard as an enemy someone with whom he has raised a single voice to God? So even the greatest of [?] and [?] what is sick [?]

[?] it peoples the deserts and brings the marketplaces to sobriety. For beginners it is a first lesson, for those making progress it is growth, for those being made perfect it is a firm support; it is the voice of the Church. It brightens the feasts, and it creates the grief that is according to God. For a psalm calls forth tears even from a heart of stone. A psalm is the work of angels, the life of heaven's citizens, spiritual incense. Oh, the wise design of the Teacher, who contrived that we should sing and at the same time learn what is profitable! In this way the teachings are somehow stamped more deeply on our souls. A lesson forced on us does not usually last, but what enters with delight and charm settles more permanently in our souls. What could you not learn here? Is not the grandeur of courage here, the exactness of justice, the dignity of self-control, the perfection of prudence? Are not the ways of repentance here, the measures of endurance, every good thing you could name? Here is perfect theology, the foretelling of Christ's coming in the flesh, the threat of judgment, the hope of resurrection, the fear of punishment, the promises of glory, the revealing of mysteries. Everything is stored up in the Book of Psalms as in some great common treasury. Although there are many musical instruments, the prophet fitted this book to the one called the psaltery. In my view, he was showing that the grace sounding in him came from above, from the Spirit, because this alone among musical instruments has the source of its sounds above. In the cithara and the lyre the bronze resonates from below against the plectrum, but this psaltery has the source of its harmonious rhythms above. So we too should practise seeking the things above, and not be carried down by the pleasure of the melody to the passions of the flesh. I think the prophetic word also shows us something deep and wise through the construction of the instrument: that those whose souls are well tuned and harmonious find the path upward easy. But let us now look at the beginning of the Psalms. 3. "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly." Builders who raise great structures to a height lay foundations in proportion to that height. Shipwrights who build a merchant ship carrying ten thousand measures fix a keel to match the weight of the cargo. And when animals are generated, the heart, which nature lays down first, receives from nature a foundation proportioned to the animal that is going to be formed. For the body is woven around its own first principles in due measure, and so the differences in size among animals come about. What the foundation is in a house, then,

the keel in a ship, and the heart in an animal's body, this short preface seems to me to be for the whole structure of the psalmody. Since, as the discourse goes on, he is going to urge many laborious things, full of countless sweats and toils, he first showed the contestants of godliness their blessed end, so that in the hope of the good things laid up for us we may bear the pains of life without grief. In the same way, for travellers on a rough and difficult road, the prospect of a comfortable inn lightens the toil; the desire for cargo makes merchants dare the sea; and the hope of a harvest steals away the farmers' labours. That is why the common corrector of our life, the great Teacher, the Spirit of truth, wisely and skilfully set out the rewards first, so that we may look beyond the toils at hand and hasten in mind toward the enjoyment of eternal goods. "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly." Properly speaking, what is blessed in the first sense is the true good, and that is God. So Paul too, when he means to speak of Christ, says, "According to the appearing of the blessed God and our Saviour Jesus Christ." For what is truly blessed is beauty itself, to which all things look and which all things desire: the unchangeable nature, the sovereign dignity, the untroubled life, the existence free of grief, in which there is no alteration and which no change touches; the gushing spring, the unfailing grace, the inexhaustible treasure. But ignorant and worldly people, who do not know the nature of the good itself, often call blessed things that are worth nothing: wealth, health, a distinguished life. None of these is good by its own nature. Not only do they easily turn into their opposites, but they cannot make their owners good. For who is just because of money? Who is self-controlled because of health? On the contrary, each of these often serves as an instrument of sin for those who use it badly. Blessed, then, is the one who possesses what is of the highest worth, who shares in goods that cannot be taken away. How shall we recognize him? "Who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly." Before I explain what it means not to walk in the counsel of the ungodly, I want to resolve a question that is raised about this passage. Someone asks: Why does the prophet single out only the man and call him blessed? Has he shut women out of blessedness? Far from it! The virtue of man and woman is one, since their creation was also of equal honour, and so the reward is the same for both. Listen to Genesis: "God made,"

it says, "man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them." Those who have one nature also have the same activities, and those whose work is equal also have the same reward. Why, then, did he mention the man and pass over the woman in silence? Because he judged it enough, since the nature is one, to indicate the whole by its leading part. "Blessed, then, is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly." Notice how precise the words are, how every expression is full of teaching. He did not say, "who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly," but "who has not walked." For someone still living is not yet to be called blessed, because the outcome is uncertain. But someone who has fulfilled what was laid on him and closed his life with an end beyond dispute can now safely be called blessed. Why, then, are "those who walk in the law of the Lord" called blessed? There the word calls blessed not those who have walked but those who are still walking. The reason is that those who do good have what is acceptable in the very work they do. But those who flee evil are not praiseworthy if they turn away from sin once or twice. They are praiseworthy only if they manage to escape the experience of evil completely. From the sequence of the passage another difficulty has come to light for us. Why does he call blessed not the one who achieves virtue but the one who has not committed sin? On that reckoning a horse, an ox and a stone will be called blessed. For what lifeless thing ever stood in the way of sinners? What irrational creature ever sat in the seat of the pestilent? Wait a little, and you will find the cure. For he goes on: "But his will is in the law of the Lord." Meditation on the divine law belongs only to a rational being. We also say this: the first step toward taking up what is good is withdrawing from what is evil. For it says, "Turn away from evil, and do [?]"

4. So, as he wisely and skilfully leads us toward virtue, he made withdrawal from wickedness the beginning of good things. If he had confronted you at once with what is perfect, you would have shrunk from the undertaking. As it is, he accustoms you to what is easier to grasp, so that you may venture on what follows. I for my part would say that the practice of godliness is like a ladder, the ladder that blessed Jacob once saw. Its lower parts were near the earth and low, while its upper parts reached up even above heaven itself. [?] those who [?] the life of virtue to set foot on the first rungs and from there always to step onto the next, until by gradual progress they climb to the height that human nature can reach. Just as, then, on the

ladder the first step up is leaving the ground, so in the life according to God the beginning of progress is separation from evil. In general, doing nothing is easier than any action whatever. For example: "You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal." Each of these requires only inaction and keeping still. But "You shall love your neighbour as yourself," and "Sell your possessions and give to the poor," and "If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two": these are deeds fit for athletes, and to carry them out requires a soul already vigorous. So admire the wisdom of the one who leads us to perfection by way of what is easier and more readily grasped. He set before us three things to guard against: not to walk in the counsel of the ungodly, not to stand in the way of sinners, not to sit in the seat of the pestilent. He gave them this order by following the nature of things. First we deliberate, then we settle our decision, then we persist in what we have decided. So what is blessed first of all is purity in our mind, since the decision in the heart is the root of the actions done through the body. Adultery, for instance, first catches fire in the soul of the pleasure-lover, and only then works corruption through the body. That is why the Lord says that what defiles a person comes from within. Since ungodliness properly means sin against God, may we never let unbelief bring us to doubt about God! For this is what walking in the counsel of the ungodly means: saying in your heart, "Is there really a God who governs all things? Is there a God in heaven who orders each thing in detail? Is there a judgment? Is there a repayment to each according to his deeds? Why, then, are the righteous poor and sinners rich? Why are these sick and those strong? Why are these without honour and those glorious? Perhaps the world is carried along by chance, and blind accidents hand out each person's life to him at random?" If you think such things, you have walked in the counsel of the ungodly. Blessed, then, is the one who has not fallen into doubt about God; who has not lost heart over present things but waits for what is hoped for; who has held no faithless opinion about the one who created us. Blessed too is the one who "has not stood in the way of sinners." Life is called a way because everyone who is born is pressing on toward his end. People asleep on ships are carried into harbour by the wind of their own accord; even if they do not notice it, the voyage drives them on to its end. So too with us. As the time of our life flows by, each of us is driven toward his own end in a continuous and unceasing movement, by the hidden course of our life. You sleep, and time runs past you; you are awake and busy

in mind, and still life is being spent, even if it escapes our notice. All of us, then, are running a kind of race, each hastening toward his own end. That is why we are all on a way. You may also understand the idea of the way like this. You have set out in this life as a traveller. You pass by everything; everything falls behind you. On the road you saw a tree, or grass, or water, or something else worth looking at. You were pleased for a moment, and then you ran on. Then again you came upon stones, ravines, cliffs, crags and stakes, or perhaps wild beasts, reptiles, thorns or some other annoyance. You were troubled for a moment, and then you left them behind. Such is life: its pleasures do not last and its sorrows do not endure. The road is not yours, and neither are the things you have now. Among travellers, as soon as the first has lifted his foot, the one behind him sets his down, and after him the one who follows. 5. Consider whether the things of life are not much the same. Today you farmed the land, tomorrow someone else will, and after him another. Do you see these fields and these costly houses? How many names has each of them changed since it was made! It used to be called So-and-so's; then it was renamed after someone else. It passed to So-and-so, and now it is called another's. Is not our life a way, then, taking up now one person and now another, and having them all follow one after another? Blessed, then, is the one who "has not stood in the way of sinners." What does "has not stood" mean? While we are in our earliest years we are in neither vice nor virtue, for that age is not capable of either disposition. But when our reason has reached its full growth, then what is written comes to pass: "When the commandment came, sin revived, and I died." For evil thoughts spring up, born in our souls from the passions of the flesh. Indeed, when the commandment comes, that is, the discernment of what is good, if it does not master the worse way of thinking but lets reason be enslaved by the passions, then sin revives and the mind dies, made dead by its transgressions. Blessed, then, is the one who has not lingered on the way of sinners, but has leapt across, by a better way of thinking, to the life of godliness. For there are two ways opposed to each other: one broad and spacious, the other narrow and hard. And there are two guides, each trying to turn people toward himself. The smooth, downhill way has a deceitful guide, an evil demon, who drags his followers through pleasure to destruction. The rough, uphill way has a good angel, who leads his followers through the labours of virtue to the blessed

end. While each of us is a child, he pursues what is pleasant at the moment and takes no thought for the future. But once he has become a man and his ideas have matured, he seems to see his life dividing toward virtue and vice. He turns the eye of his soul again and again toward each, and compares what belongs to the one with what belongs to the other. The life of sinners displays all the delights of the present age, while the life of the righteous only hints at the good things to come. The way of those being saved makes the present laborious in the same measure that it promises the future will be good. But the pleasant and dissolute life holds out enjoyment that is not expected later but is already here. So every soul grows dizzy and wavers in its thinking. When it considers eternal things, it chooses virtue; when it looks at present things, it prefers pleasure. On one side it sees bodily comfort, on the other the body brought into subjection; here drunkenness, there fasting; here unrestrained laughter, there abundant tears; on this side dancing, on that side prayer; here flutes, there groans; here fornication, there virginity. The truly good can be grasped by reason only through faith, for it is far removed, and "eye has not seen and ear has not heard." But the pleasure of sin is close at hand, and its enjoyment flows in through every sense. So blessed is the one who has not been turned toward destruction by the baits of pleasure, but waits patiently for the hope of salvation, and who, in choosing between the two ways, has not set foot on the way that leads to what is worse. 6. "And has not sat in the seat of the pestilent." Does he mean these seats on which we rest our bodies? And how could wood pass on sin, so that I should avoid as harmful a seat a sinner had sat in before me? Or should we take "seat" to mean a settled and lasting persistence in the choice of wickedness? This we must guard against, because diligently dwelling on sins produces in our souls a disposition that is hard to move. A passion of the soul that has grown old, and a practice of evil confirmed by time, is hard to cure, or even wholly incurable, since habit for the most part turns into nature. It is something to pray for, then, not to [?]

[?] slid into passions and, through habit of evil, remaining in their sins even to grey old age. Just as pigs wallowing in the mire keep plastering the mud on themselves, so these people smear on themselves, every day afresh, the shame that comes from pleasure. Blessed, then, is the one who has not even thought of evil. But if the enemy caught you off guard and you admitted ungodly counsels into your soul, do not stand in sin. And if this too has happened to you, do not settle down in evil. Do not, then, sit in the seat of the pestilent. Now that you understand what the word means by "seat", that it means continual attendance on evil, examine next whom it has called "the pestilent". Those skilled in these matters say that when a pestilence touches one person or animal, it passes from one to another and spreads to all who come near. For such, they say, is the nature of this disease, that all fill one another with the sickness. Such too are some of the workers of lawlessness. They pass the disease on one to another, sicken together, and perish together. Do you not see the fornicators sitting in the marketplace, mocking those who live chastely, telling the story of their shameful deeds and the practices of darkness, and listing their dishonourable passions as if they were feats of valour or other acts of heroism? These are the pestilent, who are eager to spread their own evil to everyone, and ambitious to make many like themselves, so that by sharing their wrongdoing with others they may escape reproach. Fire that catches inflammable material cannot fail to spread through all of it, especially if it meets a wind that carries the flame along. In the same way, when sin has touched one person, it cannot fail to pass to all who come near, since the spirits of wickedness fan it into flame. The spirit of fornication does not allow the disgrace to stop with one person. At once companions of his own age are drawn in: revels, drinking bouts and obscene stories, and a courtesan drinking with them, smiling at this one, provoking that one, and setting them all ablaze for the same sin. Is this pestilence small, or the spread of the sickness slight? And what of the one who envies the greedy man, or someone made famous by some other wickedness who has gained political power, or governs nations, or commands armies, and yet wallows in the most shameful passions? Has he not taken the pestilence into his very soul, making his own the evil of the one he envies? For the splendours of life bring to light along with them the lives of the prominent. Soldiers, for the most part, become like their commanders, and those in [?]

…in cities the common people try to copy those in power. In general, whenever the many come to think that one person's wickedness is worth imitating, we may properly and fittingly say that a pestilence of souls is spreading through life. For wickedness that draws attention pulls many who slip easily into the same eagerness. So, since one person after another is infected with the corruption, let such people be said to spread plague among souls. Do not, then, sit in the seat of the pestilent. That is, do not join a council of corrupting and destructive men, and do not stay with those who have made evil plans. But although my discourse is still in its opening, I see that it has already grown too long. It is not easy for you to retain more, and it is not easy for me to carry on the ministry of the word, because my voice fails me through my usual weakness. What has been said has been said incompletely. I have shown how to flee evil, but I have passed over how to reach perfection through good works. Nevertheless, I entrust what I have said to well-disposed ears, and I promise, God willing, to supply what is missing, unless I fall completely silent from now on. May the Lord grant us the reward for what has been said, and you the fruit of what you have heard, by the grace of his Christ, for to him belong glory and power for ages of ages. Amen.

A Psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Hushai son of Jemini.

1. The title of the seventh psalm seems in some way to conflict with the history in the Books of Kingdoms, where the account of David is [?]

[Editorial notes: (42) The third Regius manuscript reads "by the grace of our Lord Jesus." [?] "and the power" [?] is missing in the manuscripts; we have added it.]

recorded. There Hushai is described as David's chief companion and is called the Archite. Here he is Hushai son of Jemini. Yet neither he nor anyone else who appears there is a son of Jemini. So perhaps he was called son of Jemini because of the great feat of courage he performed by pretending friendship. He went over to Absalom in appearance, but in fact he undid the counsels of Ahithophel, a very shrewd and skilled strategist, who was offering his plans. "Son of Jemini" means "son of the right hand." Ahithophel advised against any delay and urged an immediate attack on the father while he was unprepared. Hushai did not allow Ahithophel's counsel to be accepted, "so that," Scripture says, "the Lord might bring all the evils upon Absalom." Instead he seemed more persuasive when he led them into postponements and delays, which gave David time to gather his forces. That is why Absalom approved him, saying, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." Meanwhile Hushai told David through the priests Zadok and Abiathar what had been arranged. He instructed him not to linger in Araboth of the wilderness, and urged him to hurry across. Since his good counsel made him David's right hand, he received his name from his brave deed. That is why he is called son of Jemini, that is, son of the right hand. It is the custom of Scripture to name the worse kind of people after their sin rather than after their fathers, and to call the better kind sons of the virtue that marks them. So the Apostle calls the devil a son of perdition: "For unless the lawless one, the son of perdition, is revealed." And in the Gospel the Lord called Judas the son of perdition: "For none," he says, "was lost except the son of perdition." But those who have been formed in the knowledge of God he calls children of wisdom: "Wisdom is justified

[Editorial notes: [?] should be read [?]. "Archite, companion" [?] a very learned man [?] "unprepared" [?] "undoing the counsels of Ahithophel"; rather: "a very shrewd man proposing his plans" [?]. The fourth [manuscript]: "is revealed," it says, "the man of lawlessness, the son of [perdition]" [?] the manuscripts; as [?]]

by her children." And again: "If a son of peace is there." So it is not surprising that here too his physical father goes unmentioned. David's chief companion is named son of the right hand, and receives from his deed a title that suits him.

2. "O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me." People think the words "O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me" are simple and that anyone at all can say them truthfully. Perhaps that is not so. Someone who hopes in a human being, or who is lifted up by something else in this life, such as power or money or any of the things most people consider splendid, cannot say, "O Lord my God, in you I have hoped." For we are commanded not to hope in rulers, and "Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man." Just as it is not right to worship anything besides God, so it is not right to hope in anyone but God, the Lord of all. "For my hope," it says, "and my song is the Lord." But why does he first pray to be saved from his pursuers, and then to be delivered? The distinction will make the passage clear: "Save me from all who pursue me, and deliver me, lest like a lion he seize my soul." What, then, is the difference between being saved and being delivered? Properly speaking, those who are sick need salvation, while those held in captivity need deliverance. So a person whose weakness lies in himself, but who has also received faith in himself, is brought to salvation by his own faith. "Your faith," it says, "has saved you," and, "Let it be done for you as you have believed." But someone who needs to be delivered waits for a ransom to be paid on his behalf by someone else. So the one who is under death knows that there is one who saves and one who redeems, and he says: "In you I have hoped; save me from weakness, and deliver me from captivity." I think that the noble athletes of God wrestle hard against invisible enemies all their lives. When they have escaped all their persecutions and come to the end of life, they are searched by the ruler of this age. If they are found to have wounds from the wrestling, or any stains or marks of sin, they are detained. But if they are found unwounded and spotless [?]

[Editorial notes: [?] as "Go in peace" and "Let it be done," etc. Where [the text] is uncertain [?]]

from those who pursue me; but deliver me there, at the time of the search, lest like a lion he seize my soul." You can learn this from the Lord himself, who said at the time of his passion, "Now the ruler of this world is coming, and he will have nothing in me." He had committed no sin, and so he said the ruler would have nothing. For a human being it is enough if he dares to say, "The ruler of this world is coming, and he will have in me few and small things." We are in danger of suffering this unless we have the one who redeems us and the one who saves us. The two things the psalm has set out are matched by the two that follow: "Save me from the multitude of those who pursue me, and deliver me," so that I may not be seized as though there were no one to redeem me.

3. "O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then may I fall empty before my enemies. Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it." Scripture usually uses the word "repayment" not only for things given in return, after some good or evil has come first, but also for things that make a beginning, as in "Repay your servant." Instead of saying "Give," it says "Repay." Giving is the beginning of kindness. Rendering back is the equal return measured out by the one who has been treated well. Repayment is a kind of second beginning, a new round of the goods or evils done to certain people. I think that when Scripture asks for repayment in the manner of a claim rather than a request, it means something like this: "Grant me the debt of care that parents, by nature, necessarily owe their offspring." For a father, out of natural affection, owes his children provision for their life. "For parents," it says, "ought to save up for their children," so that besides life itself they may also give them the means of living. This is often how Scripture uses "rendering" or "repayment" for actions that make a beginning. But here the speaker seems confident that he has not paid back those who repaid him with evil, and has not returned like for like. "If then I have done this, and if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then may I fall empty before my enemies." A person falls empty before his enemies when he has fallen from the grace that comes from the fullness of Christ. "Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground." The soul of the righteous is separated from sympathy with the body, and its life is hidden with Christ

[Editorial notes: [?] has "finds" instead of "will have." (55) [?] "those who pursue, and deliver me." [?] instead of "given in return" reads "given in exchange." [?] reads "with Christ."]

in God, so that he can say with the Apostle, "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me," and, "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith." But the sinner lives according to the flesh and is mixed up with the pleasures of the body, and his soul is rolled in the passions of the flesh as if in mud. The enemy tramples on it and strives to soil it even more and almost to bury it. He stands on the one who has fallen, and with his own feet he tramples the life of the one who has slipped into the ground, that is, into the body. "And make my glory dwell in the dust." The saints have their citizenship in heaven and store up good things for themselves in eternal treasuries, so their glory is in heaven. But of those made of dust, who live according to the flesh, it is said that their glory dwells in the dust. Someone who takes pride in earthly wealth, who chases the short-lived honor that people give, and who trusts in bodily advantages, has a glory that does not look up to heaven but stays in the dust. "Arise, O Lord, in your anger; be exalted in the borders of my enemies." The Prophet prays that the mystery of the resurrection may already be at work to abolish their sin. Or he means the lifting up on the cross, which was to take place after the wickedness of the enemies had risen to its utmost limit. Or else "Be exalted in the borders of my enemies" suggests a meaning like this: however high wickedness climbs, however far it spreads into the boundless and unlimited, you can, by the abundance of your power, act like a good physician. He gets ahead of the edges of a spreading sore, and you can halt the disease as it spreads and creeps, and cut off its advance with your corrective blows.

4. "And awake, O Lord my God, by the command you have given." These words can be applied to the mystery of the resurrection. Then the Prophet is asking the Judge to awake and punish every sin, and to bring to fulfillment the commandments laid down for us beforehand. They can also be taken of the Prophet's situation at that time. Then he is asking God to awake and avenge the command he gave. The command was "Honor your father and your mother," given by God, which [Absalom] broke [?]

[Editorial notes: [?] him; "in anger against my enemies," "in fury against my ene[mies]" [?]]

[?] will return. So punish his wickedness, so that a great assembly of peoples may surround you. "And for its sake return on high." For the sake of the assembly that surrounds you, which you gained through your gracious condescension and saving plan, return to the height of the glory you had before the world came to be.

"The Lord will judge peoples." Scripture scatters its teaching about judgment through many passages, because this teaching is most necessary and most essential for instructing in godliness those who have believed in God through Jesus Christ. But since the teaching about judgment is written in many different ways, it will seem confused to those who do not carefully distinguish its meanings. "Whoever believes in me is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged." If the unbeliever is like the ungodly, how can it be said that the ungodly will not rise up in the judgment? And if believers have become sons of God through faith, and are therefore worthy to be called gods themselves, how can "God stood in the assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges between gods"? It seems that Scripture sometimes uses "being judged" to mean being tested, and sometimes to mean being condemned. It means being tested in "Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence," because there it goes on to say, "Test me, O Lord, and try me." It means being condemned in "For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged." That is, if we examined ourselves, we would not fall under condemnation. Again, it is said that the Lord will be judged with all flesh. That is, when each person's life is examined, he submits himself to judgment. He sets his own commands against what the sinners have done, and defends himself with proofs that he did everything in his power for the salvation of those being judged. In this way the sinners are persuaded that they are guilty of their sins, accept the divine sentence, and willingly take on the penalty that falls to them.

5. The word "to be judged" has yet another meaning, as when the Lord says, "The queen of the south will rise up in the judgment and condemn this generation." Some people turn away from divine teaching, have no love for what is good, and utterly reject the corrective doctrines of wisdom. When they are compared and set beside people of their own generation who excelled in zeal for what is good, they receive, he says, for what they neglected, a heavier

condemnation. I do not think that all who have taken on this earthly body will be judged alike by the just Judge. The outward circumstances that befall each of us differ greatly, and so each person's judgment differs too. Things that are not in our power, but that come upon us against our will, either make our sins heavier or lighten them. Suppose fornication is the sin being judged. One man has committed it after being brought up from the start in bad habits. He was born to licentious parents and grew up used to vile things: drunkenness, carousing, and shameful stories. Another man had much to call him to what is noblest: his upbringing, teachers, hearing more divine words, saving readings, his parents' admonitions, stories that shape a person toward dignity and self-control, and a disciplined way of life. If he then falls into the same sin as the first and has to give an account of his life, how will he not rightly deserve a heavier punishment than the other? The first will be charged only for not using well the seeds of salvation sown in his natural understanding. The second will be charged for this and also because he received much help toward salvation, yet through lack of self-control and a moment's carelessness he betrayed himself. In the same way, consider someone raised in godliness from the beginning, who has escaped every distortion in teaching about God, and who has also been raised in the law of God, which condemns every sin and calls us to the opposite. He will not have the same defense for idolatry as someone brought up by lawless fathers, among Gentiles taught from the beginning to worship idols. "The Lord will judge peoples": the Jew in one way, the Scythian in another. The Jew relies on the law, boasts in God, and approves what is excellent. He has been instructed from the law, and besides the notions common to all he is constantly guided by its teaching as if by a charm. He has been trained in the writings of the Prophets and the Law. If he is found to have stumbled into lawlessness, his sins will be counted far heavier. But the nomadic Scythians were raised in wild and inhuman ways. They are used to robbing one another and to violence, they cannot control their anger, and they are easily provoked to rage against one another. They are accustomed to settling every quarrel with the sword [?]

[?] "Judge me, O Lord," he says, "according to my righteousness." There is much to say about righteousness, he says, and the limits of perfect righteousness are hard to reach. The righteousness of angels surpasses that of human beings. If there is any power above the angels, its superiority in righteousness matches its greatness. And the righteousness of God himself surpasses all understanding, since it is beyond words and beyond the grasp of all created nature.

6. "Judge me, then, O Lord, according to my righteousness," that is, according to the righteousness human beings can attain, which is possible for those living in the flesh. "And according to my innocence that is in me." These words show very clearly that the speaker's attitude is far from Pharisaic pride. By his "innocence" he means a kind of guilelessness and lack of experience in the things that are useful for knowledge. This agrees with what is said in Proverbs: "The innocent believes every word." We human beings fall into many things unawares through inexperience, so he pleads with God and asks for pardon on account of his innocence. This makes it clear that his words show humility rather than pride. "Judge me," he says, "according to my righteousness, and judge me according to the innocence that is in me." Weigh my righteousness against human weakness, and judge me on that basis. And when you have seen the simplicity of my ways, do not condemn me when I sin as though I were shrewd or well versed in the affairs of the world.

"Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end." Whoever prays this is plainly a disciple of the Gospel commands. He prays for those who mistreat him, and asks that the wickedness of sinners be confined within some limit and boundary. It is as if someone praying for those who are sick in body were to say, "Let the illness of the sick come to an end." He loves his enemies and wants to do good to those who hate him, and so he prays for those who mistreat him. He asks God to stop sin and set bounds to its further spread, so that it may not creep further like gangrene and spread.

"And you will guide the righteous straight." The righteous man is called upright, and a heart that has been set right is upright. What, then, does the Prophet mean by this prayer? He is praying that someone who is already upright be guided straight. For no one would say that there is anything crooked, distorted or twisted in the righteous. But perhaps this request on behalf of the righteous is necessary. The uprightness of his purpose and the straightness of his intention need to be guided straight by God's hand, so that he may never turn aside from the rule of truth, so to speak, either through weakness or through the enemy of the tru[th] [?]

[?] to be harmed by perverse doctrines. "God tries hearts and kidneys justly." Since Scripture often uses "heart" for the ruling part of the soul, and often uses "kidneys" for its desiring part, it means the same here: "O God, judge me both on the doctrines I hold about true religion and on the movements of passion, for you are the one who tries hearts and kidneys." Trying, strictly speaking, is the inquiry that judges conduct, using every kind of torture, on those they examine, so that those who hide within themselves what is being sought may, under the pressure of pain, bring what is hidden into the open. In the judge's examinations, which cannot be deceived, our thoughts are tried, and our deeds are tried as well. So let no one anticipate the true judge, and let no one judge before the time, "until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts." So in trying hearts and kidneys God displays his own justice. Abraham's heart was tried, whether he loved God with his whole soul and with his whole heart, when he was commanded to offer Isaac as a burnt offering, so that it might become plain that he did not love his son more than God. Jacob too was tried when his brother plotted against him, so that his brotherly love might shine out, undimmed by all Esau's many wrongs. The hearts of these men were tried; but Joseph's kidneys were tried when his licentious mistress was madly infatuated with him and he preferred the dignity of chastity to shameful pleasure. He was tried for this purpose: that those who watch God's judgment might agree that the honor was justly awarded to him, because his purity shone out brilliantly under great trials. 7. "My help is from God." Strictly speaking, it is in wars, when enemies attack, that those under attack look for help. Here too, then, the one who perceives his invisible enemies, and sees the danger hanging over him from the foes encamped around him, will say: "My help comes not from wealth, nor from bodily resources, nor from my own power and strength, nor from human kinship; but my help is from God." What kind of alliance the Lord sends to those who fear him we have learned elsewhere, where the psalm says: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them"; and elsewhere: "The angel who delivers me." "Who saves the upright in heart." Upright [?]. [?] The fourth [manuscript reads] "let him anticipate." [?] "seek." [?]

[?] those who miss the mean by excess and deficiency. For just as a line becomes crooked when the straight line is bent, sometimes outward into a convex curve and sometimes inward into a concave one, so too a crooked heart is now lifted up by arrogance and now brought low by griefs and dejection. That is why Ecclesiastes says: "What is crooked will not be made straight." "God is a just judge, strong and patient, and does not bring wrath every day." Here the Prophet seems to be addressing those who might one day be troubled by what had happened, as if to calm people's agitation, so that they would not lose faith in the providence that governs all things when they saw a father left unavenged when his son rose against him, and Absalom's wickedness prospering in what he had set out to do. So, correcting the folly in their thinking, he solemnly declared to them: "God is a just judge, strong and patient, and does not bring wrath every day." Nothing that happens happens without judgment; rather, God measures back to each person by the very measures that person first used in measuring out the actions of his life. "Since, then, I have committed some sin, I receive what I deserve. So do not speak injustice against God, for God is a just judge. Nor think so meanly of God as to suppose he is too weak to avenge, for he is also strong. What, then, is the reason that punishment is not brought swiftly on sinners? It is because he is patient, 'not bringing wrath every day.'" "If you do not turn back, he will burnish his sword." The words are a threat, urging those who are slow to repent to turn back. He does not at once threaten wounds and blows and deaths, but the burnishing of weapons, a kind of preparation for retaliation. For just as those who polish their weapons signal by this their eagerness for war, so too the text, wishing to show God's movement toward punishment, said that he burnishes his sword. "He has bent his bow and made it ready, and in [?] Eccl. 1:15: "What is crooked will not be able [to be made straight]." it he has prepared instruments of death." It is not a bowstring that bends God's bow, but his punishing power, which is sometimes drawn taut and sometimes slackened. The text threatens the sinner that what is to be sent forth for his punishment is ready for him if he persists in sin. For instruments of death have been made ready on the bow. The instruments of death are the powers that destroy God's enemies. "He has made his arrows for those who are burning." Just as fire was made by the Creator for material that burns (for it was not created for the sake of adamant, which fire cannot melt, but for the sake of wood that is burned up), so also God's arrows were made by him for souls that catch fire easily, in which much fuel has been gathered, ready for destruction. So those who have already received and hold within themselves the fiery arrows of the devil are the ones who receive God's arrows. That is why he says: "He has made his arrows for those already burning." Fleshly lusts set the soul on fire, as do desires for money, fiery fits of anger, griefs that inflame and consume the soul, and fears that are foreign to God. But the one who is unwounded by the enemy's arrows and clothed in the full armor of God remains untouched by the deadly arrows. 8. "Behold, he has travailed with injustice, conceived toil, and given birth to lawlessness." As far as order goes, the wording seems confused, since women who bear children first conceive, then travail, and last give birth, whereas here first comes the travail, then the conception, then the birth. But as an image of what the heart conceives it is extremely vivid. For the irrational impulses of the licentious and their mad, frenzied desires are called travail because they arise in the soul with sharpness and pain. In line with such an impulse, the one who has not mastered his evil plans has "conceived toil," and the one who has fanned the evil in his heart into flame through wicked deeds has "given birth to lawlessness." He seems to say this in shame at being the father of a lawless child: "The child is not mine," he says, "but has become the son of the father into whose family he adopted himself through sin." For according to John, "Whoever commits sin is born of the devil." So, behold, he travailed with him through injustice and conceived him, as it were, in the most intimate [?] 1 John 3:8. into which Joseph was thrown by his brothers. And when there is struck down "from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the captive woman in the pit." And in the Psalms: "I was counted among those who go down into the pit." And in Jeremiah he says: "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and dug for themselves broken pits that will not be able to hold water." And in Daniel too a pit of lions is recorded, into which Daniel is thrown. But Abraham digs a well, as do Isaac's servants; and Moses, when he had gone out, rested by a well. And from Solomon we receive the command to drink water from our own vessels and from the spring of our own wells. And the Savior talks with the Samaritan woman about divine mysteries beside the well. The reason pits are assigned to worse things and wells to better ones we take to be this: in pits the water is brought in from outside, falling from heaven, whereas in wells veins of water that were buried before the places were dug are revealed once the soil covering them is removed, along with whatever substance lies on top, all of which is earth. So in souls too there is, as it were, a dug pit, into which better things fall and are changed and counterfeited, when someone turns the thoughts about good things that have fallen into him, twisting them toward greater wickedness and toward what is opposed to the truth, having resolved to hold no good of his own. And again there are wells, when the worse things covering them are removed and light shines out, and a spring of water fit to drink in word and doctrine. That is why each person must make a well for himself, so as to keep the commandment cited above, which says: "Drink water from your own vessels, and from the spring of your own wells." For in this way we will be called children of those who dug the wells, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But we must not make a pit, so that we do not fall into the hole, as is said here, nor hear what is written in Jeremiah in reproach of sinners, where God says about them what we quoted a little earlier: "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and dug for themselves broken pits that will not be able to hold water for them."

[?] the one who is to attain the beatitudes, using a certain order and path in what he considers concerning him, has made his beginning from the nearer and first things. "Lord, who shall sojourn in your tent?" Sojourning is a temporary way of life, indicating a life that is not settled but passing through, in hope of moving on to better things. It is the mark of a holy man to pass through this life while hastening toward another life. That is why David too says of himself: "I am a sojourner with you, and a stranger, as all my fathers were." For Abraham was a sojourner, owning not even a foot's breadth of land of his own; but when he needed a burial place, he is seen acquiring one with silver. By this the text shows that while one lives in the flesh it is fitting to be a sojourner, but when one passes on from this life, to rest in one's own places. That is why in this life he sojourns among foreigners, but for burial he purchased for himself land of his own to receive his body. It is blessed [not] to be attached to the things on earth as if they were one's own, nor to cling to the things here as to some natural homeland, but to know that one has fallen from better things and, weighed down by living here under sentence, to sojourn as those do who have been driven out of their native land into exile by judges for some offenses. Rare is such a man: one who does not attend to present things as his own; who knows that the use of wealth is temporary; who considers the body's good health short-lived; who recognizes that the flower of human glory is unstable. "Who, then, shall sojourn in your tent?" The flesh given by God to the human soul as a dwelling is called God's tent. Who will attend to this flesh as something not his own? Just as tenants who lease another's land farm it according to the wishes of the one who let it out, so the care of the flesh has been entrusted to us by a kind of contract [?], so that, having worked on it properly, we may return it fruitful to the one who gave it. And if the flesh is worthy of God, it truly becomes God's tent, by his dwelling in the saints. Such is the flesh of the one who sojourns. That is why it says, "Lord, who shall sojourn in your tent?" Then comes progress and advance toward what is more perfect: "And who shall dwell on your holy mountain?" The earthly-minded Jew, when he hears "mountain," runs off to Zion. "Who shall dwell on [?] Two [manuscripts read] "holy" (hosiou) instead of "holy" (hagiou). The Septuagint has it slightly differently: "I am a sojourner in the land."

your holy mountain?" The one who has sojourned in the flesh will dwell on the holy mountain. That mountain is the region above the heavens, renowned and radiant, of which the Apostle says: "You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is a festal gathering of angels and the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven." 2. So when someone passes through this flesh without attachment, sojourning in it as something not his own and not clinging to it as his own, he, having achieved holiness by putting to death his members that are on earth, is worthy to dwell on the holy mountain. Longing for this, the Psalmist said: "I will pass into the place of the wonderful tent," and, "How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts!" There we are brought to dwell both by [?] toward our neighbors, for the sake of that dwelling on the mountain, and by the friendship that comes from the mammon of unrighteousness: "Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings." Of that way of life the Lord spoke in the form of a prayer: "Holy Father, grant that where I am, they too may be." Rare is the one who sojourns in the body, and the one who dwells on the mountain. That is why the text speaks as if at a loss: "Who shall sojourn?" and "Who shall dwell?" just as in "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" and "Who will tell you that a fire is burning?" and "Who will tell you of the eternal place?" and "Who, then, is the faithful and wise steward?" But perhaps the "Who" is also a question, as from one seeking an answer from the holy Lord with whom he is speaking. And what does the divine voice say to him, resolving the question? "He who walks blameless and works righteousness." If the blameless person is one who lacks none of the good things and leads his life without stumbling into any wickedness, what difference is there between him and the one who does righteousness? Does it, then, express the same meaning in two phrases, "He who walks blameless and works righteousness"? Or does each of the expressions present a distinct sense of its own, so that the blameless person is the one who, in the hidden inner self, is fitted out for every perfection of virtue, while the one who works righteousness is the one who perfects his practical life through bodily actions? For we must not only do the just deed but also do it from a just disposition, as it is said: "You shall pursue what is just justly";

that is, he must carry out the deed with the principle of righteousness. For example, a layman may do something medical that benefits the sick, but such a person has not acted medically, because nothing of the art accompanies his action. So "he who walks blameless" is the one perfect in mind, and "he who works righteousness" is, in the Apostle's words, the Lord's "workman who has no need to be ashamed." Pay attention to the precision of the wording. He did not say "having walked blameless" but "walking blameless," nor "having worked righteousness" but "working." For a single deed does not make the earnest person perfect; rather, virtuous activity must extend through his whole life. "Speaking truth in his heart, who has not practised deceit with his tongue." Here again, speaking truth in the heart and not practising deceit with one's tongue are related to each other in the same way that being blameless was related to working righteousness. For just as there the text presents both the one perfect in hidden things and the one who succeeds in practical life, so here, since what is spoken comes from the abundance of the heart, the word flowing as from a spring of the inner disposition, he first mentioned the truth in the heart, then the absence of deceit in the word put into action through the tongue. We will find that truth has two meanings: one is the grasp of the things that lead to the blessed life; the other is sound knowledge about any matter whatever in life. That truth, the one that works with salvation and is in the heart of the perfect person, must be handed on to one's neighbor without deceit in everything. But in the matters of life, even if the earnest person should sometimes miss the truth, this will be no obstacle to him in reaching what lies before him. For how many stades there are of land or sea, how many stars move, and how much one exceeds another in speed—if we do not know the truth about these things, it will not hinder us at all from attaining the blessedness held out in the promises. But perhaps the text is also showing us something like this: that it is fitting to speak of the things of truth, that is, the mystical things, not to everyone but to one's neighbor—meaning not to reveal them to just anyone, but to those who have shared in the mysteries. And if our Lord is the Truth, let each of us hold this truth stamped and, as it were, sealed in our own heart; and speaking of it in our hearts, let us not adulterate the word of the Gospel when we proclaim the message to our neighbors. "Who has not practised deceit with his tongue." In many places [?] as an enemy of God, the [?] [Some manuscripts] have "of Christ" instead of "of the Lord."
