deceit has been denounced in Scripture. "May the Lord destroy," it says, "all deceitful lips"; and, "Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil." Anything better is said to be adulterated when something worse is mixed into it: wine is adulterated when something worse is mixed with it or water is blended into it, and gold is adulterated when combined with silver and bronze. So too truth is adulterated when more blasphemous words are woven in with the holy words. 4. "Nor has he done evil to his neighbor." Whom the text calls "neighbor," no one doubts who has heard the Gospel's reply to the man who asked, "And who is my neighbor?" To him the Lord told the parable of the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and then asked him, "Which of these do you think proved to be a neighbor?" And he answered, "The one who showed mercy to him." By this he taught us to regard every human being as a neighbor. But this too is hard to achieve and calls for much care: not to harm one's neighbor in anything small or great; not to injure him by a word; not to deprive him of anything that is his due; not to wish him ill; not to indulge in envy at the good fortune of those around us. "And has not taken up a reproach against those nearest him." The wording is ambiguous: either he himself did nothing deserving of reproach from those nearest him, and so received no reproach from them; or he himself reproached none of those nearest him, whether they had fallen into human failings or were found to have bodily defects or some other shortcomings of the flesh. For the sinner is not to be reproached, as it is written: "Do not reproach a man who is turning away from sin." Indeed, we have never known reproach to be used for the benefit of offenders, since the Apostle, in his instructions to his disciple Timothy, allowed rebuke, exhortation, and admonition, but nowhere adopted reproach, as being contrary to these. And it seems that rebuke has as its aim the correction of the sinner, while reproach serves to shame the one who has stumbled. To reproach someone for poverty, low birth, ignorance, or bodily illness is altogether irrational and foreign to the earnest person. For what happens to us not by our own choice is involuntary, and for involuntary shortcomings pity [?] The Basel edition and five manuscripts: "may [he] destroy." [?] The fourth Royal [manuscript]: "as wine is adulterated with something worse." [?] Gen. 29.

[?] …it was fitting that the unfortunate be [?] rather than insulted. 5. "In his sight the evildoer is set at nought, but he honours those who fear the Lord." It belongs to a lofty mind, one that bows to no human need, and to a man who has brought the habit of justice to perfection, to give each person what he deserves. He sets evildoers at nought, even if they happen to be clothed with great power, even if they flourish in wealth or in the distinction of their family, even if they claim splendour for themselves. If wickedness alone is found in them, he sets such people at nought, that is, he counts them as nothing. Conversely, those who fear the Lord, even if they are poor, low-born, unskilled in speech or weak in body, he honours, exalts and counts blessed, for he has been taught by the Spirit to call such people blessed. "For blessed," it says, "are all who fear the Lord." It belongs to the same mind to set the evildoer at nought, even if he is raised high in splendour, and to honour the one who fears the Lord, even if he is lowly, poor in his way of life and despised, and possesses none of the outward things that win people's approval. "He who swears to his neighbour and does not break faith." Why is it that here keeping one's oath is allowed among the noble deeds befitting the perfect man, while in the Gospel swearing is entirely forbidden? Here: "Who shall sojourn, and who shall dwell? He who swears to his neighbour and does not break faith." But there: "But I say to you, do not swear at all." What then do we say? That everywhere the Lord holds to the same aim: he forestalls the consequences of sins and cuts wickedness out at its very root. The old law said, "You shall not commit adultery," but the Lord, "You shall not even desire"; the law said, "You shall not kill," but he who gives the more perfect laws, "You shall not even be angry." In the same way, here the law is content with keeping oaths, while the Lord cuts off the occasion of perjury. For the man who swears truly might perhaps at some point slip against his will, but the man who does not swear has escaped the danger of perjury. In many places Scripture also calls an unalterable affirmation about any matter an oath, as in "I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness" [?].

[?] …"and will not repent." This is not because he brought in God as a witness to make what was said credible and remove ambiguity [?], but because he confirmed the grace of the promise to David by unchangeable and immovable decrees. So here too it may be said: "He who swears to his neighbour," that is, who gives his neighbour a firm assurance, "and does not break faith." This agrees with what the Lord said: "Let your word be yes, yes, and no, no." Give your assurance and assent about things that are so; and about things that are not so, even if everyone begs you, never let yourself be persuaded to affirm something against the truth of the facts. Has the thing not happened? Let denial follow. Has it happened? Let assent affirm it. Try to present the truth by itself, without tying anything else to it, and use plain affirmations. Let the one who refuses to believe bear the harm of his own disbelief. For it is utterly shameful and foolish to accuse yourself of being untrustworthy by bringing in the security of oaths. There are some expressions that have the form of oaths but are not oaths; they are courtesies to the hearers. So Joseph, winning the Egyptian's goodwill, swore "by the health of Pharaoh." And the Apostle, showing his love for the Corinthians, said, "By the boasting in you that I have in Christ Jesus our Lord." For the man entrusted with the Gospel did not disobey the Gospel's teaching. He gave a plain statement in the form of an oath, showing in this way that his boasting in them was worth everything to him [?].

6. "Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow." The word calls us to what is sociable, to mutual love, and to what is proper to our nature. For man is a social animal that lives in community. In the common life of society and our dealings with one another, a readiness to share is needed to relieve those in want. "Give to the one who asks you." He wants you to be open-handed and simple toward those who ask, out of love, but also to use reason to discern the need of each of those

who beg. We have learned in the Acts how this can be done well by those who fulfil the aim of godliness wisely: "For as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, brought the price of what was sold, and laid it at the apostles' feet. And it was distributed to each as any had need." Many go beyond the use of necessities and make begging a source of trade and a means of shameless luxury. So it was necessary for the money to be collected with those entrusted with the care of the poor, so that from there the necessities could be distributed wisely and prudently according to each person's needs. With the sick there is often need of wine, but not everyone can judge the right time, amount and kind; a physician is needed to give the wine. In the same way, not everyone can manage the care of the needy so that it does good. For those who compose mournful songs to deceive women, and who put their bodily deformities and sores on show as a means of trade, generous giving is by no means helpful; the supply will become an occasion of vice for them. We should drive off the barking of such people with a small gift, and show our compassion and brotherly love to those who have learned to bear affliction with patience. On their account it will be said to us, "I was hungry and you gave me food," and the rest. "And do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow." This command too is connected with the earlier ones. For the person who asks here is poor and asks you for a loan, pointing you to the one who is rich in heaven, who will pay you the debt on his behalf. "For whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God," it says. And the pledge for the loan is the kingdom of heaven. May we all be found worthy of it by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory and power to the Father and the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

[?] …the hour did not allow us. But now we have come like grateful debtors to pay you what we left owing. What remains is short to listen to, or so it may seem, and perhaps it escaped many of you, so that no part of the psalm was thought to have been left out. But we have come to see that this short phrase has great force for the affairs of life, and so we did not think we should give up the benefit of examining it. In sketching the perfect man, the one who is to rise to the unshaken life, the Prophet counted among his noble deeds that he did not give his money at interest. This sin is condemned in many places in Scripture. Ezekiel puts taking interest and increase among the greatest evils, and the law plainly forbids it: "You shall not lend at interest to your brother and your neighbour." And again it says, "Deceit upon deceit, and interest upon interest." And what does the psalm say about a city flourishing in a multitude of evils? "Interest and deceit have not departed from its streets." And now the Prophet has taken this very thing as a mark of human perfection, saying: "He did not give his money at interest." It truly is the height of inhumanity that one man, lacking the necessities of life, seeks a loan to ease his life, while the other is not content with the principal but schemes to gather income and wealth for himself out of the poor man's misfortunes. The Lord gave us a clear command: "And do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you." But the money-lover sees a man bent down by necessity, pleading at his knees. What humble thing does he not do, what does he not say? Yet the lender does not pity him in his undeserved plight. He gives no thought to their shared nature and does not yield to his pleas. He stands unbending and implacable, not giving way to entreaties or softened by tears. He persists in refusing. He swears and calls curses on himself that he truly has no money at all and is himself looking around for someone to lend to him. He backs up the lie with oaths, and so gains perjury as a wicked side-trade to his inhumanity. But when the one seeking the loan mentions interest and names securities, then he relaxes his frown and smiles. Somehow he even remembers a friendship with the man's father, and calls him acquaintance and friend. "We'll see," he says, "whether we have any money put by. There is a deposit

that a friend placed with us to invest. But he set heavy interest on it. We, though, will certainly let something go and give it to you at lower interest." With such pretences and words he fawns on the wretched man and lures him in. He binds him further with written contracts, and on top of the poverty that already crushes him he takes away the man's freedom as well, and off he goes. For the man who has made himself liable for interest he cannot bear to pay has accepted a slavery of his own choosing for life. Tell me, do you look for money and income from a man without means? If he could make you richer, why would he be seeking help at your door? He came looking for an ally and found an enemy. He searched for remedies and came upon poisons. You ought to relieve the man's poverty, but you multiply his want and try to harvest a crop from the desert. It is as if a physician visited the sick and, instead of restoring them to health, took away even the little strength they had left. In the same way you make the misfortunes of the wretched a source of income. Just as farmers pray for rain to multiply their seed, you look for people in want and need so that your money can be put to work. Do you not know that you add more to your sins than you contrive to add to your wealth by interest? The one seeking the loan is caught between two impossibilities. When he looks at his poverty, he despairs of repaying; when he looks at his present need, he ventures on the loan. Then the one is defeated, bowing to need, and the other goes off [?]

[?] …"When the lender and the debtor meet each other," it says, "the Lord watches over both." The one runs at his prey like a dog; the other cowers at the meeting like game ready to be caught. For poverty robs him of his boldness. Both of them reckon on their fingers: the one rejoices at the growth of the interest, the other groans at the increase of his misfortunes. "Drink water from your own vessels"; that is, look to your own resources. Do not go to other people's springs, but gather what you need to live from your own fountains. Do you have bronze vessels, clothing, a beast of burden, household goods of every kind? Sell them. Agree to part with everything except your freedom. "But I'm ashamed to sell them in public," he says. Why, then, when a little later someone else will bring them out, auction off your things, and dispose of them cheaply before your very eyes? Do not go to other people's doors. For truly "another's well is narrow." It is better to meet your need little by little with small expedients than to be puffed up all at once by other people's goods and later be stripped of everything you have together. If you have the means to repay, why not relieve your present want from those resources? But if you lack the means to repay, you are curing one evil with another. Do not let a lender lay siege to you. Do not put up with being hunted and tracked down like some other kind of game. Borrowing is the beginning of lying, the occasion of ingratitude, unfairness and perjury. The borrower says one thing, and the man being pressed for payment says another: "I wish I had never met you then; I would have found a way out of my need by now. Didn't you thrust the money into my hand against my will? Your gold was mixed with copper and the coin was counterfeit." So if the lender is a friend, do not lose his friendship; if he is an enemy, do not put yourself in a hostile man's power. You will show off for a little while in other people's goods, and afterwards you will give up even what you inherited from your father. You are poor now, but free. If you borrow, you will not become rich, and you will lose your freedom. The borrower is the lender's slave, and a hired slave at that, bearing a service he cannot escape. Dogs grow tame when they are given something; the lender, when he is given something, is provoked all the more. He does not stop barking but demands more. If you swear, he does not believe you. He searches your house, your dealings

he pries into. If you go out [?], he drags you off to himself; if you hide yourself inside, he stands over the house and knocks at the door. He shames you before your wife, insults you before your friends, throttles you in the marketplace. He is an evil encounter at a festival [?], and he makes your life unliveable. "But the need is great," he says, "and there is no other source of money." What then is the gain in putting it off for today? Poverty will come at you again like a good runner, and the same need will be back, only greater. For a loan does not give complete release from helplessness, only a short postponement. Let us suffer the hardships of want today and not put them off to tomorrow. If you do not borrow, you will be just as poor today as later; but if you borrow, you will be worn down more harshly, for the interest will intensify your poverty. Now no one blames you for being poor, since the evil is involuntary; but if you are liable for interest, there is no one who will not blame your [?]

3. So let us not, on top of evils we cannot help, bring upon ourselves through our own folly an evil we choose. It is the mark of a childish mind not to make do with what one has, but to trust in uncertain hopes and venture on obvious and undeniable harm. Think now: where will you repay from? From what you receive? But that is not enough both for your need and for the repayment. And if you also reckon in the interest, how will the money be multiplied so far that one part meets your need, another makes up the principal, and on top of that it produces interest? No, you will not repay the loan from what you receive. From somewhere else, then? Then let us wait for those other hopes and not come to the bait like fish. For just as they swallow the hook with the food, so we are pierced by interest for the sake of money. Being poor brings no disgrace. Why then do we heap on ourselves the reproaches that come from owing? No one heals wounds with a wound or cures evil with evil, and no one repairs poverty with interest. Are you rich? Do not borrow.

Are you poor? Do not borrow. If you are well off, you do not need a loan; if you have nothing, you will not repay the loan. Do not hand your life over to regret, or someday you will call the days before the interest happy ones. In this one thing we poor are better off than the rich: freedom from care. We laugh at them lying awake while we sleep, and at them always tense and anxious while we are carefree and at ease. But the debtor is both poor and full of care. He is sleepless by night and sleepless by day, brooding all the time. Now he appraises his own property, now the costly houses and the fields of the rich, the clothes of the people he meets, the dishes of those who give dinners. "If these were mine," he says, "I'd sell them for so much and so much and be rid of the interest." These thoughts sit in his heart by night and fill his mind by day. If you knock at the door, the debtor is under the bed. Someone comes running in, and his heart pounds. The dog barks, and he is drenched in sweat, gripped by anguish, and looks around for a way to escape. When the due date draws near, he worries about what lie he will tell, what excuse he will make up to put the lender off. Do not think of yourself only as receiving the money, but also as being pressed to repay it. Why do you yoke yourself to a beast that breeds so prolifically? They say that hares give birth, suckle their young and conceive again all at once. So too with usurers, money is lent, begets and grows all at the same time. You have not yet got it into your hands, and already you are asked for this month's interest. And this, lent again, has bred another evil, and that another, and so the evil goes on without end. That is why this kind of greed has been given its name. For it is called tokos, "offspring," I think, because the evil is so prolific. Where else would the name come from? Or perhaps it is called tokos, "birth," because of the birth-pangs and griefs it naturally causes in the souls of borrowers. For as the pangs come upon the woman giving birth, so the due date comes upon the debtor. Interest upon interest: the wicked offspring of wicked parents. Let these products of interest be called a brood of vipers. They say vipers are born by eating through their mother's belly. And interest is born by devouring the houses of debtors. Seeds sprout over time and animals reach maturity over time, but interest

is born today and today begins to give birth. Among animals, those that breed quickly also stop breeding quickly. But money, which begins to increase quickly, admits of endless increase. Each growing thing stops growing once it reaches its proper size; but the silver of the greedy keeps growing as long as time goes on. Animals hand on breeding to their offspring and themselves stop conceiving; but lenders' money both breeds the new increments and makes the old ones young again. May you never come to know this monstrous beast by experience. 4. You see the sun as a free man. Why do you begrudge yourself the freedom of life? No boxer dodges his opponent's blows the way a borrower dodges meeting his creditor, hiding his head behind pillars and walls. "How then shall I live?" he says. You have hands, you have a craft. Work for wages, take service. There are many ways of making a living, many resources. But you are unable? Beg from those who have. But begging is shameful? Defrauding a lender after borrowing is more shameful still. I do not say this as though I were laying down a law, but to show you that anything is more bearable than borrowing. The ant can feed itself without begging or borrowing, and the bee gives what is left of its own food to kings, though nature gave them neither hands nor crafts. Will you, man, the inventive creature, not find a single one of all the ways to get through life? Yet we see that it is not those lacking necessities who come to borrow (for they have no one to trust them). Rather, the people who borrow are those who give themselves up to unrestrained spending and fruitless extravagance, slaves to a wife's love of luxury. "For me," she says, "costly clothing and gold jewellery; for the children, fine clothes to set them off; and for the servants too, bright and embroidered cloaks; and plenty on the table." The man who serves his wife in such things goes to the banker, and before he has even used what he got, he takes one master after another. Forever transferring his bonds from lender to lender, he escapes being exposed as insolvent by keeping the evil going. And just as

…paying off what came before, and so winning himself the credit to borrow again through the very persistence of the evil. Then, just as in cholera those who keep vomiting up whatever is in them, and take in fresh food before they are fully purged, vomit again with pain and convulsions, so these people too take interest upon interest and bring in a second loan before clearing the first; they live in luxury for a little while on what belongs to others, and afterwards lament the loss of their own as well. Oh, how many have been ruined by other people's goods! How many, rich only in a dream, have reaped the penalty beyond measure! “But many,” someone says, “have grown rich from loans.” More, I think, have hanged themselves. You see those who grew rich, but you do not count those who strangled themselves, who could not bear the shame of being pressed for payment and preferred death by hanging to a life of disgrace. I have seen a pitiful sight: freeborn children dragged to the auction block for their father's debts. You have no money to leave your children? Then do not rob them of their free birth as well. Preserve for them this one possession, their freedom, the deposit you received from your own parents. No one has ever been charged with his father's poverty, but a father's debt leads to prison. Do not leave behind a bond that comes down like a father's curse upon children and grandchildren. 5. Hear, you rich, what advice we give the poor because of your inhumanity: to endure their hardships rather than accept the calamities that come from interest. But if you obeyed the Lord, what need would there be for these words? And what is the Master's counsel? “Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive anything back.” “And what kind of loan is this,” someone says, “that carries no hope of repayment?” Consider the force of the saying, and you will marvel at the lawgiver's love for humankind. When you are going to give to a poor man for the Lord's sake, it is at once a gift and a loan: a gift, because you have no hope of getting it back; a loan, because of the generosity of the Master who repays on the poor man's behalf, who receives little through the poor man and will repay much in return. For “whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God.” Do you not want the Master of all to be bound to you for repayment? If some rich man in the city promises to pay you on behalf of others, you accept his guarantee; yet you will not accept God, who pays back the poor man's debt and more? Give the money that is lying idle,

without weighing it down with additions, and it will go well for both of you. You will have the safety of having it kept, and the borrower the profit of using it. And if you are looking for an increase as well, be content with what comes from the Lord. He himself will pay the surplus on behalf of the poor. Look for kindness from the one who is truly kind. For what you take falls short of no extreme of inhumanity. You profit from misfortunes, you collect money from tears, you strangle the naked, you beat the starving. There is no mercy anywhere, no thought that the sufferer is your kin, and you call the profits you make from this “kindness.” “Woe to those who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter,” and who call inhumanity humanity. Not even the riddles of Samson that he put to his fellow drinkers were like this: “Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness”—and out of the inhuman came humaneness! “They do not gather grapes from thorns, nor figs from thistles,” nor humaneness from interest. “For every rotten tree bears bad fruit.” There are “hundredth-collectors” and “tenth-collectors,” names dreadful even to hear; monthly exactors who, like the demons that cause epilepsy, fall upon the poor according to the phases of the moon. It is an evil giving for both, for giver and receiver alike: it brings the one a loss in money, the other a loss in his very soul. The farmer, once he has the ear of grain, does not go digging under the root again for the seed; but you both have the fruits and will not let go of the principal. You plant without land; you reap without sowing. It is uncertain for whom you are gathering. The one weeping over the interest is plain to see, but who will enjoy the wealth that comes from it is doubtful. For it is uncertain whether you will leave the enjoyment of the wealth to others, having stored up for yourself only the evil of the injustice. So do not turn away the one who wants to borrow, and do not give your money at interest, so that, having been taught what is profitable from the Old and New Testaments, you may depart to the Lord with good hope, there to receive the interest on your good works, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 28. A Psalm of David, at the departure from the tabernacle. 1. The twenty-eighth psalm shares the common title, for it says, “A Psalm of David”; but it also has something peculiar to it, for there is added, “at the depar- (Matt. 5:42)

-ture from the tabernacle.” What does this mean? Let us consider what the departure is and what the tabernacle is, so that we may be able to enter into the intent of the psalm. As far as the historical sense goes, this instruction will seem to be given to the priests and Levites when they leave off their work, so that they remember what they ought to have prepared for the service. For as they depart from the tabernacle and go out, the word solemnly charges them with what they ought to have made ready, and with what they should come to the next service: sons of rams; glory and honor; glory to his name; and that they ought to worship nowhere else but in the court of the Lord and in the place of the sanctuary. But for our understanding, which contemplates lofty things, and according to the elevated sense befitting divine Scripture, the ram is not understood as the male among the sheep, nor the tabernacle as the dwelling put together from this lifeless material, nor the departure from the tabernacle as a withdrawal from the temple. Rather, the tabernacle for us is this body, as the Apostle taught us when he said, “We who are in this tent groan”; and again the psalm: “And no scourge shall come near your dwelling.” The departure from the tabernacle is our withdrawal from this life, for which the word bids us prepare by bringing such and such things to the Lord, since the work done here is provision for the journey to the life to come. And whoever here brings glory and honor to the Lord through good works stores up glory and honor for himself according to the just recompense of the Judge. In many copies, however, we find added, “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.” Not everyone's gift is acceptable to God, but only that of one who offers it from a pure heart: “For vows paid from a harlot's hire are not pure,” it says; and again Jeremiah says, “Will vows and holy flesh take away your wickedness, or will you be made clean by these?” Therefore the psalm wants us first to be sons of God, and only then to come forward to bring gifts to God, and not just any gifts, but such as he himself has prescribed. First say “Father,” then ask for what follows. But test yourself: from what sort of life have you come, and are you worthy to call the holy God your father? Our kinship with the Holy One comes through sanctification. If you wish always to be a son of the Holy One, let sanctification adopt you. “Bring to the Lord,” then—not just anyone, nor those sprung from just anyone, but “sons of God.” He is about to ask for great gifts; that is why he chooses great people to offer them. For so that he may not cast your thoughts down to the ground, and make you look for a ram, this irrational, four-footed, bleating animal, as if [?]

you expected to appease God by sacrificing it, he says, “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.” It is not that a son is needed in order to offer up a son; rather, if the son is something great, it is fitting that what is offered should also be something great, worthy both of a son's disposition and of the father's dignity. “Bring,” then, he says, “sons of rams,” so that those offered by you may themselves be changed from being sons of rams into sons of God. 2. The ram is an animal that leads; it guides the sheep to nourishing pastures and to restful waters, and back again to folds and pens. Such too are those who preside over Christ's flock. They lead the way to the flowering and fragrant food of spiritual teaching; they water the flock with living water through the supply of the Spirit, raising it up and nurturing it to bear fruit; and they guide it to rest and to safety from those who plot against it. It is the sons of these that the word wants the sons of God to bring to the Lord. And if the rams are those who lead the rest, their sons would be those whom the teaching of the leaders has formed for the life of virtue through zeal for good works. “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams.” You have learned to whom he is speaking; you have learned about whom he speaks. “Bring to the Lord,” he says, “glory and honor.” How then do we, who are earth, bring glory to the great Lord? And how do we bring honor? Glory, through good works, when our works shine before men, so that men see our works and glorify our Father in heaven. It is also possible to glorify God through self-control and the holiness that befits those who profess godliness, according to the exhortation of Paul, who says, “Glorify God in your members.” This is the glory the Lord demands from those who believe in him and have been honored with the gift of adoption. “For a son,” it says, “glorifies his father”; and, “If I am a father, where is my glory?” And he brings honor to God who, as Proverbs says, honors God from his own just labors and offers him the firstfruits of his fruits of righteousness. Everyone, too, who speaks of God with due order, so as not to fall away from the right understanding of the Father, and concerning [?]

the divinity of the Only-begotten, and concerning the glory of the Holy Spirit—such a person brings glory and honor to the Lord. And he increases the glory who can explain the principles by which all things were created and by which they are held together, since God's providence reaches down to the very smallest things, and the principles by which, after the order of things here, they will be brought to judgment. Whoever has been able, with clear and unconfused reasoning, to contemplate each of these things himself, and after contemplating them can also set forth to others the truth about God's goodness and his just judgment—he is the one who brings glory and honor to the Lord, provided he also leads a life in keeping with such contemplation. For the light of such a person shines before men, and the Father in heaven is glorified by his word and deed and by every kind of noble action. But the one infatuated with human glory does not bring glory and honor to the Lord; nor does the one who honors money; nor the one who honors the pleasures of the body; nor the one who admires doctrines foreign to true religion. For just as we bring glory to the Lord through good works, so through evil works we do the opposite. For what does he say to sinners? “Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations.” And again the Apostle: “Through transgression of the law you dishonor God.” For disregard and contempt of the laws is an insult to the lawgiver. And in a badly run household, where there is anger and shouting, insolence and laughter, luxury and debauchery, impurity and licentiousness, the dishonor and shame of what goes on there falls back upon its master. It follows that we should understand that, just as God is glorified in good works, so the enemy is glorified in evil ones. For when I take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot, I have transferred the glory from the one who saves me to the one who destroys me. And the unbeliever exchanges the glory of the incorruptible God for an image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things of the earth. And whoever reveres and serves the creature rather than the Creator brings glory not to God but to created things. So let whoever calls something a creature and then worships it recognize the company in which he will be ranked. Let us fear, then, lest by offering glory and boasting to the devil through our sin we be handed over with him to eternal shame. That our sin becomes glory for the one who works it in us, understand from an illustration. When two generals advance against each other, whenever this army wins, its commander carries off the glory; but whenever the other side prevails, the honor passes over to that one instead. So in your good works it is the Lord who is glori-

-fied, and in their opposites, the Opponent. And do not, I beg you, imagine the enemies to be far off, or look for the generals somewhere outside; examine yourself, and you will find the illustration entirely true. For when the mind wrestles with passion, if it prevails through vigor and vigilance, it carries off the prize of victory over the passion and, as it were, crowns God through itself. But when it is weakened [?] by pleasure and becomes a slave and captive to sins, it adds boasting and exaltation and arrogance to the enemy. 3. “Worship the Lord in his holy court.” After bearing the fruits that are required, worship is necessary—worship performed not outside the Church but in the very court of God. “Do not,” he says, “imagine private courts and assemblies of your own. There is one holy court of God.” Formerly the synagogue of the Jews was a court; but after their sin against Christ, “their habitation was made desolate.” That is why the Lord too says, “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold.” Speaking of those from the Gentiles who were predestined to salvation, he shows that he has a court of his own, distinct from that of the Jews. So one must not worship God outside this holy court, but having come inside it; so that no one, by being outside it or by being drawn away by those outside, may lose his place in the court of the Lord. For many stand in the posture of prayer and yet are not in the court, because their mind wanders and their thoughts are pulled away by anxiety over vain things. It is also possible, rising higher still, to understand the court as the heavenly way of life. That is why “those who are planted” here “in the house of the Lord,” which is the Church of the living God, will there “flourish in the courts of our God.” But whoever makes a god of his belly, or of glory, or of money, or of anything else he has honored above all things, neither worships the Lord nor is in the holy court, even if he seems worthy of the visible assemblies. “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” You will find the word “voice” used in many places. So in order to understand what the voice of the Lord is, it is worth our while to gather, as far as we can, what is written about the voice in divine Scripture: as in the oracle given to Abraham: “And immediately a voice came, saying: [?]

‘This man shall not be your heir’”; and in the case of Moses: “And all the people saw the voice and the torches”; and again in Isaiah: “The voice of one saying, Cry out.” Our own voice is either struck air, or the form produced in the air, shaped as the speaker wishes. What, then, is the voice of the Lord? Should it be understood as a striking of the air? Or as struck air that reaches the hearing of the one to whom the voice comes? Or is it neither of these, but something of a different kind: an impression made on the ruling faculty of those people whom God wishes to hear his own voice, so that this impression is analogous to the one that often occurs in dreams? For just as in our dream images, without any striking of the air, we receive a memory of certain words and sounds, not taking in the voice through our hearing but because our heart itself has received an impression, so we must suppose that the voice from God that comes to the prophets is something of this kind. “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” In the sense perceptible to us: since the clouds, when they are full of water, make a roar and crash as they collide with one another, it says, “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” But also, whenever there is the crash of waters breaking against some obstacle, and whenever the sea, stirred up by winds, surges and sends out a violent roar, these lifeless things have their voice from the Lord. The word shows that all creation all but cries aloud, proclaiming its own Creator. And when thunder bursts from the clouds, we must think nothing else than that “the God of glory has thundered,” and that it is the Lord who by himself holds together the liquid element. “The Lord is upon many waters.” For in the account of creation we have learned of water above the heavens, of the water of the abyss as well, and of another, the gatherings of the seas. Who, then, holds these together and does not let them be carried downward by their natural tendency, but the Lord, who stands upon all things and also holds power over the waters? But perhaps, in a more mystical sense, “the voice of the Lord is upon the waters” when, after Jesus was baptized, a voice came from above: “This is my beloved Son.” For then the Lord was upon many waters, sanctifying the waters through baptism, and the God of glory thundered from above with the loud voice of his testimony. And over those being baptized the voice that the Lord left behind is pronounced: “Go,” he says, “baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” So “the voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” [?]

Thunder occurs when a dry and violent wind, trapped in the hollows of a cloud and whirling forcefully about in the cavities of the clouds, seeks some outlet to the outside. The clouds, resisting because they are so tightly compressed, produce that harsh sound from the friction of the wind; but when, stretched around the wind like bubbles, they can no longer hold out and contain it, they burst violently and let the wind escape outward, producing the crashes that accompany thunder. This also naturally produces lightning. It is the Lord, then, who is upon the waters and who causes the great crashes of thunder, producing so tremendous a noise in the soft substance of the air. You may also, in keeping with the Church's interpretation, call “thunder” the teaching handed down after baptism, which comes from the loud voice of the Gospel in the souls of those already being perfected. That the Gospel is thunder is shown by the disciples whom the Lord renamed and who were called sons of thunder. That is why the voice of such thunder is not found in just anyone, but in one who is worthy to be called a wheel. “For the voice of your thunder,” it says, “was in the wheel.” That is, if someone, straining toward what lies ahead, is like a wheel that touches the earth with only a small part of itself, and is altogether like the one Ezekiel spoke of: “And I looked, and behold, one wheel on the earth beside the four living creatures, and their appearance and their workmanship were like the appearance of Tharsis.” 4. “The God of glory has thundered; the Lord is upon many waters.” The saints too are waters, since rivers flow from their belly, that is, spiritual teaching that waters the souls of those who hear. And again, they receive water springing up to eternal life, which in those who receive it well becomes a spring of water springing up to eternal life. It is over such waters, then, that the Lord is. Remember too the story of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months; when, though the sky was clear, he heard on the summit of Carmel the sound of many waters, and then there followed thunder from the clouds and water pouring down. So “the Lord is upon many waters.” “The voice of the Lord is in power.” Just as the voice occurs in the wheel, so the voice of the Lord is found in power. For the one who is able to do all things in Christ who strengthens him [?]

…the working of deeds, such a person is called magnificent. So when a soul that is not enslaved to the mind of the flesh takes on the greatness and dignity that befit it, from awareness of the gifts it has received from God, the voice of the Lord comes to be in it. Those, then, who have lofty conceptions of God, who have contemplated the principles of creation in an exalted way, and who have been able to grasp at least in some measure the goodness of God's providence; who besides are unsparing in their spending and generous in relieving the needs of their brothers: these are the magnificent, in whom the voice of the Lord makes its home. For truly the magnificent person looks down on all bodily things, judging them worth nothing compared with the things that are unseen. No circumstance will grieve the magnificent person; the sins of base and contemptible little men will not move him, nor will impurity of the flesh bring him low. For he is hard to approach for the passions that debase, and they cannot even look at him because of the loftiness of his mind. A magnificence is also ascribed to God, as in: "Your magnificence is exalted above the heavens." So those who think great things of God exalt his magnificence.
5. "The voice of the Lord who breaks the cedars." Scripture sometimes praises the cedar as lasting, resistant to rot, fragrant, and able to give ample shelter; but sometimes it censures it as fruitless and hard to bend, so that it even serves as an image of the ungodly: "I saw the ungodly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon." It is in this sense that the word has been taken here too. For the voice of the Lord breaks cedars. Just as it comes to be in the magnificent soul, so it is said to break those who are puffed up for no reason, who exalt themselves in what pass for the heights of this world: wealth, or glory, or power, or bodily beauty, or might, or strength. "And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon." Those who stand on things not their own and draw their arrogance from them are the cedars of Lebanon. Cedars are tall in themselves, but because they grow on a high mountain the mountain is added to their height and they become more conspicuous. In the same way those who lean on the perishable things of the world are cedars because of their arrogance and the elation of their minds, but they are called cedars of Lebanon because they glory in a height not their own, and are lifted up to arrogance by the earth and earthly things, as if by the summit of Lebanon. Yet the Lord does not break all cedars, but only those of Lebanon. Since Lebanon was a place of idolatry, all souls that are lifted up against the knowledge

of God are named after Lebanon and are judged worthy of being broken. For there are certain cedars of God, which are covered by the tendrils of the vine transplanted from Egypt, as we have learned in the Psalms: "Its shadow covered the mountains, and its tendrils the cedars of God." Among the other titles given to Christ, our Lord is also called a vine: "I am the vine," he says, "you are the branches." The cedars of God, then, are those who were once fruitless and fit only for burning, but who have come under the vine of Christ and, as it were, clothed themselves with him, and who by the grace that comes from him cover the fruitlessness of their own lives. So fruitful tendrils twine around the cedars of God and protect them, but the cedars of Lebanon the Lord breaks. "And he will grind them fine like the calf, Lebanon." Remember the calf in Exodus, which they fashioned in their idolatry, and which Moses ground fine and made the people drink. Like that calf, then, he will wipe out all of Lebanon, together with the custom of idolatry that prevails in it. "And the beloved is like the son of unicorns." When the only-begotten Son, who gives life to the world, offers himself to God as a sacrifice and offering for our sins, he is called the Lamb of God and a sheep: "Behold," it says, "the Lamb of God"; and again, "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter." But when he must take vengeance and pull down the tyranny that has fastened itself on the human race, a power that has turned bestial and savage, then he is called the son of unicorns. For the unicorn, as we have learned from Job, is an animal of invincible strength that will not submit to human beings. "You will not bind him with a strap," it says, "nor will he lie down at the manger." And in that part of the prophecy much is said about the animal's freedom and its refusal to yield to human beings. It has also been noticed that Scripture uses the image of the unicorn in both ways, sometimes in praise and sometimes in censure. "Deliver my soul from the sword," it says, "and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns." He says this in censure of the warlike people who rose up against him at the time of his passion. And again: "Exalt [?]…" [John 1:29; Acts 8:32; Isaiah 53:7.]

It seems, then, that because of the animal's power to defend itself it is often used as an image of what is worse, but because of its high horn and its freedom it is drawn into an image of what is better. And in general, one can find that Scripture frequently uses "horn" for glory, as in "He will exalt the horn of his people," and "His horn will be exalted in glory"; or again "horn" is often used for power, as in "My protector and the horn of my salvation"; and Christ is the power of God. For this reason, as having one horn, that is, one power, the power of the Father, he has been called a unicorn.
6. "The voice of the Lord who divides the flame of fire." According to the story, the flame of fire was divided in the case of the three young men in Babylon, when the furnace poured out its fire forty-nine cubits beyond its mouth and burned all who stood around it. But divided by the command of God, it took a breeze into itself, giving the young men a most pleasant breath of cool air, as if in the shade of trees, in a state of peace. "For it became," it says, "like a whistling wind of dew." And it is far more wonderful for the nature of fire to be divided than for the Red Sea to be cut into separate parts. Yet the voice of the Lord divides even what in fire is by nature continuous and unified. Though to human thinking fire seems impossible to cut or divide, it is nonetheless divided and separated at the Lord's command. And I think that the fire prepared for the punishment of the devil and his angels is divided by the voice of the Lord. There are two powers in fire, one that burns and one that gives light, so the sharp and punishing part of the fire will remain for those who deserve burning, while its light and brightness will be allotted to the radiance of those who rejoice. So it is the voice of the Lord that divides and apportions the flame of fire, so that the fire of punishment is without light, while the light of rest remains without burning.
"The voice of the Lord who shakes the desert." The Lord arranges the shaking of the desert for its benefit, so that it may change from being a desert and become an inhabited land; so that, putting away the reproach of childlessness, it may receive praise for its many children ("For many are the children of the desolate, more than of her who has a husband"); and so that, filled with the waters of the Spirit, what was once a desert may become pools of water. "And the Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh." The Lord will not shake every desert, but that of Kadesh, that is, of sanctification; for Kadesh is interpreted as "sanctification." "The voice of the Lord preparing the deer." In keeping with what precedes

we must also interpret what is said about the preparing of the deer, which the voice of the Lord brings about. The deer is so made that it is proof against harm from reptiles; indeed, as those who have observed such things say, eating a viper even serves it as a purge. And all venomous creatures are taken as an image of the evil and hostile powers: the Lord says, "I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy"; and the psalm in turn promises the prophet, "You will tread on the asp and the basilisk." So whenever we hear the name of the deer in Scripture, we must draw the passage toward the better image. "The high mountains are for the deer"; and, "As the deer longs for the springs of water." Every righteous person also spends his time on the heights, "pressing on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call," and runs up to the springs of fresh water, seeking out the first principles of theology. The deer draws out the venomous creatures lurking in their holes with the breath of its mouth, and by the force of its breath brings them out of their hiding places. So just as the saint is called an eagle because he soars aloft and is raised far above the earth; and a sheep because he is gentle and ready to share what he has; and a ram because he is fit to lead; and a dove because he is guileless; so too he is called a deer because he opposes what is evil. That is why Solomon says, "Let the deer of friendship and the colt of your graces keep company with you," teaching us that the deer we have described are fit for teaching theology.
7. "The voice of the Lord preparing the deer." So when we see a man of God who is perfect and fully prepared, let us seek the benefit of his company. For where a deer is present, all the malice of reptiles is put to flight. Venomous creatures cannot bear the animal's smell; they even retreat when its horns are burned as incense. "And he will uncover the thickets." First the voice of the Lord prepares the deer; then it uncovers the thickets, places overgrown and dense with wild and fruitless growth, where venomous creatures naturally take refuge most of all. Since, then, the deer has already been perfected through the preparation that came from the Lord, the [?]

[?] good fruit is cut down by the axe and thrown into the fire, the thickets are necessarily cleared: the overgrown souls in which, like wild beasts, the various passions of sin make their lairs are cleared by the Word, which is sharper than any two-edged sword. And since many people, weighed down with the cares of life, have souls like thorny ground and do not let them be nourished to bear the fruit of the Word, the Lord uncovers the thickets, that is, he shows how ugly, unseemly and harmful the concerns of this life are. Then, once the account of good and evil has been made clear, people will not through ignorance have their judgments about things turned upside down. For many think good things are evil when they involve toil, and pursue evil things as good because of the pleasure that comes with them; and people's error in such matters is beyond telling. Fruit-bearing trees and all cedars belong to the nature of good things, and these are also called on to give praise. But the thickets belong to evil things, and the voice of God uncovers and exposes them so that those who expect to find some useful fruit in them may not be deceived. "And in his temple everyone speaks glory." Let those who give themselves over to long chatter hear the words of the psalm and be ashamed. What does the psalm say? Whoever is in the temple of God does not utter slander or empty talk or words full of shameful things, but "in his temple everyone speaks glory." Holy angels stand by, writing down the words; the Lord is present, watching the dispositions of those who come in. Each person's prayer lies open to God: he sees who seeks heavenly things from the heart, who with understanding, and who mouths the words perfunctorily with the tips of his lips while his heart is far from God. Even when such a person prays, he asks for bodily health, material wealth and human glory. But none of these is needed, as the passage teaches; rather, "in his temple everyone speaks glory." "The heavens declare the glory of God." The work of angels is to glorify God. For the whole host of heaven this is the one work: to send up glory to the Creator. All creation, silent and speaking, above the world and on the earth, glorifies the Creator. But wretched human beings leave their houses and flock to the church as though to gain some benefit, and yet they do not lend their ears to the words of God, they gain no awareness of their own nature, they are not grieved at having been overtaken by

[?], and when they come to remember their sins they do not tremble at the judgment. Instead, smiling and clasping one another's hands, they turn the house of prayer into a place for long conversations, ignoring the psalm that solemnly testifies, "In the temple of God everyone speaks glory." But you not only fail to speak it; you also become a hindrance to someone else by turning him toward you, and you drown out the teaching of the Spirit with your own noise. Take care that you do not leave, instead of receiving a reward for giving glory, condemned along with those who blaspheme the name of God. You have a psalm, you have prophecy, the commandments of the Gospel, the preaching of the apostles. Let the tongue sing, let the mind search out the meaning of what is said, so that you may sing with the spirit and sing with the mind as well. For God does not need glory; but he wants you to be worthy of being glorified. For "whatever a person sows, that will he also reap." Sow glorification, so that you may reap crowns and honors and praises in the kingdom of heaven. This digression on "In his temple everyone speaks glory" has not been made to no purpose; it is because of those who chatter endlessly in the temple of God and come in without profit. Would that it were only without profit, and not to their harm!
8. "The Lord will make the flood a dwelling." A flood is an inundation of water that wipes out everything beneath it and cleanses everything that is soiled. So he calls the grace of baptism a flood, because the soul that has washed away its sins and been cleansed of the old man is from then on fit to be a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. What is said in Psalm 31 agrees with this. For after saying, "I acknowledged my iniquity and did not hide my sin," and, "For this every holy one will pray to you," he added, "Yet in a flood of many waters they shall not come near him." For sins will not come near the one who has received the baptism for the forgiveness of trespasses through water and the Spirit. Akin to this is what is said in the prophecy of Micah: "For he delights in mercy; he will turn back and have mercy on us; he will sink our sins, and they will be cast into the depths of the sea." "And the Lord will sit as king for [?]…"

[?] strength. For "to everyone who has, more will be given." And once strengthened to do good works, he becomes worthy of the blessing that comes from God. Peace seems to be the most perfect of blessings, since it is a kind of stability of the soul's ruling faculty. So the peaceable man is marked out by the settledness of his character, while the one who is still at war with the passions has not yet shared in the peace that comes from God, the peace the Lord gave to his disciples, which surpasses all understanding and will guard the souls of the worthy. This is what the Apostle prays for the churches when he says, "Grace to you, and may peace be multiplied." May it be granted to us, then, having fought the good fight and overthrown the mind of the flesh, which is enmity against God, and with our souls brought into a calm state free of waves, to be called sons of peace and to share in the blessing of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 29
A Psalm of an ode, for the dedication of the house.
1. Figuratively speaking, the psaltery, an instrument tuned musically for hymns to our God, is the structure of the body; and the psalm is the actions performed through the body and offered for the glory of God, when, tuned by reason, we produce nothing out of tune in our movements. The ode is whatever belongs to lofty contemplation and theology. So the psalm is a musical utterance when it is struck rhythmically on the instrument according to the laws of harmony, while the ode is a melodious voice sung harmoniously without the accompaniment of the instrument. Here, then, since the title is "A Psalm of an ode," we think the text hints at action that follows from contemplation. According to its title, this psalm of an ode contains certain words about the dedication of the house. In the bodily sense, the text seems to have been composed in the time of Solomon, when the famous temple was built, and to have been sung to the psaltery. But in the spiritual sense it seems to signify the incarnation of God the Word and the dedication of the house that was built for him in a new and wondrous way,
[Notes: [?] "…you, Lord, for you have upheld me"; some manuscripts read θεωρίᾳ τῶν λόγων; a codex reads εὕραμεν ἐν.]

as the title shows. For we have found many things in this psalm spoken in the person of the Lord. Or perhaps we should understand the house as the Church built by Christ, as Paul writes in his letter to Timothy: "So that you may know how one ought to behave in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God." The dedication of the Church should be taken as the renewal of the mind that comes about through the Holy Spirit in each of those who make up the body of the Church of Christ. This divine and musical harmony does not consist of words that please the ear, but of words that restrain and calm the evil spirits that harass [?] souls with their malicious assaults [?]. "I will exalt you, Lord, for you have upheld me, and you have not let my enemies rejoice over me." How is he who dwells on high exalted by those who have been allotted the lowly region? If God is in heaven above and you are on the earth below, how could you exalt God? What, then, does the prophet's promise mean? Or perhaps God is said to be exalted by those who are able to think great things about him, worthy of God, and by living for the glory of God? So the one who presses on through knowledge toward blessedness exalts God; but the one who turns the opposite way, though it is not even right to say it, humbles God as far as lies in him.
2. We also, as it were, attach to God every state that fits our circumstances. So when we are drowsy and act sluggishly, God is said to sleep, judging us unworthy of his watchfulness over us. But when at some point we feel the harm that comes from sleep and say, "Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?" then "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep." Others, as it were, make God turn his eyes away, because what they do is shameful and unworthy of God's eyes; and when they repent they say, "Why do you turn your face away?" Besides these there are others who have been cast out of God's memory and have, as it were, made him forget them; they say, "You forget our poverty and our affliction." In short, the things said about God in human terms [?] …

And where does my power to exalt come from? From the fact that you came to me first and upheld me. He chose the word “You upheld” deliberately, meaning “You lifted me up and set me above those who rose up against me.” It is as if someone took hold with his hand of a child who did not yet know how to swim and held him up above the water. So the one who, by God's help, has raised himself up from his fall promises out of gratitude to exalt God through good works. Or it is as if someone propped up a weak wrestler who was in danger of falling and set him above his opponent: to the one he gave the opening for victory, and from the other he took away the pleasure of seeing him fall. The afflictions brought on the saints to test them do not give joy to our invisible enemies. But when we give up under affliction, and our thoughts are hemmed in because we have grown weary of the constant blows, then they rejoice and clap and gloat. Take the case of Job. He had lost his property, he had been robbed of his children, his flesh seethed with pus and worms; yet this was still no joy to the adversary. But if he had given way under his sufferings and spoken a blasphemous word, as his wife advised, then his enemies would have rejoiced over him. So too with Paul, hungry, thirsty, naked, beaten, toiling, homeless: the enemy did not rejoice. On the contrary, he was crushed to see him bearing his contests so well that he could say with contempt, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” 5. “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.” Blessed is the one who recognizes the wound deep within himself, so that he can approach the physician and say, “Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled,” and, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” Here, however, it is thanksgiving for the healing that has been applied to him, for he says, “O Lord my God.” God is not the God of all, but of those who have become his own through love. For he is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. If he were the God of all, this would not have been attested of them as something special. And again Jacob says, “My God has helped you.” And Thomas, once fully convinced, embraced the Master and said, “My Lord and my God.” So the cry “O Lord my God” comes from the heart. For “while you are still speaking,” he says, “I will say, Here I am.” So when we pray to God we must ask for great things, so that healing may spring up for us quickly. “O Lord, you brought my soul up from Hades.” For this healing he gives thanks to God. He had gone down into Hades through weakness, but [?] came back up from Hades by the power of him who for our sake wrestled down the one who holds the power of death. “You saved me from those who go down into the pit.” In many places the word “pit” is used for the underground holes designed for keeping prisoners. Every action either drags us down, weighing us down through sin, or lifts us up and gives us wings toward God. So you saved me, who once lived an evil life, by separating me from those who go down into the dark and frozen place. This, then, is what “You upheld me” means: you brought me back from my downward course, so as to give my enemies no chance to rejoice over me. So elsewhere he says, “He makes my feet like a deer's and sets me on the heights.” The return to the heights is what he calls deliverance from the pit and being upheld. “Sing to the Lord, you his holy ones.” It is not whoever recites the words of the psalm with his mouth who sings to the Lord. Rather, those who send up their psalmody from a pure heart, and who are holy and keep righteousness toward God, can sing to God, keeping fittingly to the spiritual rhythms. How many are standing here fresh from fornication, how many from theft! How many hide deceit or lies in their hearts! They think they are singing, though in truth they are not. For the word calls the holy one to sing psalms. A bad tree cannot bear good fruit, and a bad heart cannot bring forth words of life. Make the tree good, then, and its fruit good. Cleanse your hearts, so that you may bear fruit in the Spirit and, once you have become holy, be able to sing to the Lord with understanding. 4. “And give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.” [?] …followed for the most part [?]: [?] “So you saved me, who was formerly in a life [?]…”

He did not say, “Give thanks to his holiness,” but “to the remembrance of his holiness.” The word “confess” here is used in place of “give thanks.” Give thanks, then, that you have come to remember his holiness. Before this, by sinking deep into wickedness and defiling yourselves with the impurities of the flesh, you had forgotten the holiness of the one who made you. So, to atone for your sins, confess the things you have done amiss in the past. “For wrath is in his anger, and life in his will.” First he mentioned the grim thing, wrath in God's anger, and then the brighter one, life in his will. To those who cannot grasp exact distinctions of meaning, it seems a tautology when the prophet says that wrath is in God's anger, as though wrath and anger were the same thing. But the difference is very great. Anger is the decision that certain painful things should be inflicted on someone who deserves them. Wrath is the actual pain, the punishment inflicted by the just judge in proportion to the wrong done. An example will make my meaning clearer. A physician notices an inflamed and festering part and decides that the patient needs surgery. This is what Scripture calls anger. After the physician's decision about the treatment comes the operation that carries out what was decided, and the knife that cuts and causes pain to the one being cut. This is called the wrath of God. Now come to the text before us, and you will see how the thought follows. “For wrath is in his anger”: that is, punishment according to God's just judgment. “But life is in his will.” What does he mean? That what God wills is for all to share in his life. Calamities are not brought about by his will, but are inflicted on sinners as they deserve. God grants life to each person by his own will, but each person stores up wrath for himself “on the day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment is revealed.” Scripture is accustomed to put the grim things before the kinder ones, because enjoyment is sweeter when painful things come before it. “I will kill,” he says, “and I will make alive.” The kindness comes second, after the punishment. “I will strike, and I will heal.” “For he causes pain, and he restores again; he struck, and his hands healed.” He sends the hardships first so that his gifts may last longer with us, since then we hold on tightly to what we have been given. “Weeping will lodge in the evening, and in the morning there will be gladness.” Remember the time of the [?]… [?]σθαι. …of the Lord, and you will find what is meant. In the evening weeping lodged with the Lord's disciples, when they saw him [?] on the cross. [7.] “But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved.” A city's prosperity is an abundance of goods for sale in the market, and we say that a land prospers when it bears many fruits. In the same way there is a prosperity of the soul, when the soul is filled with every kind of good work. It must first be farmed with hard work, and then enriched with plentiful streams of heavenly water, so that it may bear fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold, and receive the blessing that says, “Blessed are your storehouses and what you have left over.” So the one who is aware of his own steadfastness will speak with confidence and declare that he will not be overthrown by the adversary, being “like a full field which the Lord has blessed.” [8.] “Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty.” Those who have spent their time examining the doctrine of the virtues [?] have said that some virtues consist of principles, while others are not based on principles. Prudence, they say, consists of principles in the topic of good and evil things; temperance of principles concerning what is to be chosen and what avoided; justice of principles concerning what is to be distributed and what is not; and courage of principles concerning what is to be feared and what is not.
