…virtues, which follow upon the virtues based on principles. Some wise men have understood beauty as the proportion and harmony of the soul's principles, and strength as the power to carry out what the virtues based on principles suggest. But for beauty to come into the soul, along with the power to do what is required, we need divine grace. So, just as he said above, “For life is in his will,” he now exalts God through thanksgiving, saying, “In your will you gave strength to my beauty.” For I was beautiful by nature, but weak, because through the serpent's plot I had died by my transgression. So to my beauty, which I received from you at my first creation, you added the strength to do what is required. Every soul is beautiful when its own powers are seen to be in proportion. But true and most lovable beauty, which only someone with a purified mind can see, is the beauty that surrounds the divine and blessed nature. Whoever gazes steadily at its radiance and its graces receives something from it, as if from a dye, and his own face takes on a blooming brightness. That is why Moses' face was glorified: he had shared in that beauty while speaking with God. So the one who perceives his own virtue utters these words of thanksgiving: “Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty.” And just as beauty and strength, which are not based on principles, follow the virtues that are, so there are certain vices [?] that make the passionate soul uglier and more hideous. Look, I ask you, at the angry man and the savagery in him. Observe the man in grief, and how low and collapsed his soul is. And the man in the grip of lust or gluttony, or panicked by fears: who could even bear to look at him? For the soul's condition spreads to the very extremities of the body, just as the traces of the soul's beauty also shine through in the bearing of a saint. We must therefore take care of our beauty, so that the Bridegroom, the Word, may receive us and say, “You are all beautiful, my beloved, and there is no flaw in you.” 6. “You turned your face away, and I was troubled.” As long as the rays of your care were shining on me, he says, I lived in a [?] steady…

…and untroubled state. But when you turned your face away, the passionate and disturbed condition of my soul was exposed. God is said to turn his face away when, in times of hardship, he leaves people exposed to temptations, so that the vigor of the contestant may be made known. So if “the peace that surpasses all understanding” guards our hearts, we can escape the turmoil and confusion of the passions. Since turning away is the opposite of God's will, and trouble is the opposite of beauty, comeliness, and strength, trouble must be the ugliness and weakness of the soul that comes from being estranged from God. Let us pray, then, that the face of God may always shine on us, so that we may be in a [?] fitting state, gentle and in every way untroubled, because we are ready for what is good. For he says, “I was prepared, and I was not troubled.” “To you, O Lord, I will cry, and to my God I will make my plea.” It has often been said about crying to the Lord that crying out belongs only to one who desires great and heavenly things. But if someone asks God for small and earthly things, the voice he uses is small and lowly. It does not rise on high or reach the Lord's ears. “What profit is there in my blood, if I go down to corruption?” Why, he says, did I cry out? And what did I ask of you, my Lord and my God? What need do I have, he says, of a pampered body and plenty of blood, when it will soon be handed over to the dissolution that comes to every body? “But I pummel my body and make it my slave,” so that a well-fed body and blood boiling with health may not give me an occasion for sin. Do not flatter your flesh with sleep, baths, and soft bedding, but keep repeating these words: “What profit is there in my blood, if I go down to corruption?” Why do you pamper what will soon decay? Why do you fatten yourself and pile on flesh? Do you not know that the fatter you make your flesh, the heavier the prison you build for your soul? “Will the dust give thanks to you, or declare your truth?” For how will the earthy, fleshly man give thanks to you, O God? And how will he declare the truth, when he has given no time to learning and keeps his mind buried under so heavy a weight of flesh? This is why I waste away my flesh and do not spare the blood that naturally congeals into flesh, so that nothing [?] may stand in my way, either in giving thanks or in understanding the truth…

…[the Lord] became my helper. After telling what he cried to God about, he at once felt God's help, and to urge us to ask for the same things he says, “The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper.” So let us pray too, and raise the spiritual cry, asking for great things and not clinging to the flesh (for “those who are in the flesh cannot please God”), so that the Lord may hear us too and have mercy on our weakness, and that we too, having enjoyed God's help, may say, “You turned my mourning into joy for me.” Joy from God does not come into just any soul. But if someone has wept much over his own sin with loud lamentations and constant dirges, and has mourned for himself as for a dead man, his mourning is turned into joy. That there is a praiseworthy kind of mourning is shown by the children sitting in the marketplaces, who say, “We sang a dirge for you, and you did not mourn; we played the flute for you, and you did not dance.” The flute is a musical instrument that uses breath as its partner in making melody. That is why, I think, every holy prophet is figuratively called a flute, because he is moved by the Holy Spirit. So he says, “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance.” For the words of the prophets urge us toward the well-ordered rhythm of holy prophecy, and this is what is called dancing. But the prophets also lament for us and call us to mourning, so that the prophetic words may bring us to an awareness of our own sins, and we may bewail our ruin, subduing our flesh with toil and hardship. For someone like this, the mourning garment that he put on while bewailing his sin is torn away. Instead he is dressed in the tunic of gladness and the robe of salvation, those bright wedding garments, and whoever is adorned with them will not be thrown out of the bridal chamber. “You tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness.” Sackcloth helps us toward repentance, since it is a symbol of humility. For he says, “They would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” But since the Apostle [?] …with unveiled face [?] is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, he calls the grace given him by the Lord his own glory. “So that my glory may sing to you.” The glory of a righteous man is the Spirit within him. So let the one who sings with the Spirit say, “So that

my glory may sing to you, and I may not [?].” [?] I will no longer do anything, he says, that deserves to have my heart [?] pierced at the memory of my sin. “O Lord my God, I will acknowledge you forever,” in place of “I will give thanks.” For since you gave me the [?] pardon that comes through repentance, and brought me back to glory, taking away the shame of my sins, I will acknowledge you for all ages. For what span of time could be so long as to make my soul forget such great kindnesses?

BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON PSALM 32. “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright.” The word “rejoicing” is common in Scripture, and it indicates a very [?] vigorous and joyful state of a soul delighting in things worthy of delight. “Rejoice, then, you righteous, in the Lord”: not when things go well for you at home, not when your body is healthy, not when your fields are full of every kind of crop, but because you have a Lord who is so great in beauty, so great in goodness, [?] so great in wisdom. Let your gladness in him be enough for you. Just as someone exults with gladness and joy over things he has eagerly sought, so [?] should one rejoice in God. That is why the word urges the righteous to realize what an honor it is that they have been found worthy to be servants of such a Master, and to exult in his service with unspeakable joy and leaping, the heart leaping, as it were, in the rapture of love for the Good. If ever something like [?] a light has fallen into your heart, given you a sudden awareness of God, and lit up your soul, so that you loved God and despised the world and bodily things, then from that faint and brief [?] experience learn the whole state of the righteous, who maintain their gladness in God steadily and without interruption. For to you that rejoicing comes [?] rarely, by God's providence, so that by giving you a small taste he may make you aware of what you have been missing. But for the righteous man the divine and heavenly gladness is continual, since the Spirit has once come to dwell in him, and “the first fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace.” “Rejoice, then, you righteous, in the Lord.” The Lord is, as it were, a place spacious enough to hold the righteous, and whoever has come to be in him cannot help being cheerful and glad. The righteous man also becomes a place for the Lord, receiving him into himself. But the sinner gives place to the devil, disobeying the one who says, “Do not give place to the devil,” and Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, do not leave your place.” So in him [?]… Many manuscripts read [?] ἀγαλλιᾶν. The Paris edition, with the fourth Colbert manuscript, reads ἀγάγοι ὧν ἐστέρησαι. [?] ἄρουραι πλήθωσι: the Colbert manuscript and the fourth read πλήθουσι; [?] other manuscripts read πληθύνωσι.

[?] having become [?] to the Lord, and contemplating his wonders as far as we are able, let us in this way gather gladness for our hearts from that contemplation. "Praise befits the upright." Just as a crooked foot does not fit a straight shoe, so the praise of God does not befit perverse hearts. For this reason, I think, since speech about the Savior did not befit the mouth of demons, he takes away their liberty to speak, so that they might not make him known. And Paul rebukes the Pythian spirit, so that the holy one might not be commended by the unclean. Of the same kind is this: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my statutes?" Let us strive, then, to flee every crooked and twisted deed, and let us set straight our mind and the judging faculty of our soul like a straight rule, so that, once we have become upright, the praise of the Lord may befit us. For the serpent who led the way into sin is called crooked, and the sword of God is brought against the dragon, the crooked serpent, because it makes many turns and swerves as it goes. The body of a serpent drags itself unevenly along the ground: the front parts push one way, the parts behind follow sideways, and the tail veers off again in the opposite direction. So he who follows the serpent will show his life to be crooked, uneven and full of contradictions; but he who walks after the Lord God makes his paths straight and the tracks of his feet right. For the Lord our God is upright, and his face has looked upon uprightness. If two rulers are laid side by side, their straightness fits together; but if a warped piece of wood is laid beside a ruler, the bent is found not to fit the straight. Since, then, the praise of God is upright, an upright heart is needed, so that the praise may befit it and fit it. And if no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit, how could you offer praise without having a right spirit renewed in your inmost parts

2. "Give praise to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery." First one must give praise to the Lord on the lyre; that is, render the actions of the body in harmony. For since we sinned in the body, when we presented our members as slaves to sin for lawlessness, let us also confess with the body, using the same instrument to undo the sin. Have you reviled? Bless. Have you been greedy? Give it back. Have you been drunk? Fast. Have you been boastful? Be humbled. Have you envied? Give comfort. Have you murdered? Bear witness as a martyr, or, by what is equivalent to

martyrdom, subdue your body [?] through confession. And then, after confession, you are worthy to sing to God on the ten-stringed psaltery. One must first set right the actions of the body, so as to perform them in harmony with the divine word, and in this way ascend to the contemplation of intelligible things. For perhaps the mind that seeks the things above is called a psaltery because of the construction of this instrument, which has its sounding part above. The works of the body, then, give praise to God as it were from below; but the mysteries proclaimed through the mind have their source above, as though the mind were made to resound through the Spirit. He, then, who looks to all the commandments, and makes of them, as it were, a single concord and harmony, sings to God on the ten-stringed psaltery, because the general commandments written at the first giving of the law are ten. "Sing to the Lord a new song." That is: serve God not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit. He who does not take the law in a bodily sense, but discerns its spiritual meaning, sings the new song. For what was growing old and aging in the covenant has passed away, and the new and ever-renewed song of the Lord's teaching has succeeded it, which renews our youth like the eagle's, when we let the outer man waste away and are renewed day by day. Moreover, he who strains forward to what lies ahead always becomes newer than himself. So he who is always becoming newer than himself sings an ever newer song to God. In ordinary usage "new" is said either of what is strange or of what has recently come into being. If, then, you recount the wondrous manner of the Lord's incarnation, which surpasses all nature, you sing a new and strange song; and if you describe the regeneration and renewal of the whole world, which had grown old through sin, and proclaim the mysteries of the resurrection, then too you sing a new and fresh song. 3. "Sing well to him with a shout." Hear the command: Sing well, with an undistracted mind and a sincere disposition. With a shout: like good soldiers after their victories over the enemy, offer hymns to the author of the victory. "Take courage," he says, "I have overcome the world." Who among men is able to wage war against the evil one, unless under the shelter of the commander-in-chief

[?] of faith in him we strike our enemy and shoot him with arrows? Sing well, then, with a shout. A shout is a kind of inarticulate cry, raised in unison by those who stand shield to shield in battle. Sing, then, in concord, in unity of spirit, and in the union of love. What, then, must those who sing say? "That the word of the Lord is upright." This is why he first calls the upright to praise: because the one who is to be glorified is upright, the Word, the Word of the Lord, who was in the beginning with God and is God. Upright, then, is the Father; upright is the Son; upright is the Holy Spirit. "And all his works are in faith." What does he mean? The heaven is a work, the earth is a work, the sea is a work, so is the air, and all things inanimate and animate, rational and irrational. How, then, are all of them in faith? What faith is there in inanimate things? What faith in irrational creatures? What faith is there in the horse? What faith in the dog? Nothing inanimate or irrational is in faith. Yet the statement made no exception but embraced everything, saying: "All his works are in faith." What, then, does he mean? If you look at the heaven, he says, and the order in it, it is a guide to faith, for through itself it reveals the craftsman. If you look at the arrangements of the earth, again through these your faith in God grows. For we did not come to believe in God by learning of him with eyes of flesh; rather, by the power of the mind we discern the invisible through the visible. "All his works," then, "are in faith." Even if you study a stone, it too contains some proof of the power of the one who made it; so does an ant, a gnat, a bee. Often the Creator's wisdom shines out even in the smallest things. For he who spread out the heaven and poured out the boundless expanses of the seas is the same who hollowed the very fine sting of the bee like a pipe, so that its venom is discharged through it. "All his works," then, "are in faith." Let nothing furnish you with an occasion for unbelief. Do not say: "This happened by chance," and "That came about of itself." Nothing among existing things is disorderly, nothing undetermined, nothing done at random or carried along by chance. Or: "Bad luck," or "An evil hour." These are the words of the uneducated. "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall without the divine will." How many are the hairs of the head? Not one of them is forgotten. Do you see the divine eye, how not even the smallest thing escapes its oversight? "The Lord loves mercy and judgment; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord." If God's judgment stood by itself, and he repaid us severely, as we deserve, for what we have done, what hope would there be? Who among us all would be saved? But as it is, "He loves

mercy and judgment." Having made mercy, as it were, his assessor, and set it before the royal throne of judgment, in this way he brings each person to judgment. "If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand?" Mercy is not without judgment, nor is judgment without mercy. Before judgment, then, he loves mercy, and after mercy he comes to judgment. These are yoked together, mercy with judgment, so that neither mercy alone may produce slackness nor judgment alone produce despair. The judge wishes to have mercy on you and to share his own compassion with you. If, after your sin, he finds you humble and contrite, having wept much over your evil deeds, having made public without shame what was done in secret, having asked the brethren to labor with you for your healing; if he sees that you have become wholly pitiable, he supplies his mercy to you ungrudgingly. But if he sees an unrepentant heart, a proud mind, unbelief in the age to come, and no fear of the judgment, then in your case he loves judgment. A skilled and kindly physician first tries to reduce a swelling with fomentations and gentle plasters; but when he sees the mass resisting stubbornly and hard, he throws away the oil and the gentle treatment and resorts at last to the knife. So he loves mercy toward those who repent, and he loves judgment toward the obstinate. Isaiah says something similar to God: "[I will set] my mercy in the balance [?]." For he too presents mercy joined with judgment, since God measures out to each by balance, number and weight according to each one's deserts. 4. "The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord." Here mercy is separated from judgment. For the earth is full of the Lord's mercy alone, while judgment is reserved for the appointed time. Here, then, there is mercy without judgment, for he came not to judge the world but to save the world. But there, there is no judgment without mercy, because no human being can be found clean from defilement, not even if his life has lasted a single day. So if someone sees wickedness spreading day by day, and the mortal race of men, as far as their sins go, deserving ten thousand deaths, he will marvel at the riches of God's goodness and forbearance [?]

[?] We are called earth, we who heard from God, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return"; we who are full of the compassion of God. For when we were dead in sins and trespasses, God had mercy on us and made us alive together with Christ. "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth." Where are those who despise the Spirit? Where are those who separate him from the creative power? Where are those who cut him off from his union with the Father and the Son? Let them hear the psalm saying: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth." For the Word is not to be thought of as this common speech, made up of nouns and verbs, nor the Spirit as a vapor dispersed into the air. Rather, the Word is he who was in the beginning with God, and the Spirit is the Holy Spirit, who has received this name as his own. As the creative Word, then, established the heaven, so the Spirit who is from God, who proceeds from the Father (that is, who is from his mouth, so that you may not judge him to be something external or one of the creatures, but may glorify him as having his subsistence from God), brought along with it all the powers in it. By the Spirit, then, all the heavenly power was established; that is, from the help of the Spirit they have their vigor, firmness and steadfastness in holiness, and every virtue fitting for the holy powers. Here, then, "Spirit of his mouth" is written; but elsewhere we shall also find "Word of his mouth," so that the Savior may be understood, and his Holy Spirit from the Father. Since, then, the Savior is the Word of the Lord, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of his mouth, and both worked together in the creation of the heavens and the powers in them, it is therefore said: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth." For nothing is sanctified except by the presence of the Spirit. The creative Word, the maker of all things, granted the angels their entrance into being, but the Holy Spirit conferred holiness on them along with it. For the angels were not created as infants and then perfected by gradual practice, and so made worthy to receive the Spirit; rather, in their first constitution, and as it were in the very blending of their substance, they had holiness laid down in them. That is why they are hard to turn toward evil: they were tempered at once by sanctification, as if by a kind of dipping, and have steadfastness in virtue by the gift of the Holy Spirit

5. "Gathering the waters of the sea like a wineskin, placing the depths in storehouses." He did not say, "Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin," but, "Like a wineskin," so gathering the waters of the sea. Consider, I ask you, the nature of a wineskin: now it is blown up, when the skin is stretched by the air shut up inside it; now it shrinks, when what stretches it withdraws. So too the sea at one time swells and seethes, made wild and swollen by the winds; at another it is settled down low again by calm. Like a wineskin, then, the Lord contracts and lowers the water of the sea. But we have found in some copies, "Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin," in which case the passage points us back to the ancient history, when the Red Sea, with nothing dividing it or holding it in, stood up against itself as if tied up in a wineskin, because the divine command would not let it pour out. "Placing," he says, "the depths in storehouses." It would have been more in keeping with ordinary thinking to say, "Placing the treasures in the depths," that is, keeping his own wealth hidden in mystery. But as it is, he says that the depths are like precious objects worthy of the divine storehouses. Might it be, then, that the principles of divine judgment, being ineffable and incomprehensible to human thought, are called depths, since the principles by which he governs each thing are laid up in the knowledge of God alone? For that the judgments concerning each thing are called a deep, we have been taught by another psalm, which says: "Your judgments are a great deep." If, then, you ask why the sinner's life is prolonged while the days of the righteous man's sojourn are cut short; why the unjust man prospers while the just is afflicted; why the child was snatched away before reaching maturity; where wars come from; why there are shipwrecks, earthquakes, droughts and floods; why things destructive to human beings were created; why one person is a slave and another free, one rich and another poor (and there is a great difference also in sins and good deeds: for the girl sold to a brothel-keeper is in sin under compulsion, while the girl who from the start found a good mistress was brought up in virginity); why the one was favored and the other condemned; and what recompense the judge makes in each of these cases: taking all these together into one [?]

[?] But to the one who [?] a promise has been given by God: "I will give you hidden treasures, unseen." When, then, we are counted worthy of knowledge face to face, we shall also see the depths in the storehouses of God. And if you gather together what is said in Scripture about wineskins, you will gain a better grasp of the prophet's meaning. Those who are renewed day by day and hold the new wine from the true vine are called new wineskins in the Gospel; but those who have not yet put off the old man are old wineskins, which cannot be trusted to receive the new wine. For no one puts new wine into old wineskins, lest the wine be spilled and those wineskins perish completely, no longer deemed worthy of any pardon if they spill the good new wine. New wine must be put into new wineskins. The new and spiritual wine, seething with the Holy Spirit, the never-aging understanding of the truth, must be put into the new man, who, because he always carries about in his body the dying of Jesus, may justly be called a new wineskin. 6. "Let all the earth fear the Lord; and let all who inhabit the world be shaken by him." Since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of perception, let those whose minds are on earthly things be trained by fear. For fear is necessarily taken up as the introduction to piety; but love then takes over those who have been shaped by understanding fear and brings them to perfection. So the word enjoins fear upon all the earth. "And let all who inhabit the world," he says, "be shaken by him." That is: let every movement in them, whether carried out by the mind or by bodily action, be set in motion according to the will of God. This is how I understand "Let them be shaken by him." As if to say: let not the eye move without God; let not the hand stir without God; let not the heart devise what is displeasing to God. In short, let them be shaken by nothing else, and let nothing move them except the fear of God. "For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created." To the two preceding statements he added two more: to "Let all the earth fear" and "Let all who inhabit the world be shaken," he added "He spoke, and they came to be" and "He commanded, and they were created." Since man is a composite of the earthly frame and the soul that dwells in the body, what was formed from the earth is called earth, while the soul, which has been allotted its life in the body, is the inhabitant of the world. Fittingly, then, "He spoke, and they came to be" is assigned to the earth: to our

frame, formed from the earth, belongs "came to be"; to what was created after the image of God belongs "was created." But since "creation" is often used of transformation and improvement, as in "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation," and "that he might create the two into one new man," perhaps "came to be" is said of man's first coming into existence, [?] and "was created" of the regeneration through Christ. As great as the difference is between bare speech and a command of God, so great is the difference between creation and coming-to-be. "The Lord scatters the counsels of nations; he sets aside the reasonings of peoples." This explains the preceding verse: how God created those who have believed in him, by scattering the foolish counsels the peoples held about idolatry and every vanity, and by setting aside the counsels of rulers. These words can also be referred to the time of the passion, when they thought they were crucifying the King of glory, while he, through the dispensation of the cross, was renewing humanity. For in the resurrection the counsel of the nations was scattered, that of Pilate and the soldiers and all who carried out the work of the cross; and the counsels of the rulers were set aside, those of the chief priests and scribes and the kings of the people. For the resurrection undid their whole design. And if you gather from each history all that God has done regarding the unbelieving nations, you will find that the saying has great force even in its bodily sense. For when Joram son of Ahab reigned in Israel, the king of Syria, the son of Hadad, having led his army with great force and a heavy hand, besieged Samaria, so that the necessities of life failed them, and an ass's head cost fifty shekels of silver, and a quarter of a kab of dove's dung five shekels of silver. Then, so that Elisha's promise might be fulfilled, the counsels of Syria were scattered: they abandoned their tents and all their possessions and fled, leaving such plenty in Samaria that a measure of fine flour sold for a shekel and two measures of barley for one shekel. In this way, then, the Lord knows how to scatter the counsels of nations. And how he sets aside the counsels of rulers we have learned from the case of Ahithophel, when David prayed, saying: "Scatter, I pray, the counsel of Ahithophel." So when you hear someone making great threats and promising to bring every kind of harm upon you, fines, blows or death, look to the Lord, who scatters the counsels of nations and sets aside the reasonings of peoples.

7. “But the counsel of the Lord abides forever, the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation.” Do you not see the doctrines of the nations, this vain philosophy? See how subtle and elaborate they are in devising doctrines: in logical theorems and ethical precepts, in certain kinds of natural science, and in other doctrines that they call “contemplative.” How has all this been scattered and made useless, while the truth of the Gospel alone now holds citizenship in the world? “For many are the counsels in the hearts of men,” but the counsel of the Lord has prevailed. And it is indeed necessary that human reasonings first be scattered within us if the counsel that comes from God is to remain abiding and firm in our souls. Someone about to write on wax first smooths it and then impresses on it whatever letters he wishes. In the same way, a heart that is to receive the divine oracles clearly must first be shown to be clean of opposing reasonings. “The thoughts of his heart from generation to generation.” There are two chosen peoples, and two covenants have been granted to them. So the words “the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation,” in which “generation” is named twice, can be understood to mean two thoughts. By one of them we received the former Covenant. The other has graciously given us the new and saving teaching of Christ. “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen as his inheritance.” He does not call the people of the Jews blessed, but the people chosen for their merit out of all peoples. For we are the nation whose God is the Lord. We are the people whom he chose as his inheritance. We are a nation because we have been gathered from many nations, and a people because we have been called in place of the people that was cast off. And since “many are called, but few are chosen,” he calls blessed not the one who is called but the one who is chosen. For “blessed is he whom he has chosen.” What is the reason for this blessedness? It is the inheritance of eternal goods that we look forward to. Or perhaps it follows the Apostle: since “when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved,” he first calls blessed the fullness of the Gentiles, and then the Israel that is saved afterward. Clearly, though, it is not just anyone who is saved, but only “the remnant chosen by grace.” That is why he says, “the people whom he has chosen as his inheritance.” 8. “The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the sons of men from his prepared dwelling place.” Those who remain in their own dignity

and do what befits human nature, the Lord watches over from above. But those who have sunk to the depths of wickedness he visits in another way, by coming down himself. “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah,” he says, “has grown great, and their sins are very grievous. So I will go down and see whether they are doing what the outcry that has come to me reports.” And again: “He came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men had built.” But here it says: “The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the sons of men.” Consider the Spectator on high; consider him who stoops down from above to look upon human affairs. Wherever you walk and whatever you do, in darkness or in daylight, the eye of God is watching over you. “From his prepared dwelling place.” No gates are opened, no curtains drawn aside; the dwelling place of God stands ready for viewing. He looks upon all the sons of men. Not one escapes his sight. Neither darkness nor concealing walls nor anything else is an obstacle to the eyes of God. [?] He is so far from failing to look on each person individually that he even looks upon hearts, which he himself fashioned without any admixture of what is worse. God, the creator of men, fashioned the heart simple, preserving the image by itself alone. Afterward it was we who made the heart many-colored and manifold by entangling it with the passions of the flesh, destroying its godlike, simple and uniform character. Since he is the creator of hearts, he therefore also understands all our works. By “works” we mean words and thoughts too, and in short every movement of a human being. For with what disposition and with what purpose we act, whether to please men or to serve the commandments God has given us, only he knows who understands all our works. That is why we shall give account even for every idle word. And we shall not lose our reward even for a cup of cold water, because the Lord understands all our works. 9. “A king is not saved by great power.” It is not the protection of military power that secures salvation for a king, nor city walls, nor an infantry phalanx, nor a force of cavalry, nor a fleet fitted out with naval strength. For the Lord sets up kings and removes them, and there is no authority except that appointed by God. A king is saved,

then, not by great power but by divine grace. So for kings too the saying holds true: “By grace you have been saved.” In the same way, a farmer obtains his share of the harvest not so much through his care in farming as through God, who makes the crops grow. “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth.” And if “the heart of the king is in the hand of God,” he is saved not by armed might but by divine guidance. But it is not just anyone who is in the hand of God, only the one who is worthy of the title of king. Some have defined kingship as lawful government, or as rule over all that is not liable to sin. “And a giant shall not be saved by the greatness of his strength.” By “giant” he means one endowed with natural power and bodily vigor. So a king does not have in his troops enough help to be saved, and a brave man cannot be sufficient to himself for everything. For all human things together are weakness and powerlessness when compared with true power. That is why “God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame,” and “out of the mouths of infants and nursing babes he has perfected praise, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.” For divine grace has shone most brightly when it works in infants and in the simple. “The horse is a false hope for safety, and by its great strength it shall not be saved.” The horse has been excluded from the use of the saints. Israel, when it prospered in war, never appears to have used cavalry, and none of the saints in his private life accepted the use of horses as fitting for himself. But Pharaoh uses horses, and Sennacherib in his arrogance prides himself on his wealth of horses. Therefore Pharaoh's horse and rider he threw into the sea, and of Sennacherib's army all who were mounted on horses fell asleep. Hence the law given through Moses, when it legislates concerning kings, says: “He shall not multiply horses for himself.” “And by its great strength it shall not be saved.” For “when I am weak,” he says, “then I am strong.” Great bodily strength is an obstacle to the salvation of the spirit. 10. “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him.” Elsewhere it is said, “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous”; but here, “on those who fear him.”

When we look to the Lord and our eyes are turned toward him, we can say, “Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, so our eyes look to the Lord our God.” Then we draw the Lord's eye, as it were, to watch over us. “Those who hope in his mercy.” He shows the humility of those who serve the Lord in that they hope in his mercy. For the one who does not trust in his own good deeds, and does not expect to be justified by works, has God's compassion as his only hope of salvation. He considers the words, “Behold, the Lord comes, and his reward with him, to repay each according to his work,” and he reckons up his own evil deeds. Then he fears punishment and cowers at the threats. Yet so as not to be swallowed up by grief, he stays hopeful, looking to God's compassion and love for mankind. And he hopes that his soul will be delivered from death and that he will be fed by him in famine. “Our soul shall wait for the Lord, for he is our helper and protector.” These words encourage us to endure. Even if we are ever seized by one of those who afflict us, we are not to be separated from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus. Instead we are to endure hardships with all our soul as we wait for help from God. “For in him our heart shall rejoice, and in his holy name we have hoped.” This agrees with the beginning of the psalm, “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous,” and here, “In him our heart shall rejoice.” And it seems to me that the Apostle spoke in keeping with these words when he said, “In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us,” and, “Not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions.” The Psalmist has said, “Our soul shall wait for the Lord.” But he wants to show that the soul does not display its endurance under compulsion or because afflictions have crushed it. Rather, it welcomes with all joy the sufferings it bears for the name of the Lord. So he says that we not only endure, but also “in him our heart shall rejoice, and in his holy name we have hoped.” It is enough for us to be called Christians to escape every

abuse from our adversaries. God's name is said to be holy, not at all because its syllables have some power to sanctify, but because every property of God, and every idea of what is contemplated as belonging uniquely to him, is holy and pure. “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, even as we have hoped in you.” Do you see how skillfully he prayed? He made his own disposition the measure of the compassion God supplies. “Let your mercy upon us be as great,” he says, “as the hope we have already placed in you.” And our whole hope is to return to rest. Then, when the body of our humiliation has been transformed, we shall see it become conformed to the body of glory.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON PSALM 33. Of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he let him go, and [?]

1. The meaning of the psalm points to two events. Both what David did at Nob, the city of the priests, and what he did at Gath before Achish, king of the foreigners, seem to fit the title. He changed his countenance when he was speaking with Abimelech the priest, concealing his flight and pretending to be hurrying to carry out a royal command. That was when he also took the loaves of the presentation and the sword of Goliath. And he changed his countenance again when he was caught in the midst of his enemies and noticed them talking with one another and preparing to take revenge. For the servants of Achish, it says, said among themselves: “Is this not David, the king of the land? Was it not of him that the women sang as they led the dance, saying, ‘David has struck down his tens of thousands, and Saul his thousands’?” “And David,” it says, “was afraid of Achish, and changed his countenance before their eyes.” How is it, then, that the title names Abimelech, while the history gives Achish as king of the Gittites? We have an account handed down to us by tradition: the kings of the foreigners had Abimelech as a common name, but each also had his own name by which he was called. The same can be seen in the Roman empire, where the emperors are all called Caesars and Augusti but have other proper names of their own. Pharaoh among the Egyptians is a name of the same kind.

For the king in Joseph's time is clearly called Pharaoh. So is the king of Egypt who arose four generations later, in the time of Moses. So is the king in the time of Solomon, for “he took,” it says, “the daughter of Pharaoh.” And the king in the time of Jeremiah's prophecy was also called Pharaoh. In the same way there was an Abimelech in Abraham's time, another in Isaac's time, and the one now named, in David's time. For in Abraham's time it is said: “And Abimelech, with Ahuzzath his groomsman and Phicol the commander of his army, spoke to Abraham, saying.” And again concerning Isaac: “He stayed there a long time. And Abimelech, the king of the Philistines, looked out through the window and saw Isaac playing with Rebekah.” So too in David's time the title gives Abimelech, the common name of the kingship, while the history records Achish, the name that was properly his from birth. It was before this king, then, that he changed his countenance. He was carried about in the hands of servants, he drummed on the gates of the city, and he let his spittle run down, it says, onto his beard. So Achish said to his servants: “Why have you brought him to me? Am I short of madmen, that you have brought him to play the madman before me?” And so he was released from there and escaped, it says, to the cave of Adullam. Having escaped a great danger, he offers up this thanksgiving to God who rescued him. “I will bless the Lord at all times,” he says. Having escaped death, he lays down rules for his life, as it were, shaping his soul to a strict way of living. He resolves to let no moment pass without blessing, and to trace the origin of things great and small alike back to God. “I will not think,” he says, “that things come about through my own care, or that they happen by mere chance. Rather, ‘I will bless the Lord at all times,’ not only when life goes well but also in times of distress.” Taught by this, the Apostle says: “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything.” Do you see how great the man's love was? He did not chafe at one misfortune following another. He had been driven not only from his homeland, his kindred, his household and his possessions, but had even been handed over to his enemies by [?]

[?] knowing that “affliction produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope.” For truly, to those who are well prepared, afflictions are like an athlete's diet and training, advancing the contestant toward the glory of his fathers. This happens when we bless when we are reviled, entreat when we are slandered, give thanks when we are worn down, and boast in our affliction when we are afflicted. It is shameful for us to bless God in pleasant circumstances but keep silent in gloomy and painful ones. On the contrary, that is when we must give thanks all the more, knowing that “the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.” “His praise shall continually be in my mouth.” The prophet seems to promise something impossible. How can the praise of God be continually in a person's mouth? When he takes part in ordinary, everyday conversation, he does not have God's praise in his mouth. When he sleeps, he will certainly be silent. And when he is eating and drinking, how will his mouth offer praise? To this we reply that the inner man also has a spiritual mouth. Through it he is nourished by partaking of the word of life, which is the bread that came down from heaven. The prophet speaks of that mouth too when he says, “I opened my mouth and drew in breath.” It is that mouth the Lord also calls us to keep wide open, so that it can take in the food of truth more abundantly. For he says, “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” So the thought of God, once it has been imprinted and as it were sealed upon the governing part of the soul, can be called the praise of God, since it remains continually in the soul. Also, following the Apostle's instruction, the earnest person can do all things to the glory of God, so that every action, every word and every activity of the mind has the force of praise. For whether the righteous man eats or drinks, he does everything to the glory of God. When such a man sleeps, his heart keeps watch, as the one in the Song of Songs says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” For the images we see in sleep are, for the most part, echoes of what we thought about during the day. 2. “My soul shall be praised in the Lord.” “Let no one,” he says, “praise the cleverness by which I was saved from danger. For salvation lies not in human power or wisdom but in the grace of God.” “Let not the rich man boast in his wealth,” it says, “nor the wise man in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength; but let him who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows the Lord his God.” Do you see how the Apostle praises his fellow workers in the Gospel? “Who is a fellow servant and minister of yours in the Lord.” If, however, someone is praised for bodily

[?], or for the distinction of his parents, his soul is not praised in the Lord. Each such person is praised in the vanity of those things. Nor do the intermediate arts have anything truly praiseworthy: pilots, physicians, orators, or architects who build cities, pyramids, labyrinths, or other costly or enormous buildings. Those who are praised for these things do not have their soul praised in the Lord. It is enough for us, in place of every honor, to be called servants of so great a Master. Surely, if someone who serves a king is proud because he has been given that rank of service, will one who has been found worthy to serve God look elsewhere for praise for himself? As if the title of the Lord's servant were not enough to surpass every glory and distinction! “My soul, then, shall be praised in the Lord.” “Let the meek hear and be glad.” “Since my salvation was won without war,” he says, “simply by changing my countenance, and the enemies were defeated with God's help, let the meek hear this. Let them learn that it is possible to raise a trophy even while keeping still, and to be proclaimed victors in battle. And let them be glad, strengthened in meekness by my example. For I received this grace from God because I had attained meekness.” “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness.” Meekness is the greatest of the virtues, which is why it is included among the Beatitudes. For “blessed are the meek,” it says, “for they shall inherit the earth.” That earth, the heavenly Jerusalem, is not spoil for those who fight. It is set before long-suffering and gentle men as their inheritance. “Let the meek hear” means the same as “Let the disciples of Christ hear.” And perhaps he also wishes, in a prophetic way, that the wonder of God's kindness toward him should pass down even to us. Let them hear, he means, who were to become disciples of Christ many generations later. For he called “meek” those to whom the Lord says, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart.” Those whose characters are settled and who are free from every passion, so that no turmoil dwells in their souls, are the ones called meek. That is why Moses too is testified to have been meek above all men on earth. 3. “Magnify the Lord with me.” He gathers a chorus befitting himself to glorify the Lord

[?]. Let no one who is turbulent or agitated, or who drives his soul into frenzy through the passions of the flesh, join with me. But you who are meek, who have made your souls steady and stable and who shake off sluggishness and drowsiness in doing your duties, you magnify the Lord with me. One who magnifies the Lord is one who endures trials for the sake of godliness with a great mind and a [?] and exalted spirit. Since, then, a single mind and the study of a single man is not adequate even for a little while to grasp the great works of God, he calls all the meek together to share in this activity. Our life is full of the tongue's slips: obscene talk, coarse jesting, foolish talk, unfitting words, slander, idle words, perjury, false witness. All these evils, and more besides, are the tongue's handiwork. And those who open their mouths against the glory of God and speak unrighteousness on high: what instrument do they use to commit their impiety, if not the tongue? Since, then, “by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned,” keep your tongue from evil, so that you do not lay up treasures with a lying tongue, which are vain. And keep your lips from speaking deceit. In other words, make the whole instrument given to you for the service of speech rest from evil activity. Deceit is a hidden way of harming one's neighbour under the pretence of something better. [Apparatus:] “your tongue… lips” com- [?]. The word “your” is missing in the edi[tions] [?].

When you are about to rush into some sin, think, I ask you, of that dreadful and unbearable judgment seat of Christ. There the judge presides on a high, exalted throne, and all creation stands by, trembling at his glorious appearing, and we are to be brought forward one by one to have the lives we have lived examined. Then, beside the one who has done much evil in his life, stand fearsome and gloomy angels. Fire is in their gaze and fire in their breath, because their purpose is bitter, and their faces are like night, because they are grim and hate humankind. Then comes a deep pit, impenetrable darkness, and a lightless fire, which in the darkness keeps its power to burn but has lost its brightness. Then a breed of venomous, flesh-eating worms, which devour insatiably and are never full, inflicting unbearable pain as they gnaw. Then the hardest punishment of all: that reproach and that everlasting shame. Fear these things. Let this fear train you, and use it as a bridle to check your soul's desire for base things. This fear of the Lord is what the father promised to teach us. He did not promise to teach just anyone, but those who choose to listen to him; not those who have fallen far away, but those who run to him out of a desire to be saved; not those who are strangers to the covenants, but those made kin to the Word through the baptism of adoption. That is why he says, “Come,” meaning: draw near to me through good works, children, you who have been counted worthy to become sons of light through rebirth. “Listen,” you whose hearts have their ears open: “I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” This is the fear that the word [described] to you a little earlier [?]…

9. “Who is the man who desires life, who loves to see good days?” If anyone desires life, he says. He does not mean this common life that even the irrational animals live, but the true life, which death does not cut short. For now, it says, “you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, our life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed with him in glory.” So Christ is the true life, and our conduct in him is true life. In the same way, the good days are other days, which the Prophet sets out as a promise: “Who is the man who desires life, who loves to see good days?” For the days of this age are evil, since this age too… [Apparatus:] The first Colbert manuscript reads “opened” [?].

…[?] him. When we [?] to the Lord [?] at the beginning of the psalm: “in the Lord”; and, “In him our heart will rejoice.” It seems to me that the Apostle had this in mind when he said, “In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us,” and, “Not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions.” The Psalmist said, “Our soul waits for the Lord.” He wanted to show that the soul does not endure under compulsion or crushed by its afflictions, but welcomes with all joy the hardships suffered for the name of the Lord. So he says: not only do we endure, but also “In him our heart will rejoice, and we have hoped in his holy name.” Being called Christians is enough to let us escape every [attack] [?] from our adversaries. [Apparatus:] [?] mercies. Two manuscripts read “into the mercies.” But then the Paris edition reads “reward” [?]… [?] manuscripts read “of the name of the Lord.” The editions read “of his name.”

10. “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.” These exhortations are elementary, an introduction to godliness. They teach us carefully to control the tongue, to keep away from deceitful schemes, and to turn away from evil. Abstaining from evil is not what marks the perfect. It is what suits someone just beginning to learn: he must turn aside from the pull toward evil and get free of the habits of a wicked life, as if leaving a bad road, and only then take up the practice of good. It is impossible to lay hold of the good without first departing from evil and turning away from it completely. In the same way, you cannot recover your health without being rid of the disease, and someone who has not completely stopped being chilled cannot become warm. These things cannot exist together. So too, anyone who is to enter on a good life must [be free] from every [inclination] toward [?]… [Apparatus:] […]being dragged about [?]. But the fifth Regius [?]… “dragged about” [?], which suits the sense [?]. In the same place the third Regius reads “calling to.”

…place. They are called eyes because our oversight is entrusted to them, and ears because they receive our prayers. So here he has called eyes and ears the power that watches over us and the power that takes up our prayers. “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer.” Every action of a righteous man is worthy of God's attention. Every word of his is effective and active, because he says nothing idly. That is why Scripture says the righteous man is always watched over and always heard. “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth.” By “face” I think Scripture means the Lord's open and manifest coming at the judgment. That is why the eyes of the Lord are said to look on the righteous, since they still watch over us from afar, while the face itself will appear in order to cut off from the earth every memory of wickedness. Do not, I ask you, think of God's face as having a bodily shape. If you did, what Scripture says would seem absurd: that the eyes shine on the righteous separately, and the face is turned against the wicked separately. Yet there are no eyes without a face, and no face without eyes. Now, “no man shall see the face of the Lord and live,” but the angels of the little ones in the Church “always behold the face of our Father who is in heaven.” For now, because of the weakness of the flesh that wraps us round, we cannot take in the sight of the glorious appearing. The angels, however, have no covering like our flesh, so nothing hinders them from gazing continually on the face of God's glory. So we too, once we become sons of the resurrection, will be counted worthy of knowing face to face. Then the righteous will be counted worthy to see the face with exultation, and sinners to see it in judgment, since God's just judgment is going to destroy all sin. 12. “The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their afflictions.” The cry of the righteous is a spiritual cry. Its loudness lies in the secret place of the heart, and it can reach the very ears of God. Whoever asks for great things and prays for heavenly things is the one who cries out and sends up an audible

prayer to God. So the righteous cried out. They sought nothing [unbecoming] [?], nothing earthly, nothing lowly. [So] the Lord accepted their voice and delivered them from all their afflictions. He frees them from troubles by making them [untouched] [?] by what happens to them. “The Lord is near to the broken-hearted, and he will save the humble in spirit.” By his own goodness he draws near to all, but we put ourselves far away through sin. “For behold,” it says, “those who put themselves far from you will perish.” That is why Moses is said to draw near to God. Anyone else who is like him comes near to God through noble deeds and good actions. The verse is a direct prophecy of the Lord's coming, and it agrees with the verse before it. There it said, “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil,” meaning that his appearing at the judgment will bring the destruction of all wickedness. Here, “The Lord is near to the broken-hearted” foretells the Lord's coming in the flesh, already drawing near and not standing far off. Let Isaiah's prophecy confirm this for you: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me. He has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind.” Since he was sent as the physician of the broken-hearted, it says, “The Lord is near.” It is as if he said, “I say this to you who are humble and have crushed your pride,” cheering them and leading them to patience through joy in what they await. Brokenness of heart is the destruction of human reasonings. Someone who has despised [the things of the present] [?], given himself over to the word of God, and offered his ruling mind to thoughts that are higher than human and more divine: he is the one whose heart is broken, and he has made it a heart that the Lord does not despise. “A broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” So “the Lord is near to the broken-hearted, and he will save the humble in spirit.” Whoever has no conceit and takes pride in nothing human is broken in heart and humble in spirit. The one brought low by sin is humbled too, since sin humiliates more than anything else. In the same way we say that a woman who has been corrupted and has lost the holiness of virginity has been humbled: “Amnon,” it says, “rose up against Tamar and humbled her.” So all who have lost the uprightness and loftiness of the soul, cast down to the earth by sin and dashed to the ground, as it were… [Apparatus:] [?] The editions read “for, he says” [?]; “he says” in the manuscripts [?]. The sixth [manuscript] reads “of the Holy Spirit.”

…stoop over as they go along bent down [?], unable to straighten up completely. These are humbled, but not in spirit, because their humiliation is nothing to praise. But there are others who have the grace of the Holy Spirit and willingly humble themselves beneath those lower than they. With the Apostle they call themselves servants of some in Christ, and “the scum of all things until now,” and again, “We have become like the refuse of the world.” These people use humility in a spiritual way, making themselves last of all so that they may become first of all in the kingdom of heaven. These are the ones the Lord calls blessed when he says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all.” “Afflicted in every way,” it says, “but not crushed.” That is why the Lord also says to his disciples, “In the world you have affliction; but take heart, I have overcome the world.” So if you ever see righteous people in sickness, in bodily disability, in the loss of their families, under blows, in disgrace, in every kind of want and lack of necessities, remember that “many are the afflictions of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all.” Anyone who says affliction is not fitting for the righteous is saying nothing other than that an athlete should have no opponent. But if the athlete does not compete, what occasion will he have for winning crowns? This is now the fourth time this psalm tells how the Lord delivers from affliction those he wishes to deliver. First: “I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my afflictions.” Second: “This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him, and saved him from all his afflictions.” Third: “The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their afflictions.” And last: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all.” 13. “The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken.” Should we stay with the letter and be content with the meaning that first strikes our ears? Should we take it that these bones, the supports of the flesh, will not be broken in the righteous because of the protection the Lord has given them? And will the righteous man's bones be kept unbroken only while he is alive and in this life? Or, even after the bodily [?] has been dissolved, will nothing happen to the righteous man that could break them? Yet experience has taught us of many righteous people whose bones were broken: those who, bearing witness to Christ, handed themselves over to every kind of suffering. Persecutors have already broken the legs of some, and [their hands]… [Apparatus:] [?] or “not suit” [?]. Other manuscripts agree with “ought” [?]… “of those in Christ” [?]… reading [?]. The first Bellovacensis manuscript reads “will be kept” in the plural.

…and they have often pierced hands and heads with nails. Yet who would deny that those perfected in martyrdom are the most righteous of all? But perhaps it works like this. The word “man” is used for the soul, [that is,] the human mind, and in the same way its members are given the same names as those of the flesh. Scripture often names [the members] of the hidden man in this way, as when it says, “The eyes of the wise man are in his head,” meaning that the hidden man of the wise is far-seeing and circumspect. Again, it speaks of eyes in the same way, whether of the soul or of the flesh, not only in the passage we have cited but also when it says that the commandment of the Lord is far-shining and enlightens the eyes. Need I mention “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear”? Clearly some people have better ears, able to hear the words of God. And what does it say to those who lack those ears? “You deaf, hear, and you blind, look up!” And, “I opened my mouth and drew in breath.” And, “You have broken the teeth of sinners.” All these are said of the powers that serve spiritual food and spiritual speech. Of the same kind are “My belly pains me” and “The foot of the righteous will not stumble.” All such terms are borrowed from the outer man. By the same reasoning, the man in secret would also have certain bones, in which the bond and harmony of the soul's powers are held together. Bones protect the softness of the flesh by their own firmness. In the same way, some people in the Church are able, because of their [firmness] [?], to bear the failings of the weak. And just as the bones are joined to one another at the joints by sinews and ligaments grown onto them, so the bond of love and peace would produce a kind of natural union and oneness among the spiritual bones in the Church of God. When these bones are loosed from their harmony and, as it were, dislocated, the Prophet says of them: “Our bones were scattered beside Hades.” And if disturbance and [trembling] [?] ever seize them, he prays: “Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled.” But when they keep their proper harmony and are guarded by the Lord, not one of them will be broken, and they are worthy to give glory to God. For “all my bones,” it says, “will say: Lord, Lord, who is like you?” Have you seen
[Apparatus:] […]an is said, the soul, etc. [?] The editions read “he speaks likewise of those both of the flesh and of the soul.”

…the nature of the rational bones? Perhaps the Church might say this, “All my bones will say,” with reference to the mystery of the resurrection. For “thus,” it says, “says the Lord to these bones: Behold, I am bringing the breath of life into you. I will put sinews upon you and bring flesh up upon you, and you shall live, and you shall know that I am the Lord.” So these bones, once they have received life, will give thanks to the one who raised them and say, “Lord, Lord, who is like you?” 14. The words “The death of sinners is evil” are added with precision. Among the righteous there is a death that is not evil by nature but good. Those who have died with Christ have entered a good death, and those who have died to sin have died the good and saving death. But the death of sinners is evil, because punishment follows it, as it did for the rich man who was dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. “And those who hate the righteous will go wrong.” It is because they live in wrongdoing that they hate the righteous man. Just as [crooked things] are exposed by the straightness of a ruler, so they are exposed by the righteous man's way of life when they are set beside what is better. Because they live in sin, they behave with hatred toward the righteous man for fear of being reproved; and because they hate, they entangle themselves in sin once more. There are many reasons the righteous man may be hated. One is his frankness in reproving: “They hate the one who reproves in the gate, and they abhor a holy word.” Love of preeminence and love of power have also moved many to hate their betters. And sometimes it is ignorance of what the righteous man stands for, and of who the righteous man is. “The death of sinners is evil.” Or perhaps he calls the whole of life death, since the Apostle called this flesh death when he said, “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” Those who misuse this body and make it the servant of every sin prepare an evil death for themselves. “The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, and none who hope in him will go wrong.” Those who were created to serve the Lord were held captive by the enemy, so he will redeem their souls with his precious blood. Therefore none who hope in him will be found guilty of wrongdoing. [Apparatus:] The Paris edition is fuller: “flesh, and I will stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit into you.” But these [?]… “The death of sinners is evil. Precisely,” etc. But the third [manuscript] [?] reads “is truly added.” (46) So five manuscripts. The editions read “frankness in [?]”.

ON PSALM 44. For the end, for those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding; a song for the beloved.

1. This psalm too appears to be one that brings human nature to perfection, offering its benefit toward the end set before those who have chosen to live according to virtue. For those who are making progress need the teaching that leads to perfection, and this psalm provides it, bearing the title: For the end, for those who will be changed. By this he meant, in a veiled way, "for human beings." For we, more than all other rational beings, are subject to alterations and changes almost every day and every hour. Neither in body nor in mind are we the same as ourselves. Our body, ever flowing and dispersing, is in constant motion and change, either growing from small to greater or shrinking from its full state to something less. The boy who already goes to school and is fit to take up the arts and studies is not the same as the newborn infant; and the youth, now able to take part in the pursuits of young men, is admittedly different again from the boy. And the grown man differs from the youth in firmness and size of body and in the full development of his reason. Having reached his prime and attained the stable point of life, he begins once more, little by little, to decline toward less, the condition of his body imperceptibly ebbing away and his bodily vigor diminishing, until, bowed down by old age, he suffers the final loss of his strength. We, then, are the ones who are changed, and the psalm wisely hinted at us human beings by this expression. For angels do not admit of change. Among them there is no child, no youth, no old man; they remain in the very state in which they were created from the beginning, their constitution preserved whole and unalterable. But we are changed: in body, as has been shown, and in soul and the inner man, shifting our thoughts along with whatever circumstances befall us. We are one sort of people when we are cheerful and everything in life flows smoothly along, and another in times of hardship, when we stumble upon something we did not want. We are changed also in our anger, taking on a beastlike [?] state. We are changed also in our desires, becoming like cattle through a life of pleasure. Those who rage with lust for their neighbors' wives have become stallions mad for mares. The crafty man is likened to a fox, like Herod; the shameless one is called a dog, like Nabal the Carmelite. Do you see how varied and manifold our change is? Marvel, then, at the one who so fittingly applied this name to us. [?]

2. That is why one of the translators seems to me to have rendered the same thought well and aptly by another term, saying, instead of "For those who will be changed," "For the lilies." He thought the short life of flowers worthy to be compared with the perishability of human nature. But since the word is cast in the future tense (for it says, "For those who will be changed," as though this change will appear to us at some later time), let us consider whether it may be hinting to us at the doctrine of the resurrection, in which change will be granted to us, a change for the better and toward the spiritual. For, it says, it is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption. Do you see the change? It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. At that time the whole bodily creation will also be changed along with us. For indeed, the heavens will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak God will change them, and they will be changed. Then the sun too will be sevenfold brighter than itself, according to Isaiah, and the moon will be like the present greatness of the sun. And since the words of God are not written for everyone, but for those who have ears in the inner man, he inscribed it "For those who will be changed": that is, I think, for those who take care of themselves and constantly advance toward what is greater through the exercises of piety. For this is the most beautiful change, which the right hand of the Most High bestows. Blessed David perceived it when, having tasted the good things of virtue, he strained toward what lay ahead. For what does he say? And I said, Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High. So the one who advances in virtue is never not being changed. When I was a child, he says, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. And again, having become a man, he did not cease from his effort, but forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead, he pressed on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward calling. It is, then, a change of the inner man, who is being renewed day by day. Since, then, he is about to proclaim to us the things concerning the beloved, who took upon himself the dispensation of the incarnation for our sake, for those worthy of this grace [?] of the sons of Korah [?]

the Prophet says he has delivered this song to the sons of Korah. For it is a song, and not a psalm, because it was delivered with the bare voice and melodious utterance, no instrument sounding along with it. [?] "For the beloved." Shall I tell you who the beloved is whom the text means? Or do you know it even before our words, remembering the voice in the Gospel: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him? For he is beloved to the Father as the Only-begotten, and to all creation as a loving father and a good protector. The beloved and the good are by nature the same; hence some have already defined the good well as that which all things desire. It is not for just anyone to advance to the perfection of love and to come to know the one who is truly beloved, but for one who has already put off the old man, corrupted according to the deceitful desires, and put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator. For the one who loves money, who is infatuated with the perishable beauty of bodies, and who prizes this paltry glory too highly, has spent his power of loving on things it should not be spent on, and has been blinded to the vision of the one who is truly beloved. That is why it says: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. "With all" admits no division toward other things. For however much of your love you squander on things below, so much will necessarily be lacking to you from the whole. That is why few out of all have been called friends of God: as Moses is recorded to have been a friend, and as John, for, he says, the friend of the bridegroom, who stands, rejoices greatly. That is, the one who keeps his friendship for Christ steady and immovable is worthy of his friendship. Therefore the Lord also says to his disciples, who were now being perfected: No longer do I call you servants, but friends, because the servant does not know what his master is doing. It belongs to the perfect, then, to know the one who is truly beloved. And in truth only the saints are friends of God and of one another; no one who is wicked or ignorant is a friend. For the good of friendship does not fall within a depraved disposition, since nothing shameful and discordant can enter into the harmony of friendship. For evil is opposed not only to the good, but also to itself. But now let us proceed to the examination of the words.

3. My heart has poured forth a good word. Some have thought that these words are spoken in the person of the Father [?]

concerning the Word who was in the beginning with him, whom, they say, he brought forth as it were from his heart and his very inward parts, so that from a good heart a good word came forth. To me, however, these words seem to refer to the person of the prophet. For what follows the passage no longer makes the interpretation concerning the Father run smoothly for us. The Father would not have said of his own tongue, My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe. You are comely in beauty beyond the sons of men. For he does not have his surpassing beauty by comparison with human beings. And going on, it says: Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness. It did not say, "I, God, anointed you," but, "He anointed you," so that from this it is shown that the person speaking is another. Who, then, is this, if not the Prophet, who received the working of the Holy Spirit that came upon him? My heart, he says, has poured forth a good word. For a belch is a hidden breath which, as the bubbles burst while the food is digesting, is breathed out upward. So the one who has been fed on the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world, and who has been filled with every word that proceeds from the mouth of God (that is, in Scripture's customary figurative language, the soul nourished on sacred teachings), gives forth a belch suited to the food he has eaten. Therefore, since the food was rational and good, the Prophet pours forth a good word. For the good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth what is good. Let us too, then, seek the nourishment that comes from the word to fill our souls (for the righteous man, it says, eats and satisfies his soul), so that, in proportion to what we are fed on, we may send forth not just any word, but a good one. For the wicked man, raised on depraved doctrines, belches forth from his heart an evil word. Do you not see what the mouths of the heretics belch out? How offensive and foul-smelling it is, betraying a great sickness deep within those wretches! For the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth what is evil. Do not, then, with itching ears, heap up for yourself teachers who can work sickness in your inward parts and bring upon you a belching of evil words, for which you will be condemned on the day of judgment. For by your words, it says, you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. I speak my works to the king. This phrase too draws us strongly to the sense of the prophetic person: "I speak my works to the king" in place of "I will confess to the judge, and I forestall the accuser by declaring my own deeds." For we have received the commandment [?]

that says: State your iniquities first, that you may be justified. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe. Just as the pen is an instrument for writing, while the hand of a skilled writer moves it to set down what is being written, so also the tongue of the righteous, when the Holy Spirit moves it, writes the words of eternal life on the hearts of believers, dipped not in ink but in the Spirit of the living God. The scribe, then, is the Holy Spirit, because he is wise and able to teach all things; and swift-writing, because the movement of thought is swift. The Spirit writes thoughts for us not on tablets of stone, but on fleshly tablets of the heart. And in proportion to the breadth of the heart, the Spirit writes more or less on our hearts, either plain to all or more obscure, according to the prior preparation of purity. And because of the speed of what is written, the whole inhabited world has at last become full of the Gospel. What follows the passage seemed to us to take its own beginning, and not to be joined to what precedes but attached to what follows. For we take "comely in beauty" to be said to the Lord, by a change in the person addressed.

4. You are comely in beauty beyond the sons of men; grace was poured out on your lips. Both Aquila and Symmachus lead us to this sense: the one says, "In beauty you have been made beautiful beyond the sons of men"; and Symmachus, "In beauty you are fair beyond the sons of men." He who has gazed upon the Lord's divinity, then, calls him comely in beauty. For he is not praising the beauty of the flesh. For we saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was without honor, inferior to the sons of men. It is clear, then, that the Prophet, having gazed on his splendor and been filled with the radiance that shone from it, was struck in soul by this beauty and moved to the divine love of intelligible loveliness. When that loveliness appears to the human soul, everything loved before shows itself shameful and worthless. That is why Paul too, when he saw the one who is comely in beauty, counted all things as refuse, that he might gain Christ. Those outside the word of truth call the preaching of the Gospel foolishness, despising the plainness of the Scriptures' diction; but we who boast in [?]
