the cross of Christ, to whom the things freely given us by God have been revealed through the Spirit, not in words taught by human wisdom, know that it is a rich grace poured out from God upon the words about Christ. That is why in a short time the preaching went through nearly the whole inhabited world: because a rich and abundant grace has been poured out upon the heralds of the Gospel, whom Scripture also called the lips of Christ. That is why, in contemptibly plain little words, the preaching of the Gospel has great power to lead and draw people toward salvation. And every soul has been mastered by immovable doctrines, being made firm through grace in unshakable faith in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: Through whom we have received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith; and again: I labored more abundantly than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.

5. Grace was poured out on your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. It is written in the Gospel that they marveled at the words of grace that proceeded out of his mouth. Therefore the psalm, wishing to represent vividly the abundance of grace in the words of our Lord, said, Grace was poured out on your lips, because of the abundance of grace in his speech. God has blessed you forever. It is clear that these words must be referred to his humanity, in so far as he advances in wisdom and stature and grace. In this sense it is clear that we understand the grace to have been given to him as a prize for his noble deeds. Similar to this is: You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions. Close to this also is what Paul wrote to the Philippians: He humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross; therefore God also highly exalted him. So it is clear that these things are said of the man in the Savior. Or else: since the Church is the body of the Lord, and he himself is the head of the Church, then just as we explained that those who serve the heavenly word are the lips of Christ (like Paul, who had Christ speaking in him, and anyone who resembles him in virtue), so also the rest of the members of Christ's body are we, each one of those who have believed. Whoever, then, refers to the Lord the blessing given to the Church will not err. So "God has blessed you" means: he has filled your members and your body with his own good things

[?] forever, that is, without end. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty. We take this, then, figuratively, to refer to the living Word of God as being joined to the flesh, the Word who is active and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. For the thigh is a symbol of generative activity: For these, it says, are the souls that came out of Jacob's thighs. Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is called life, and way, and bread, and vine, and true light, and countless other things, so too he is called a sword that cuts through the passionate part of the soul and puts to death the impulses of desire. Then, since God the Word was about to be joined to the weakness of the flesh, "O mighty one" is fittingly added, because the ability of God to come to be in human nature is a demonstration of the greatest power. For the constitution of heaven and earth, of sea and air, and the coming into being of the greatest elements, and whatever is conceived above the world or beneath the earth, do not display the power of God the Word so much as the dispensation of the incarnation and his condescension to the lowliness and weakness of humanity. In your comeliness and your beauty. Comeliness differs from beauty. "Comely" is said of what has been brought to completion in its season, at the fitting time for its proper prime: as wheat is comely when it is already ripe for harvest, and the fruit of the vine is comely when it has received its proper ripening to completion through the season of the year and is fit for enjoyment. Beauty, on the other hand, is the harmonious composition of the members, with grace blooming upon it. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness, that is, in the fullness of the times; and in your beauty, that is, in the divinity that is contemplated and grasped by the mind. For that is the truly beautiful: what surpasses all human comprehension and power, and is contemplated by the mind alone. The disciples, to whom he explained the parables in private, came to know his beauty. Peter and the sons of thunder saw his beauty on the mountain, outshining the brightness of the sun, and were deemed worthy to receive with their own eyes the preludes of his glorious coming. And bend your bow, he says, and prosper, and reign. That is: having begun the care of humankind through the flesh, make your care intense, lasting, and never

slackening. For this will open a road and a course for the preaching, and will subject all to your kingdom. Let it not surprise us that "prosper" is spoken in the imperative, since Scripture is accustomed always to frame wishes in this way: Your will be done, in place of "may it be done"; and Your kingdom come, in place of "may it come."

6. Because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and your right hand will guide you wondrously. Again the sentence is framed in a similar way, as though the Lord were receiving these things, prospering and reigning, as a reward for truth and meekness and righteousness. But we must understand it this way: since human affairs had already been perverted by falsehood, reign among men who are ruled by sin, so that you may sow truth in its place; for you are the truth. And "because of meekness": so that by your example all may be led on to gentleness and kindness. That is why the Lord also said: Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart. And he gave proof of his meekness in his very deeds: when he was reviled, he was silent; when he was scourged, he endured it. And your right hand will guide you wondrously: not a pillar of cloud, nor the light of fire, but your right hand itself. Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one. The sharpened arrows of the mighty one are the well-aimed words that reach down to the hearts of the hearers, striking and wounding souls that are sensitive. For the words of the wise, it says, are like goads. That is why the Psalmist too, praying once to be delivered from the deceitful men of his generation, seeks the sharpened arrows of the mighty one as a cure for a deceitful tongue. He also asks that the desert coals be present, so that for those whom the arrows of the word do not touch because of the hardness of their hearts, punishment may be ready; and this punishment he called desert coals. For those who have turned themselves into deserts empty of God need the desert coals to be made ready for them. Now, then: Your arrows are sharpened. By these arrows the souls that have received the faith are wounded, and, kindled to the highest love of God, they say like the bride: I am wounded with love. Indescribable and ineffable is the beauty of the Word, and the comeliness of Wisdom, and the form of God in his image. Blessed, then, are those who love to behold the true beauty. For, as though bound to it by love, and burning with that heavenly and blessed passion, they forget their relatives and friends; they forget home and all their possessions; and forgetting even the bodily [need] to eat [?]

[?] … of necessity to drink, they cling to the divine and pure love alone. You will also understand the sharpened arrows to be those sent out to sow the Gospel throughout the whole world. Because they were sharpened, they shone with the works of righteousness and slipped subtly into the souls of those they taught; and these arrows, sent forth everywhere, made the peoples fall beneath Christ. It seems to me that the phrase is more coherently restored by a transposition, so that the sense is this: "Bend your bow, and prosper, and reign, and your right hand will guide you wonderfully, and peoples will fall beneath you, because your arrows are sharpened in the heart of the king's enemies." No one who fights against God, no boaster and no proud man, falls beneath God, but only those who have accepted the submission that comes from faith. And the arrows, falling into the hearts of those who were once the king's enemies, draw them to a longing for the truth, draw them to the Lord, so that, though they were enemies of God, they are reconciled to him through the teachings. 7. "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." Since he has spoken at length with reference to what is human, he now leads the discourse back up to the heights of the glory of the Only-begotten. "Your throne, O God," he says, "is forever and ever"; that is, your kingdom lies beyond the ages and is older than every [?]. And it is fitting that, after the submission of the peoples, he hymns the magnificence of God's kingdom. "A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." This is why he has also given him his proper title, plainly proclaiming him God: "Your throne, O God." The rod of God is a rod of discipline, and in disciplining it brings judgments that are straight and not perverted. That is why the rod of his kingdom is called a rod of uprightness. "For if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod." Do you see the just judgment of God? He does not use the rod on anyone at random, but on those who sin. It is also called a rod of comfort: "For your rod," he says, "and your staff, these have comforted me." It is also a rod of crushing: "You will shepherd them with a rod of iron; you will shatter them like a potter's vessel." But what is earthy and made of clay is shattered for the benefit of those being shepherded, just as a man is handed over "for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved." 8. "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions."

Since the figurative anointing, and the figurative high priests and kings, had to be given their pattern, the Lord's flesh was anointed with the true anointing, when the Holy Spirit came to dwell in it; and this is what is called the oil of gladness. He was anointed above his companions, that is, above all men who share in Christ. For to them some partial communion of the Spirit was given, but the Holy Spirit came down upon the Son of God and, as John says, "remained upon him." The Spirit is fittingly called the oil of gladness, since joy is one of the fruits that the Holy Spirit cultivates. Because the discourse about the Savior is mixed, on account both of the nature of the Godhead and of the economy of the incarnation, he looks again to the human side of God and says: "You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness." That is: other men often achieve a disposition toward the good and an aversion from evil only through toil, discipline and constant attention; but in you there is a natural affinity for the good and estrangement from lawlessness. Yet for us too it is not hard, if we are willing, to take up love of righteousness and hatred of lawlessness. For God has given every faculty to the rational soul for a useful purpose, the faculty of hating as well as that of loving, so that, guided by reason, we may love virtue and hate vice. There are times when hatred can be used in a praiseworthy way: "Did I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and pine away over your enemies? I hated them with a perfect hatred." 9. "Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments, from ivory palaces, from which the daughters of kings have gladdened you in your honor." The prophetic discourse, descending in due order and having touched on everything in the economy, gazing intently at the Spirit who was revealing hidden things to him, has come to the Passion: "Myrrh," he says, "and stacte and cassia from your garments." That myrrh is a symbol of burial the evangelist John has also taught us, when he says that Joseph of Arimathea buried him with myrrh and aloes. Stacte too is a kind of myrrh, the finest kind. For when the aromatic substance is pressed, whatever of it runs off is set apart as stacte, while the thicker part that remains is (92) … "and I pined away over your enemies"; that last phrase, "they became my enemies," [?] is believed …

called myrrh. So the fragrance of Christ breathes out myrrh because of the Passion, and stacte because he did not remain motionless or inactive during the three days and three nights, but went down into Hades for the sake of the economy of the resurrection, so that he might fill all things with himself. It breathes out cassia because cassia is a very fine and fragrant bark wrapped around a woody stalk. Perhaps, then, the word has deeply and wisely hinted, through the name of cassia, at the Passion of the cross, which he underwent for the benefit of all creation. So you have myrrh for the burial, stacte for the descent into Hades (since every drop moves downward), and cassia for the economy of the flesh upon the wood. And for this reason, he says, "the daughters of kings have gladdened you in your honor." Who could the daughters of kings be but noble, great and royal souls, which, having come to know Christ through his condescension to human things, gladdened him in honor, glorifying his Godhead with true faith and perfect love? He says that these spices are present in Christ's garments (that is, in the figurative language of his words and the structure of his doctrines) not sparingly, but that they are carried from whole [?] buildings. For by "palaces" he means the greatest of houses, and these built of ivory; by this the prophet teaches, I think, the richness of Christ's love toward the world. "The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a robe woven with gold, richly adorned." He now speaks of the Church, about which we have learned in the Song that she is Christ's one perfect dove, who takes into the place at Christ's right hand those who are known for good works, separating them from the wicked as the shepherd separates the lambs from the kids. So the queen stands—the soul joined to the Word as her Bridegroom, not ruled by sin but sharing in the kingdom of Christ—at the Savior's right hand in a robe woven with gold; that is, she adorns herself majestically and in a manner befitting holy things with spiritual doctrines, interwoven and richly varied. And since the doctrines are not of one form but varied and manifold, containing moral, natural and so-called contemplative teachings, the word says for this reason that the bride's robe is richly adorned. 10. "Listen, daughter, and see, and incline … are called the greatest of houses. But the Paris edition and …

… and they will worship him." He calls the Church to hear and keep what is commanded, and makes her his own by the way he addresses her, calling her daughter, as though begetting her as his child through love. "Listen, daughter, and see." By "see" he teaches her to keep her mind trained for contemplation. Consider creation, he says, and, having profited from the order within it, rise in this way to the contemplation of the Creator. Then, bending the lofty neck of her arrogance, he says, "Incline your ear." Do not run off to the myths of those outside, but accept the humble voice of the word of the Gospel. Incline your ear to the teaching here, so that you may forget those wicked customs and the teachings of your fathers. Therefore: "Forget your people and your father's house." For everyone who commits sin has been born of the devil. Cast out, he says, the teachings of demons; forget sacrifices, night-time dancing, and myths that inflame to fornication and every kind of licentiousness. That is why I have called you my own daughter: so that you may hate the father who first begot you for destruction. For if by forgetting them you wipe away the stains of evil lessons and recover your own beauty, you will appear desirable to the Bridegroom and King. "For he is your Lord, and they will worship him." By "He is your Lord" he points to the necessity of submission. And all creation will worship him; for "at the name of Jesus Christ every knee [?] of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth." "And the daughter of Tyre with gifts. The rich among the people will entreat your face." The excess of idolatry seems to have been practiced in the land of Canaan, and Tyre is the chief city of Canaan. So the word, urging the Church to obedience, says, "Even the daughter of Tyre will come one day with gifts, and the rich among the people will worship your face with gifts." He did not say, "They will worship you with gifts," but, "your face." For it is not the Church that is worshiped, but the head of the Church, Christ, whom Scripture has called "face." 11. "All the glory of the king's daughter is within; she is clothed and richly adorned with golden fringes. Virgins will be brought to the king after her." Since she has been cleansed of the … Basil and six manuscripts: "you will worship him." … [?] "calls." But other manuscripts, with the editions, "calling." … the third: "of the ancestral traditions," ancestral … "they will worship him." (4) The third and sixth Royal manuscripts: "and he will worship him,"

old teachings of wickedness, has obeyed the teaching, and has forgotten her people and her father's house, the Holy Spirit tells what concerns her. And since he saw her hidden purity, he says, "All the glory of the king's daughter"—that is, of the bride of Christ, who has now become the king's daughter through adoption—"is within." The word urges us to advance into the innermost mysteries of the Church's glory, since the bride's beauty is within. For whoever prepares himself for the Father who sees in secret, and prays, and does everything not in order to be seen by men but to be made manifest to God alone, has all his glory within, like the king's daughter. So the golden fringes too, with which she is clothed and wholly adorned, are within. Look for nothing in outward gold and bodily finery; but understand a garment worthy to adorn one made after the image of the Creator, as the Apostle says: "Having put off the old man and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created him." And whoever has put on "heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, patience, gentleness" is clothed inwardly and adorned in the inner man. Paul also exhorts us to put on the Lord Jesus, not in the outer man, but so that the remembrance of God may cover our mind. I think the spiritual garment is woven when the action that answers to it is interlaced with the word of teaching. For just as a bodily garment is woven when the weft is interlaced with the warp, so, when the word has been laid down first, if actions follow accordingly, the soul would have a most dignified garment, with its life of virtue made complete in word and deed. Fringes hang down from the garment, and these too are to be understood spiritually; that is why they are said to be golden. Since word goes beyond deed, it is like a fringe overhanging the fabric woven for action. Certain souls follow the Lord's bride, souls that have not received the seeds of alien words; these will be brought to the king, following the bride. Let those who vow their virginity to the Lord hear that virgins will be brought to the king—but virgins who are near the Church, following after her and not straying from the Church's good order. "The virgins will be brought with gladness and rejoicing; they will be led into the king's temple." Not those who have taken up virginity under compulsion, nor those who … (8) The whole phrase "of the king's daughter, that is" … manuscripts: "seeds."

accepted the life of chastity out of grief or necessity, but those who always rejoice with gladness and exultation at such an achievement—these will be brought to the king, and will be led not to some ordinary place but into the king's temple. For the priestly vessels, which human use has not defiled, will be carried into the Holy of Holies and will have the right of entry into the inner sanctuary, where profane feet will not tread. How great a thing it is to be led into the king's temple the Prophet shows when he prays for himself and says: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple." 12. "In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will make them rulers over all the earth." Since above she was commanded to forget her people and her father's house, now, in return for her obedience, she receives sons in place of fathers, sons distinguished by such high dignities that they are appointed rulers over all the earth. Who, then, are the sons of the Church? Surely the sons of the Gospel, who have ruled the whole earth. For "their voice," it says, "has gone out into all the world"; and, "They will sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel." And if one takes the bride's fathers to be the patriarchs, even so the interpretation referring to the apostles does not fail. For in place of the patriarchs sons were born to her through Christ, who do the works of Abraham and are therefore reckoned equal in honor to them, because they have done the same things for which the fathers were deemed worthy of great honors. The saints are rulers of the whole earth because of their affinity with the good, since the very nature of the good confers the first place on them, as it conferred on Jacob authority over Esau: "Be lord," it says, "over your brother." Those, then, who have become equal in honor to the fathers, and have gained preeminence over all through the practice of virtue, are sons of the bride of Christ and are appointed by their own mother as rulers over all the earth. Consider, I ask you, how great the queen's authority is: she appoints rulers over all the earth. "I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore peoples will confess you forever, and forever and ever." Last of all, the word is spoken as though in the person of the Church: "I will remember your name in every generation and generation." And what is the Church's remembrance? The confession

ON PSALM 45. For the end; on behalf of the sons of Korah; concerning hidden things. A psalm. 1. The psalm seems to me to contain a prophecy about the things at the end. Paul also knew of this end when he said: "Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father." Or else: our actions lead us to the end, each to the end proper to it, good action to blessedness and evil action to eternal condemnation, and the counsels the Spirit hands down in this psalm lead those who obey them to the good end. For this reason it is entitled "For the end," since the teachings point to the blessed end of human life. "On behalf of the sons of Korah." This psalm too is addressed to the sons of Korah, whom the Holy Spirit does not distinguish from one another, because they uttered the prophetic words as though with one soul and one voice, in complete harmony with one another. None of them prophesied anything beyond the rest, but the prophetic gift was granted to them equally, because their disposition toward one another in good things was equal. The psalm is spoken "concerning hidden things," that is, concerning things secret and hidden in mystery. When you come to the individual words of the psalm, you will learn what is hidden in them, and that it is not for just anyone to look into the divine mysteries, but only for one who can become a harmonious instrument of the promise [?], so that his soul, like a psaltery, is moved by the Holy Spirit who works in it. "God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the afflictions that have come upon us exceedingly." Every man needs much help because of the weakness that belongs to him by nature, since many painful and toilsome things befall him. So, seeking a refuge from all his troubles, like someone fleeing to an inviolable sanctuary, or taking refuge on some steep peak encircled by a strong wall when enemies invade, he flees to God, believing that the only rest is to abide in him. Now, that refuge is to be found in God is agreed by all; but the enemy has produced much error and confusion

… unbelievers take refuge in idols, robbed of the knowledge of the true God by the confusion the devil has brought upon them. And even those who know God go astray in judging things, making their requests for what is good for them without instruction: they ask for some things as good which are often not to their benefit, and flee from others as evil which sometimes bring them great benefit. For example, is someone ill? Fleeing the pain of the illness, he prays for health. Has he lost money? He is in anguish over the loss. Yet illness is often beneficial, when it is going to discipline the sinner; and health is harmful, when it becomes provision for sin to the one who has it. In the same way money has already served some as a means to licentiousness, while poverty has brought to self-control many who had set out on an evil course. So do not flee what you should not flee, nor take refuge where you should not. Let there be one thing for you to flee: sin; and one refuge from evils: God. Do not trust in rulers; do not exalt yourselves on uncertain wealth; do not pride yourselves on bodily strength; do not chase after the splendor of human glory. None of these things saves; all are temporary, all are deceptive. There is one refuge: God. "Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man," or in anything human. 2. "God, then, is our refuge and strength." To one who can say, "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me," God is strength. Many can say, "God is our refuge," and, "Lord, you have become our refuge"; but to say it with the same disposition as the Prophet belongs to very few. For few are those who do not admire human things, but depend wholly on God, breathe God, and have all their hope and confidence in him. And our deeds convict us, when in afflictions we run to anything rather than to God. Is your child ill? You look around for the charmer, or for the man who hangs strange inscribed characters around the necks of innocent infants; or at the very least you go to the doctor and his medicines, neglecting the one who is able to save. If a dream troubles you, you run to the dream interpreter. If you fear an enemy, you contrive to get some human patron. In short, in every need you stand convicted: in word you call God your refuge, but in deed you draw help from useless and vain things. But for the righteous man God is a true help. Just as a general, equipped with a fine force of heavy infantry, is always ready to come to the aid of any part of the line that is hard pressed, so God is our helper, and … (26) The editions: "fleeing some things." But six manuscripts: "fleeing …"

…an ally to everyone who fights against the schemes of the devil, sending out the ministering spirits for the salvation of those in need. Affliction finds every righteous person because of the way of life he follows. For whoever turns aside from the broad and spacious road and walks the narrow and hard-pressed one is found by afflictions. The Prophet has shaped the phrase as though they were living things when he says, “in the afflictions that have found us exceedingly.” For like living creatures they overtake us, producing endurance, and through endurance proven character, and through proven character hope. That is why the Apostle too says, “Through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God”; and, “Many are the afflictions of the righteous.” But whoever has endured the trial that comes from affliction nobly and calmly will say, “In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” And he is so far from [?] and shrinking back in afflictions that he even makes the excess of his troubles an occasion for boasting, saying, “And not only that, but we also boast in our…”

5. “Therefore we will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas.” The Prophet shows how great is the firmness of trust in Christ: even if everything is turned upside down, even if the earth is overturned in its turmoil, even if the mountains leave their own seats and are shifted into the middle of the sea, “we will not fear,” because we have God as our refuge and strength and helper in the afflictions that have found us exceedingly. Whose heart is so undaunted, whose thoughts so untroubled, that in such great confusion he keeps his mind fixed on God, and because of his hope in him is dismayed by nothing that happens? We, however, cannot bear even a man's anger; or when a dog rushes at us, or some other beast, we do not look to God, our helper in afflictions, but in terror turn back on ourselves. “Their waters roared and were troubled.” He spoke of the shaking of the earth and the moving of the mountains; he now speaks also of the surging and upheaval of the sea, as the mountains fall into the midst of the deep. “Their waters roared and were troubled”—that is, the waters of the seas. He makes the […] still greater in the…

…[un]shaken and firm, having our hopes set on God. “The mountains were troubled by his might.” You may also take the sense of the saying figuratively, calling “mountains” those who think highly of their own greatness but are ignorant of the might of God, who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, and then are overcome by those who proclaim the word of wisdom with power and wisdom, and who, once they become aware of their own poverty, fear the Lord and are humbled beneath his might. Or perhaps the rulers of this age, and the fathers of the wisdom that is perishing, are themselves called mountains, being troubled by the might of Christ, which he displayed through the cross in the contest against the one who has the power of death. For having stripped himself like a noble wrestler, he threw down the principalities and the powers, and made a public example of them, triumphing over them in the…

4. “The streams of the river make glad the city of God.” The salt waters, violently stirred up by the winds, roared and were troubled; but the streams of the river, advancing without a sound and flowing quietly into those worthy to receive them, make glad the city of God. Even now the righteous man drinks the living water, and later he will drink it more abundantly, when he has been enrolled as a citizen of the city of God. Now, however, he drinks through a mirror and in a riddle, because he grasps the divine contemplations only little by little; but then he will receive the river in full flood all at once, able to overflow the whole city of God with gladness. And what could the river of God be but the Holy Spirit, who comes to dwell in the worthy [?] through the faith of those who have believed in Christ? For “whoever believes in me,” he says, “out of his belly rivers will flow”; and again, “If anyone drinks of the water that I give, it will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.” This river, then, makes glad the whole city of God together, that is, the Church of those whose citizenship is in heaven; or else we should understand as the city the whole intelligible creation, from the powers above the world down to human souls, made glad by the inflowing of the Holy Spirit. For some define a city as a settled community governed according to law. And the definition of a city just given fits the Jerusalem above, the heavenly city, as well. For there too is a community, that of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven; it is settled because the way of life of the saints cannot be moved; and it is governed according to the heavenly law. To learn thoroughly, then, the order of that commonwealth and all its arrangement is beyond any human [?] “the streams make glad” (Latin: impetus laetificant); instead of “heavenly” has “heaven.”

nature. For those are the things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him”—except that there are myriads of angels there, and a festal gathering of saints, and the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. Of that city David says, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God.” To that city God makes this promise through Isaiah: “I will make you an everlasting exultation, a gladness for generation after generation; and there will be no ruin or misery within your borders, but your walls will be called Salvation.” So lift up the eyes of your soul, and seek what concerns the city of God in a way worthy of the things above. What could anyone conceive that is worthy of the blessedness there, in a city which the river of God makes glad, and whose craftsman and maker is God? “The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle.” Perhaps he means the God-bearing flesh, sanctified through its union with God. So you will understand the tabernacle of the Most High to be his manifestation through the flesh.

5. “God is in her midst, and she will not be shaken. God will help her at the break of morning.” And since God is in the midst of the city, he will grant her to be unshaken, providing her with help at the first rising of the light. Whether, then, one applies the name “city” to the Jerusalem above or to the Church below, “the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle” in her. And through this tabernacle, in which God dwelt, he came to be in her midst, granting her not to be shaken. God is in the midst of the city, sending out his rays equally from there to the farthest bounds of the circle of his providence. For in this way the justice of God is preserved, as he distributes the same measure of his [?] to all. “God will help her at the break of morning.” Our morning is made by the sun we perceive with our senses, when it peeps over our horizon; but the morning in the soul is brought about by the Sun of righteousness, who by the rising of the intelligible light makes day in the one who has received him. For during the time of ignorance we human beings are in night. When, therefore, we open wide our ruling faculty and receive the radiance of glory and are bathed all around in the eternal light, “God will help her at the break of morning.” When we become children of light, and the night is far spent for us and the day has drawn near, then we become worthy of God's help. So God helps the city by producing morning in her through his own rising and appearing. “For behold a man,” it says, “whose name is the Dawn.” To those, then, on whom the intelligible light rises, [?] … The editions read “our [morning].” Immediately after, the editions read “the morning of the soul”; but the manuscripts [?] … The editions read ἐπανατέλλῃ (“rises”); but five manuscripts read ἐπανατείλῃ [?].

…[dispelling] the darkness of ignorance and wickedness, morning comes. Since, then, the light has come into the world, so that whoever walks in it may not stumble, his help is what brings the morning. Or perhaps, since the resurrection took place at early dawn, “God will help the city at the break of morning,” he who won the victory over death in the morning, on the third day, the day of the resurrection. 6. “The nations were troubled, kingdoms gave way; the Most High uttered his voice, the earth was shaken.” Picture for me a city under attack by enemies who have marched against it, with many nations besieging it for a time, and the kings who hold the sceptre in each nation; then a general of irresistible strength suddenly appears to help this city, lifts the siege, scatters the massed nations and drives the kings to flight merely by shouting at them with power, striking their hearts with the [?] of his voice. How great a turmoil would likely arise, as the nations are pursued and the kings turn to flight; an indistinct din and an unceasing clamour would rise from their confused flight, and every place would be full of those driven off by fear, so that commotion would break out everywhere in the cities or villages that took them in! Such, then, is the help the Saviour gives the city of God which he presents when he says, “The nations were troubled, kingdoms gave way. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.” He saw God become man; he saw Emmanuel born of the holy Virgin, which is translated “God with us”; and therefore he cries out prophetically, “The Lord of hosts is with us,” showing that this is the one who appeared to the holy prophets and patriarchs. “Our protector,” he says—not some other God besides the one handed down by the prophets, but the God of Jacob, who spoke to his servant in the oracle: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” 7. “Come and see the works of God, the wonders he has set on the earth, putting an end to wars to the ends of the earth.” Those who are far from the word of truth the Word summons into nearness through knowledge… [?] “…victory over death, the morning of the third,” etc. “Who through the victory…” (41) [The editions?] and some manuscripts read ἐκβοῆσαι (“to shout out”). [?] ἐνανθρωπίσαντα (“become man”). But five other manuscripts [read] ἐνανθρω[πήσαντα] [?] … In the same place the editions read “to us … handed down,” where some are said to read “having been handed down.”

…saying, “Come and see.” For just as with the eyes of the body great distances make our perception of what is seen faint, while drawing near gives the viewers clear recognition of what they are looking at, so too with the objects of the mind's contemplation: whoever has not been made familiar with God through works and drawn near to him cannot see his works with the pure eyes of the understanding. That is why it says, “Come”: draw near first, and then see the works of the Lord, which are wondrous and astonishing; struck with amazement by them, the nations that were formerly warlike and given to strife have turned to peace. “Come, children, listen to me”; and, “Come, all you who labour and are heavy laden.” It is the voice of a father, calling to himself with outstretched arms those who until now have been unruly. So whoever has heard the call and drawn near and clung to the one who gave the command will see him who made peace for all things through the cross, “whether things on earth or things in heaven.” “He will break the bow and shatter the weapon, and burn the shields with fire.” Do you see how peaceable the Lord of hosts is, though he has with him the invisible powers of the angelic ranks? Do you see the courage, and at the same time the love for humanity, of the commander-in-chief of the hosts? Though he is Lord of the hosts and has all the companies of the angelic ranks, nowhere does he wound any of the enemy, strike any down, or lay a hand on anyone; he only breaks bows and weapons, and burns shields with fire. He breaks the bow, so that fiery arrows may no longer be shot from it; he shatters the [?] weapons of close combat, so that those nearby who are under attack may not receive wounds. And he burns the shields with fire, stripping his adversaries of their defences, and doing all things for the good of his enemies…

8. “Be at leisure, and know that I am God.” As long as we give our leisure to matters outside God, we cannot take in the knowledge of God. For who, while anxious about the things of the world and sunk deep in the [?] of the flesh, can attend to words about God and be equal to the precision of such great contemplations? Do you not see that the word which fell among the thorns is choked by the thorns? And the thorns are the pleasures of the flesh, wealth and glory, and the cares of this life. Whoever desires the knowledge of God must get outside all these things, and only when he is at leisure from the passions can he take up the knowledge of God. For how could it enter a soul cramped by the reasonings that have already taken possession of it—the thought of

God? Even Pharaoh knew that seeking God belongs to someone at leisure, and that is why he reproaches Israel: “You are idle, you are idlers, and you say, ‘We will pray to the Lord our God.’” This leisure, then, is good and profitable to the one who has it, since it creates quiet for taking in the teachings of salvation; but the leisure of the Athenians was evil, who “spent their time in nothing else but telling or hearing something newer.” Some imitate this even now, using the leisure of their lives in constantly inventing some newer doctrine. Leisure of this sort is dear to unclean and evil spirits. “When the unclean spirit,” it says, “has gone out of a man, it says, ‘I will go back to the place from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds that house unoccupied and swept.” God forbid, then, that we should leave room for the adversary to enter; rather, let us keep our inner house occupied, having first settled Christ within ourselves through the Spirit. So after granting peace to those who until then were troubled by enemies, he then says, “Be at leisure from the enemies who distract you, so that in quiet you may contemplate the teachings of the truth.” For this reason the Lord too says, “Whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” We must, then, be at leisure from married relations, so that we may give our leisure to prayer; be at leisure from our efforts after wealth, from craving this paltry glory, from pleasures sought for enjoyment, from envy and every kind of wickedness toward our neighbour, so that, with our soul calm and troubled by no passion, the illumination of God may shine in it, pure and unclouded, as in a mirror. “I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted on the earth.” Here the Lord is plainly speaking of his own passion, as it is written in the Gospel: “And I, when I am lifted up, will draw all to myself”; and that “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” on the earth. Since, then, he was to be lifted up on the cross for the nations, and to accept being lifted up for the whole earth, he therefore says, “I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted on the earth.” “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.” Exulting in God's help, he cried out the same words twice—“The Lord of hosts is with us”—as if trampling and leaping on the enemy, because of his perfect trust in the Saviour of our souls, as one who will suffer no harm from him. “For if God is for us, who is against us?” He who to Jacob [?] … “We will pray”: in the Septuagint it reads thus: “Therefore you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” Pro- … (52) The third Regius manuscript reads ἐνοικίσαντες (“having settled”).

…having granted the victory, and after the wrestling [?] … he himself fights for us. And let us keep still, for “he is our peace, who has made both one, so that he might create the two into one new man.”

ON PSALM 48. For the end; for the sons of Korah, a psalm. 1. Some even of those outside [the faith] have formed notions about the end of human life, and have been carried in different directions in their idea of the end. Some declared the end to be knowledge, others practical activity; others the varied [?] use of life and of the body; while the brutish declared pleasure to be the end. But for us the end, for whose sake we do everything and toward which we hasten, is the blessed life in the age to come. And this is fulfilled in being ruled by God as our king. For nothing better than this could be found by rational nature, even in thought; and the Apostle urges us toward it when he says, “Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father.” Zephaniah too presents this in his prophecy, speaking in the person of God: “For my judgment is upon the gatherings of the nations, to receive kings, to pour out my wrath upon them. For in the fire of my jealousy all the earth will be consumed; for then I will turn to the peoples a tongue for its generation, so that all may call on the name of the Lord, to serve him under one yoke.” To this end, then, I think, the benefits of those Psalms that bear this title are directed. In agreement with this sense are also those who gave the title “For victory,” or “Song of victory,” or “To the one who gives victory.” For since “death has been swallowed up in victory,” and has been destroyed by him who said, “I have overcome the world”; and since all things have been conquered by Christ, and “at his name every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth,” it is fitting that the Holy Spirit should proclaim beforehand in songs of victory the things that are laid up for us. “Hear this, all you nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world; both earthborn and sons of men, rich and poor together.” The audience is very great, since he summons all the nations to hear the psalm, and all who [inhabit] the world… [?] Philippians 2:10. “Hear this, all you nations,” immediately after the title-

…[who] [?] stands so high above as to see all the nations from a lookout and take in the whole world with his eye? What herald has so great a voice that he can cry out audibly to so many ears at once? What place can hold those who are assembled? How great must the teacher be, and how wise, to find teachings worthy of so great an assembly? Wait a little, and you will learn that what follows is worthy of the announcement. For the one who convenes the assembly and calls everyone together by his proclamation is the Paraclete [?], the Spirit of truth, who through prophets and apostles gathers those who are being saved. Since “their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world,” he therefore says, “Hear, all you nations, and all you who inhabit the world.” That is why the Church has been gathered from every walk of life, so that no one may be left outside its benefit. For there are three pairs among those called, in which the whole human race is contained: nations, and those who inhabit the world; earthborn, and sons of men; rich and poor. Whom, then, has he left outside the hearing? Those who are strangers to the faith are called by the term “nations.” Those who are in the Church are “those who inhabit the world.” The “earthborn” are those who set their minds on earthly things and cling to the desires of the flesh. The “sons of men” are those who give some care and training to reason, for rationality is what is proper to man. Rich and poor have a character that is recognizable at once: the one has more than he needs, the other lives in want of necessities. Since the physician of souls came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, in the call he placed first in each pair the one that stands condemned. For the nations are worse than those who inhabit the world; yet they were given precedence in the call, so that those who are badly off might be the first to share in the physician's help. Again, the earthborn were placed before the sons of men, and the rich before the poor. The class that is despaired of and whose salvation is difficult was called before the poor. Such is the physician's love for the weaker: he gives them a share in his help first. At the same time, the shared call also brings about peace, so that those who until now were at odds with one another because of their ways of life may, through the Church, grow used to loving one another. Let the rich man know that he has been called by the same proclamation, in equal honour with the poor man. For it says, “rich and poor together.” Leaving outside his superiority over those of lesser means, and the arrogance that comes from wealth, … [?] the manuscripts read “of so great an assembly,” rightly. In the same place the editions read [?] “and you will learn”; but six manuscripts read “Wait a little, and you will learn.”

…so come into the Church of God. Let the rich man not look down on the poor, and let the poor man not cower before the power of the wealthy. Let the sons of men not despise the earth-born, and let the earth-born in turn not keep themselves apart from them. Let the nations grow used to those who inhabit the world, and let those who inhabit the world welcome in love those who are strangers to the covenants.

2. “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.” According to the Apostle, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation,” and the working of both together brings about perfection. That is why the text has joined the two: the activity of the mouth and the meditation of the heart. If the good is not first stored in the heart, how will someone bring out through his mouth a treasure he does not hold in secret? And if he has the good things of the heart but does not make them public in speech, it will be said to him: “Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure, what profit is there in either?” So for the benefit of others let my mouth speak wisdom, and for our own progress let the heart meditate on understanding. “I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my riddle on the psaltery.” Again the Prophet presents himself, so that his words will not be despised as if they came from human invention. “What I am taught by the Spirit,” he says, “I announce to you. I say nothing of my own and nothing human. I have become an attentive hearer of the riddles of the Spirit, who hands on to us the wisdom of God in a mystery, and so I open the riddle to you and make it plain. And I open it no other way than on the psaltery.” The psaltery is a musical instrument whose notes sound in harmony with the melody of the voice. The rational psaltery, then, is opened most fully when actions are rendered in harmony with words. The spiritual psaltery is the one who has both done and taught. He opens the riddle in psalms, because he sets out from his own example that what he teaches can be done. Since he knows of nothing out of tune or discordant in his life, he speaks the following words with confidence: “Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel shall not surround me.” By the evil day he means the day of

judgment, of which it has been said: “The day of the Lord is incurable upon all the nations,” the day on which, the prophet says, each person’s own schemes will surround him. “Then, since I have done nothing lawless on the road of life, I do not fear the evil day. The footprints of my sins will not stand around me or surround me, bringing proof against me in a silent accusation.” For no other accuser will stand against you than your own deeds, each appearing in its own form: adultery, theft, fornication, together with the night, the manner and the particular traits that mark it. In a word, each sin will appear in its own character and bring a vivid reminder. “So the footprints of my sins will not surround me, because I inclined my ear to a parable and opened my riddle on the psaltery.”

3. “Those who trust in their own power and boast in the abundance of their wealth.” The Prophet’s words are addressed to two kinds of people, the earth-born and the rich. To the first he speaks to tear down their conceit about their power, and to the second to tear down their pride in their great possessions. “You,” he says, “who trust in your own power.” These are the earth-born, who put their hopes in bodily strength and think human nature is enough to accomplish by its own power whatever it wants. “And you,” he says, “who trust in uncertain riches, listen. You need a ransom to be set free and restored to the freedom you lost when the violence of the devil overcame you.” Once he has you under his hand, he does not release you from his tyranny until some worthy ransom persuades him and he chooses to take it in exchange for you. So the ransom must not be of the same kind as those held captive. It must far exceed them in value if he is to release the captives from slavery willingly. That is why a brother cannot redeem you. No human being can persuade the devil to set free from his power someone who has once fallen under it, since no human being can even give God a propitiation for his own sins. How then will he be able to do it for another? And what could he acquire in this age so great that it would be a sufficient exchange for the soul? The soul is precious by nature, because it was made in the image of the one who created it. What toil in the present age is enough provision for the human soul for the age to come? This is our simpler understanding of these words. Even if someone seems to be among the very powerful in this life, even if he is surrounded by a mass of possessions, the passage teaches him to come down from his conceit and humble himself under the mighty hand of God. He should neither trust in what passes for power nor boast in the abundance of his riches. But we can also rise a little higher in thought and understand “those who trust in their own power

and boast in the abundance of their wealth” as referring to the powers of the soul, since not even the soul is self-sufficient for salvation. For even if someone is perfect among the sons of men, he will be counted as nothing if the wisdom that comes from God is absent. Even if he has gathered a mass of theories from the wisdom of the world and amassed some [?] wealth, let him hear the whole truth of the matter. Every human soul has bowed under the evil yoke of slavery to the common enemy of all. It lost the freedom it had from its Creator and was led away captive through sin. Every captive needs a ransom to be set free. So a brother cannot redeem his own brother, and no one can redeem himself, because the redeemer must be far better than the one who is held and already enslaved. In fact, no human being at all has such standing before God that he could make propitiation for someone who has sinned, since he himself is answerable for sin. “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

4. “He shall not give to God a propitiation for himself, nor the price of the redemption of his soul.” So do not look to your brother for redemption. Look to one who surpasses your nature: not a mere man, but a man who is God, Jesus Christ. He alone can give God a propitiation for all of us, because “God set him forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood.” Moses was a brother of Israel, and yet he could not redeem them. How then will an ordinary man redeem? That is why the psalm states the one point outright, “A brother does not redeem,” and adds the other as a forceful question: “Shall a man redeem?” For Moses did not free the people from sin; he only turned aside God’s anger at the sin. And he could not even give a propitiation for himself, since he too fell into transgression. After all the great wonders and signs he had seen, he uttered those doubting words: “Hear me, you disobedient ones! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” Because of this saying the Lord told Moses and Aaron: “Because you did not believe me, to sanctify me before the sons of Israel, you shall not bring this congregation into the land I have given them.” “He shall not give to God a propitiation for himself.” For what could a man find so great that he could give it to redeem his soul? But one thing was found that was worth as much as all people together, and it was given as the price

of the redemption of our soul: the holy and most precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he poured out for all of us. That is why we were bought with a price. If, then, a brother does not redeem, shall a man redeem? And if a man cannot redeem us, then the one who redeemed us is not a man. He came to live among us in the likeness of sinful flesh, but do not on that account suppose that our Lord is only a man and overlook the power of his divinity. He had no need to give God a propitiation for himself or to redeem his own soul, because “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.” No one is able to buy himself back unless the one comes who turns back the captivity of the people, “not with ransoms or with gifts,” as it is written in Isaiah, but with his own blood. We were not his brothers; through our transgressions we had become his enemies. And he is not a mere man but God. Yet after the freedom he grants us, he even calls us his brothers: “I will declare your name to my brothers,” he says. So if you consider the nature of the one who redeemed us, he is neither brother nor man. But if you consider how he came down to us out of grace, he calls us brothers and descends to human nature. He “will not give to God a propitiation for himself,” but for the whole world. He needs no propitiation; he himself is the propitiation. “For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, blameless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. Unlike those high priests, he has no need to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for the people’s sins of ignorance.” Then the psalm says: “And he toiled forever, and he shall live to the end.” Life itself, Power itself, the nature that never tires, toiled in this age when, worn out from the journey, he sat down by the well.

5. He “shall not see corruption when he sees the wise dying,” for “the Father will not let his holy one see corruption,” when those who boast in the wisdom that is coming to nothing die. If you would rather take these words as applying to righteous people as well, remember Job, who says: “Man is born to toil”; and the Apostle: “I toiled more than all of them,” and: “in toils more abundantly.” So the one who toiled in this age shall live to the end. But consider the one who spends his life in luxury and every kind of self-indulgence, who in his soft living wears purple and fine linen, feasts splendidly every day and runs from the labors that virtue demands. He neither toiled in this age nor will he live in the age to come. He will see life from far off, tormented in the flame of the furnace. But the one who in countless

contests for virtue has sweated, and has toiled [?] in labors more abundantly to take it up, is the one who will live to the end. So it was with Lazarus, who toiled much in afflictions, and with Job, who was worn out in his contests against the adversary. “For there,” it says, “the weary are at rest.” That is why the Lord calls to rest those who labor and are heavy laden. How then can those who toil in good works be called heavy laden? Because “Going, they went and wept, scattering their seed; but they shall come back with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves,” full of fruit, as what they sowed is repaid to them in proportion. So they are called heavy laden because they sowed in blessings and also reap in blessings, and with eternal gladness they have loaded themselves with the sheaves of spiritual fruit. So the one who has been redeemed through the propitiation God gave [?] for him toiled in this age, but afterward he will live to the end. He also “shall not see corruption when he sees the wise dying.” He chose the narrow and toilsome road over the smooth and easy one. In the time of God’s visitation, those who disbelieved God’s words and followed the desires of their vain heart will be led away to eternal punishment. But he will not see eternal corruption, the suffering that never ends. By “the wise” the psalm means either those who are clever at villainy, of whom Jeremiah says: “They are wise in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good”; or the disciples of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing, who “claiming to be wise, became fools.” For “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” And because this wisdom makes people fools, God says that he will destroy the wisdom of the wise and set aside the understanding of the prudent. The persuasive arguments of what is falsely called knowledge become a cause of death for those who accept them. That death will not be seen by the one who has been redeemed by him who was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching.

6. “The imprudent and the mindless shall perish together and leave their wealth to strangers. And their graves are their houses for

[?] …calls “gods” those who are not gods by nature, following the usage of the deceived. In the same way he has called the imprudent and the mindless “wise.” We can, then, distinguish in thought the imprudent person from the mindless. The imprudent person is the one who lacks prudence and has no discernment in common, human affairs. So too ordinary usage calls “prudent” those who can tell the useful from the harmful in the affairs of life. The Gospel says the same: “The sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in dealing with their own generation.” They are not simply more prudent, but more prudent in conducting this life in the flesh. Such people are also called stewards of unrighteousness, because of the prudence with which they manage their own lives. In this sense even serpents are prudent: they prepare hiding places for themselves, and in danger they avoid blows to the head by every possible means. The mindless person, on the other hand, is the one who lacks what is distinctive of human beings. These are the knowledge of God the Father, the acceptance of the Word who was in the beginning with God, and the illumination that comes from the Holy Spirit. This mind is possessed by those who can say with Paul: “But we have the mind of Christ.” Scripture, however, also uses these words interchangeably. It calls the godless person imprudent in the verse “The imprudent man said in his heart, ‘There is no God,’” and again it calls what is harmful to life “mindless,” as the Apostle does when he speaks of those who fall into mindless and harmful desires. Either way, the imprudent and the mindless are swept down to one common end, destruction. One could also say that the imprudent person is the one who lives like a pagan, and the mindless person the one who lives in the Jewish manner, by the bare observance of the law. It was to this imprudent person that God said, because of the godlessness within him: “Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you.” And Israel according to the flesh is called mindless by the prophet who says: “Ephraim was like a mindless dove; he called on Egypt and went to the Assyrians.” So while both are crushed together by their own ignorance, we who were strangers to them become heirs of their wealth. The commandments are ours, the prophets are ours,

the patriarchs are ours; the righteous of old are ours. Those who perish in their own imprudence have left their wealth to us. But the houses of these, the imprudent and the mindless, are graves forever. Those whose lives are filled with the dead works of every sin have graves for houses forever. For someone who has died through his transgressions lives not in a house but in a grave, since his own soul has been put to death. Jacob, guileless and simple in character, lives in a house; of him it is written that he was “a plain and good man, dwelling in a house.” But the utterly wicked man lives in a grave. He does not lay a foundation of repentance from dead works. He is like a whitewashed tomb, which looks fine on the outside but inside is full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness. That is why, when such a person speaks, he does not open his mouth for the word of God; his throat is an open grave. So if someone who believes in Christ does not live in a way that matches his faith, he has paid attention to wicked doctrines and has not accepted [?] the intent of Scripture, and so he hews himself a tomb in the rock.

7. “Their dwellings are from generation to generation”; that is, their graves are their houses forever. Then, explaining what he means by graves, he shows that he is speaking of the bodies in which souls dwell after wickedness has put them to death. So he adds: “Their dwellings from generation to generation,” since by custom human bodies are always called dwellings. “And they have called their names upon their lands.” The name of the ungodly is not written in the book of the living, nor is it counted with the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. Their names stay on their own land, because they preferred this passing, short-lived life to the eternal dwellings. Do you not see those who build marketplaces and gymnasia in the cities, put up walls and construct aqueducts? Do you not see how their names are given to these earthly buildings? Some have even branded herds of horses with their own

names, contriving to make their memory last long beyond their lives. And after showing off their magnificence in tombs, they have left their names on their monuments. These are the people whose minds are on earthly things. They think glory here, and being remembered by others, is enough to make them blessed. And you may see some who are proud of what is falsely called knowledge, who give their assent to wicked doctrines, and who, instead of the name of Christians, call themselves after one of the founders of heresies: Marcion, or Valentinus, or one of those now in vogue. Know that these too have called their names upon their lands, since they have given themselves over to perishable men who are wholly of the earth.

8. “And man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the mindless beasts and became like them. This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them, and afterward they will take pleasure in their mouth.” Man is a great thing, and a merciful man is precious, for he has that preciousness in his natural constitution. What else on earth was made in the image of the Creator? To whom has rule and authority been given over all living things, on land, in the water and in the air? He ranks a little below the angels because he is joined to an earthly body, for God made man from the earth, and his ministers a flame of fire. Yet human beings too have the power to know and understand their Creator and Maker. For God breathed into his face; that is, he placed in man a share of his own grace, so that by what is like he might recognize what is like. Man was fashioned in the image of his Creator and held in such great honor, honored above heaven, above the sun, above the choirs of the stars. (For which of the heavens is called an image of God Most High? What image of the Creator does the sun preserve? What about the moon, or the other stars? They are lifeless and material, possessing only transparent bodies. There is no thought in them anywhere, no movements of choice, no freedom of self-determination. They are slaves to the necessity laid on them, and by it they always revolve on the same course without variation.) Man was raised above all these in honor, yet he did not understand. He gave up following God and becoming like his Creator, became a slave to the passions of the flesh, and “was compared to the mindless beasts

…[senseless beasts], and became like them: now like a horse mad after females, neighing after his neighbor's wife; now like a ravening wolf lying in wait for what belongs to others; and at other times, through his deceit toward his brother, likened to the cunning of the fox. It is truly the height of folly and of brutish senselessness neither to perceive one's own original constitution, though one was fashioned in the image of the Creator, nor to be willing to understand the great dispensations carried out on one's behalf, and from these at least to recognize one's own worth; but instead to forget that, having cast away the image of the heavenly, one has taken on the image of the earthly. And so that man might not remain in sin, for his sake the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and humbled himself so far as to become obedient unto death, even death on a cross. If you do not remember your first origin, take a notion of your dignity from the price paid for you: look at what was given in exchange for you, and know your own worth. You were bought with the precious blood of Christ; do not become a slave of sin. Understand your own honor, so that you may not be compared to the senseless beasts. This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them. God, who orders our affairs, hinders us as we walk in wickedness, setting stumbling blocks and obstacles before us, so that, having turned away from a senseless life, afterward we may take delight in our mouth, as those who believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation. Paul persecuted and ravaged the Church of Christ; he gave free rein to his course toward wickedness. Afterward he took delight in his mouth, proclaiming in the synagogues that this is the

9. Like sheep they are laid in Hades; death will shepherd them. Those who are brutish and have been compared to the senseless beasts, like sheep that have neither understanding nor the strength to defend themselves, the one who carries them off into captivity, being an enemy, has already cast down into his own stronghold and handed over to Death to shepherd. For death shepherded from Adam until the commonwealth under Moses, until the true shepherd came, who lays down his own life for the sheep, and

…from the prison of Hades into the morning of the resurrection, he handed them over to the upright, that is, to his holy angels, to shepherd them. And the upright will have dominion over them in the morning. For to each of the faithful an angel is assigned, worthy to behold the Father who is in heaven. These upright ones, then, will have dominion over them once they have been freed from the most bitter slavery; and they will have dominion over those who have come into the morning, that is, those who have come under the rising of the light. Observe the whole sequence of the words of Scripture. Man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts. He who has worth by virtue of his constitution, yet because of the sin dwelling in him does not perceive himself—this man was compared to the beasts. Then, because he estranged himself from the Word of God and became irrational, the enemy seized him like a sheep without a shepherd, laid him in Hades, and handed him over to death to shepherd. For this reason the one who has been rescued from there and freed from the evil shepherd says: The Lord is my shepherd. And there is no longer death, but life; no longer a fall, but resurrection; no longer falsehood, but the truth. And their help will grow old in Hades. Either he is speaking of death, which with all its help was unable to keep hold of those it shepherded, because of him who destroys the one who holds the power of death; and all its help is old and weak. And then the help of men deceived in their minds, who pride themselves on wealth and glory and power, will be exposed. It will grow old in Hades, when their weakness is exposed. Or perhaps the help of the righteous who have been redeemed by the Lord will be prolonged in Hades. For they have not yet received the promises, since God foresaw something better for us, so that those who went before should not be made perfect apart from us. But God will redeem my soul from the hand of Hades, when he receives me. He clearly prophesies the Lord's descent into Hades, who together with the others will redeem the Prophet's own soul too, so that it does not remain there. 10. Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house is increased. Do not be afraid, he says, when a man becomes rich. This proclamation too is necessary for those who inhabit the world, both the earthborn and the sons of men, rich and poor together. Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich. When you see, he says, the unjust man rich and the just man poor, do not be afraid within yourself; do not be alarmed in your mind, as though

there were nowhere any providence of God overseeing human affairs; or as though divine oversight perhaps exists somewhere, yet does not reach as far as the earthly region so as to watch over our affairs as well. For, one thinks, if there were a providence assigning to each what is fitting, the righteous, who know how to use wealth, would be rich, and the wicked, who have wealth as an instrument of their own wickedness, would be poor. Since, then, there are many among the nations and the earthborn who think such things, and who, because of the apparent unevenness in the distribution of the goods of life, suppose the world to be without providence, the word addresses them, checking their untaught impulse—those whom he had also summoned in the opening to hear his teachings. Or perhaps he is addressing himself specifically to the poor man alone, saying: Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich. For these above all need consolation so as not to cower before those who are above them. For there is no benefit, he says, to the rich man when he dies, since he cannot take his wealth with him; he gained from his enjoyment only this much, that his soul was called blessed by flatterers in this life. But in dying, he says, he will not take all this finery with him; he will scarcely take a garment to cover his shame—and that only if the servants who lay him out see fit. He will be glad to obtain a little earth; and even this is given him out of pity by those who bury him, who provide it out of respect for our common human nature, not as a favor to him, but in honor of humanity. Do not, then, lose heart over present things, but wait for that blessed and endless life. For then you will see that poverty, obscurity, and the lack of luxury turn out for the good of the righteous man. And do not be troubled now over what are reckoned goods, as though they were distributed [?]. For you will hear how it will be said to the rich man: You received your good things in your life; and to the poor man, that he received evil things in his life. Therefore, fittingly, the one is comforted and the other is in anguish. He will give thanks to you when you do good to him. This is said of the earthly man, who thinks that only the advantages of this life—wealth, health, and power—are goods; of him he says that he will give thanks to God when he prospers, but in adversity he lets loose every kind of blasphemy. For, leaving the poor man aside, he now directs his word to God, including in his accusation against wealth also the fact that in prosperity

ON PSALM 59. 1. As I look at the eagerness of your listening and at the weakness of my own strength, there came to my mind the picture of a child already fairly sturdy, yet not yet weaned, who keeps pestering his mother's breast, though it has gone cold through illness; and even though the mother knows that the springs of her milk are dry, pulled and tugged by him she gives him the breast, not to nourish the infant but to stop his crying. So too, even if our resources have been dried up by this long and varied illness of the body, they are nevertheless set before you, offering no enjoyment worth mentioning, but a certain reassurance, since the overflowing measure of your love is content to soothe its longing for us with my voice alone. Let the Church of God, then, be addressed, and let it be taught to say what we were saying just now: Give us help out of affliction, for vain is the salvation of man. So perhaps the sense of the psalm does not even allow us to plead illness as an excuse, if affliction is the bringer of help and not an occasion of weakness. For those, then, who were rejected because of their sins and then received back again through God's love for mankind, it is fitting to say: O God, you have rejected us and broken us down; you were angry, and you had compassion on us. Or rather, since our discourse has fallen into the course of the psalm's meaning, come, let us take up its interpretation in moderate measure. 2. The history of the present psalm, word for word as the title gives it, has not yet been found set down anywhere in the divinely inspired histories; but things equivalent to it will be found by those who search diligently in the Second Book of Kingdoms, where it is written: And David struck Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to set his hand upon the river Euphrates. And David captured from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, and left of them a hundred [Note: The Paris edition reads: "By the same author, on Psalm 59. For the end, for those who will be changed; further, for an inscription for David, for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand."
