chariots. And a little further on it says: And David reigned over Israel, and David executed judgment and righteousness, and Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army. And a little after that: And the sons of Ammon sent and hired Syria of Rehob and Syria of Zobah, twenty thousand men; and Joab saw that the battle was set against him in front, and he chose men from all the sons of Israel, and they drew up in battle array against Syria. And the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated before Israel, and they deserted to Israel and served them. In this passage of the history we find the title of the psalm in agreement; except that the time of this inscription is the time when David was at his most brilliant and most renowned for his exploits in war. So it is worth asking how it begins with lamentations and dirges, when it ought to be joyful and glad at his successes. For the cries of those celebrating are one thing, and those of the downcast another. A victory is the occasion of a festival for the whole people, not only for soldiers but also for farmers, merchants, craftsmen, and all who share in the blessings of peace. How, then, can it say, O God, you have rejected us and broken us down? Surely he took the victors to himself. And how did he break down those whom he so greatly increased, adding to them weapons, chariots, horses, subjects, and tributary land—all Arabia, Phoenicia, Mesopotamia? It is worth considering whether the words do not betray some ingratitude. For he who first slew Hadadezer king of Zobah, taking from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen and twenty thousand foot; who again enslaved the king of Syria who came to the aid of the defeated man and made him tributary, and in a single moment slaughtered twenty-two thousand of his men; and who won a third victory over the sons of Ammon drawn up by the gate of the city, through Joab his commander-in-chief, who divided his force in two, meeting some face to face and going around to subdue the others from behind—how, after such exploits, does he utter such gloomy and dejected words, saying: O God, you have rejected us and broken us down; you were angry, and you had compassion on us? But although the time of the inscription was this time of successes, the force of what is written has reference to the end;

and by "the end" he means what is going to come about at the consummation of the ages. That is also why he says the psalm was written for those who will be changed. One may understand this simply of the whole human race, since the benefit of the psalm passes to all. For those are being changed and will be changed who neither keep the same condition of body nor always stand firm in the same mind, but are changed in body through the transitions of the stages of life, and shift in mind with the variety of circumstances. For we are one thing as children, another as youths, different again when grown to manhood, and when we have grown old we are altogether changed once more. We are one thing in the brighter conditions of life, and we become different from what we were when we meet with harsher times; different when sick, different when thriving; different at weddings, different in mourning. Or else, because it does not say "for those who are being changed" but "for those who will be changed," and the expression carries an indication of prophecy by turning the time toward the future, it is more consistent to understand "those who will be changed" as those who were going to abandon the vain custom of their fathers and to regulate their way of life by the strictness of the Gospel. The psalm, then, was not written for the Jews of that time, but for us who were to be changed: who exchange polytheism for piety, and [?] over idols for the knowledge of him who made us; who choose lawful self-control instead of lawless pleasure; who take up psalmody, fasting and prayer instead of pipes, dances, and drunkenness. Whoever says, then, that the psalm was written for us would not miss the truth. That is why the divine oracles are ours too, and in the Church of God they are read at every assembly as gifts sent by God, a kind of nourishment for souls supplied through the Spirit. But the psalm was also written "for an inscription"; that is, let your hearing of it not be casual; and do not, as things written on perishable material quickly vanish, engrave it on the memory of your mind for a short while and then allow it to be blurred and effaced; but keep it inscribed as on a pillar in your soul, that is, fixed immovable and firm in your memory for all time. And if the Jew pushes us away as strangers to what is written, we will put him to shame from what is written, showing the mixed character of the calling: how it gathers what was separated, calls together those who were far off, and makes the many one through faith in Christ. Gilead is mine, it says, and Manasseh is mine. And Ephraim

he named, and Judah he took to himself, and Moab he counted in. And he threatens to set foot on Idumea; and he announces the good news of the subjection of all together: The foreigners have been subjected to me. 3. O God, then, you have rejected us. Those who distance themselves from you in proportion to their sins you have rejected. You have broken down our structures of wickedness, [benefiting us through weakness]. You were angry, when we were by nature children of wrath, having no hope and without God in the world. You had compassion on us, when you set forth your Only-begotten as a propitiation for our sins, so that in his blood we might find redemption. These benefits we would not have recognized, had you not given us the wine of compunction to drink. By "wine" he means the word that brings the hardened heart to awareness. You have given to those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from before the bow. Moses marked the doorposts of the Israelites with the blood of the sheep; but you have given us as a sign the very blood of the spotless Lamb slain for the sin of the world. And Ezekiel says that the sign is given on the foreheads. For go, he says, after him, and strike; do not spare, and do not have pity. Old man, young man, infant, virgin, and women—kill them to utter destruction; but do not come near any on whom the sign is. God has spoken in his holy place: I will exult, and I will divide Shechem. Shechem, the choice portion given to Joseph by Jacob, is a type of the covenant that seemed to have been granted to Israel alone. This choice covenant and inheritance of the people, then, I will bring to division and make common to the rest. When the covenant has been divided among all, and the benefit from it has become common to all who receive God's favors, then the valley of tents will also be measured out; that is, the whole inhabited world will be divided, as if into allotments, into the Christian communities in each place. Then he will also join together what was separated—he who makes peace, whether among things on earth or things in the heavens; and having broken down the dividing wall of partition, he will make both one. 4. ON PSALM 61. "For the end, for Jeduthun, a psalm of David." 1. We know of two psalms with the title "For Jeduthun": the thirty-eighth and the one before us. We take David to be the author of the composition. But it was given to Jeduthun for his own benefit, to correct the passions of his soul, and to be sung before the people, so that God might be glorified by it and those who heard its harmony might have their characters reformed. For Jeduthun too was a sacred singer, as the history of Chronicles testifies: "And with them were Heman and Jeduthun, trumpets and cymbals for sounding aloud, and instruments for the songs of God." A little later it says: "And King David and the commanders of the army set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, harps and drums." Both psalms, then, are mostly about endurance. Endurance calms the angry part of the soul, drives out all pride and achieves humility. For a man who has not accepted being lower than everyone and the last of all cannot master his anger when he is reviled, or overcome temptations by patience when he is afflicted. The one who has achieved perfect humility has already judged himself more worthless than any insult, so words of dishonor will not stir his soul. If he is called a pauper, he knows that he is poor, lacking everything, and in need of the Lord's daily provision. If he is called low-born and of obscure family,

he has already fixed in his heart that he was made from clay. That is why in the other psalm he says, "I said, I will guard my ways," and describes the sinner's attack on him and his own patience: "When the sinner stood against me," he says, "I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent even from good things." Then, going on, he says: "Surely all things are vanity, every man living," and then, "He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it." In the psalm before us, however, he begins with a question, as if he were talking to his own soul, following on from what was said before. He does not want his soul to submit to the mind of the flesh and be provoked to anger and grief. Why, he says, should I make my soul the slave of wicked passions, when God who created it entrusted it with rule over the body and its passions? It must therefore rule the passions and serve God. It cannot be ruled by sin and by God at the same time; it must master evil and be subject to the Master of all things. So the Prophet addresses the one who brings on temptations, who stirs up a great crowd of evils against him and is eager to lead the mind of the spirit captive and throw it down beneath the flesh. As if to show him that his scheme against him is futile, he says: Why do you force me to serve what I must not serve? I have a Master; I know the true King. 2. "Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation." He has given the reason for his eagerness to be subject: salvation comes from God. It is proper for a Creator to care for the safety of what he has made. Or else he says "from him is my salvation" because he foresaw prophetically the grace that would come through the Lord's becoming man. So he says that we must serve God and love him, since he planned so great a benefit for the human race that "he did not spare even his own Son but gave him up for us all." For Scripture is accustomed to call the Christ of God "salvation," as Simeon says somewhere: "Now, Master, you let your servant depart, for my eyes have seen your salvation." Let us be subject to God, then, because from him is our salvation. He explains what this salvation is. It is not some mere activity that gives us a favor such as release from sickness and health of body. What, then, is the salvation? "For he is my God and my Savior, my helper; I shall not be shaken any further." The Son who is from God is our God. He is also the Savior of the human race,

who supports our weakness and steadies the tossing that temptations cause in our souls. "I shall not be shaken any further." As a man, he admits to being shaken, but not "any further." It is impossible for a human soul not to be shaken somewhat by temptations. As long as our sins are small and few, we are shaken gently, like plants swayed by a mild breeze. But when our evils grow more numerous and greater, the shaking naturally grows stronger in proportion to the growth of our sins. Some are shaken further. Others are even torn up by the roots and thrown down, when the spiritual forces of wickedness, more violent than any whirlwind, tear away what we might call the roots of the soul, by which it was anchored in faith in God. So he says: I was shaken, as a man is, but I shall not be shaken further, because I am held up by the right hand of the Savior. 3. "How long will you set upon a man? All of you commit murder, as against a leaning wall and a fence [?]." Again the text fights against the wicked servants of the devil and blames the excess of the plotting they bring. Men are weak creatures, but you set upon them. You are not content with the first assault but bring a second and a third, until you have so overturned the soul of the one who has fallen into your hands that it becomes like a wall that leans and a fence that is knocked down. A wall stays firm as long as it keeps standing upright. But once it leans, it must inevitably break up and fall. A single solid mass can be set upright again after it leans, but things made of many parts can no longer be straightened once they have tipped to one side. The text shows, then, that human nature, being composite, was made to lean by sin, and must be wholly dissolved. Then it will be rebuilt by the craftsman who built it in the beginning, and will receive a security and permanence that leaves it safe from a second fall. "You are God's field," he says, "God's building." The enemy shook this building, and the Creator repaired the breaches made in it. So the fall was necessary because of sin, but the resurrection is great because of immortality. "But they plotted to reject my price; they ran
that is, my enemies and those who plot against me without truth [?] made their efforts against me, having given themselves wholly over to falsehood. But a scribal error occurred in those after

in thirst; with their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed." The price of a man is the blood of Christ: "For you were bought with a price," he says; "do not become slaves of men." This is the price that the soldiers of the evil one plotted to make useless to us, by leading us back into slavery once we had been set free. "They ran in thirst." He speaks of how intense the demons' plotting is: they run against us, thirsting for our destruction. "With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed." There are many who approve of wicked deeds. They call the buffoon charming and the foul-mouthed man sophisticated. They call the bitter, irascible man someone not to be trifled with. They praise the stingy, unsociable man as thrifty, the spendthrift as generous, and the fornicator and the debauched as someone who enjoys life and is easygoing. In short, they give every vice the pet name of the virtue nearest to it. Such people bless with their mouth but curse in their heart. With their fine-sounding words they call down every curse on the lives of these people, for by approving of them they make them liable to eternal condemnation. Again he talks to his soul, tightening its subjection to God. "But be subject to God, my soul," he says, "for from him is my endurance." He shows how great the temptations are, and says what the Apostle says, that "he will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able to bear." For from him is my endurance. 4. "In God is my salvation and my glory; the God of my help, and my hope is in God." Blessed is the one who prides himself on none of the [?] things of this life but has God as his glory, who has Christ as his boast and can say with the Apostle, "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ." As it is, many take pride in the body: those who devote themselves to athletic contests, or in general those who are bursting with the vigor of youth. Many take pride in courage in war, and even count the killing of their own kind a virtue. For distinction in war, and the trophies raised by generals and cities, are awarded according to how much killing has been done. Others are glorified for building walls around cities [?]

and others for constructing aqueducts and erecting great gymnasia. So-and-so spends his wealth on men who fight wild beasts. He exults in the empty shouts of the crowds, is puffed up by their praise and thinks highly of himself, though his glory is in his shame. He even displays his own sin, written up on tablets in the most conspicuous places of the city. Another is glorified for his wealth, and another because he is a formidable and unbeatable orator, or skilled in the wisdom of this world. The glory of all these deserves pity. Those who make God their glory are the ones we should call blessed. If someone thinks highly of himself because he is a servant of the king and receives great honors from him, how much more should you magnify yourself because you are a servant of the great King? He has called you into the closest intimacy with him, and you have received the Spirit of the promise, so that, sealed by it, you have been shown to be a son of God. Having learned in himself the benefit of true hope in God, the Prophet urges the people to the same zeal as his own, saying: "Hope in him, all you assembly of peoples; pour out your hearts before him." We cannot become capable of holding divine grace unless we first drive out the evil passions that have already taken possession of our souls. I myself have seen physicians who would not give their healing medicines until they had first used emetics to empty out the diseased matter that intemperate people had stored up in themselves through a bad diet. And a vessel that is already filled with some foul-smelling liquid will not take in perfume poured into it unless it has been washed out. What was there before must be poured out, so that what is brought in can be received. "But the sons of men are vain." He saw that not everyone followed his command. They would not agree to hope in God but placed their hope in the vanities of life. That is why he says: "But the sons of men are vain, the sons of men are false." Why are they vain? Because they are false. Where is their falsehood most clearly exposed? "In the scales," he says, "so as to do wrong." What scales does he mean? Surely not all people weigh things on scales? Surely not all are wool-sellers or butchers, or deal in gold or silver, or are occupied with the kinds of goods that merchants commonly exchange by scales and weights? There is a great class of craftsmen who need no scales for their work. There are many sailors, and many who spend their time in the law courts and in public office. Falsehood is found among them, but no one cheats them with scales. What, then, does he mean? That each of us has in secret a kind of scale

that was built into us by the one who created us, and by which [?] we are able to discern the nature of things. "I have set before your face life and death, good and evil." These are two natures opposed to each other. Weigh them against each other on the balance of your own judgment. Weigh carefully what is more profitable for you: to choose passing pleasure and through it receive eternal [?], or to choose the hardship of practicing virtue and let it secure for you eternal delight. Men, then, are false, because the judgment of their souls is corrupt. The Prophet laments over them, saying: "Woe to those who call darkness light and light darkness, who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter." "The present is mine," someone says, "and who knows the future?" You weigh badly, wicked man, choosing evil in place of the good, preferring vanities to true things, putting the temporary before the eternal, and picking pleasure that passes away instead of joy that is unceasing and everlasting. So the sons of men are false in the scales, so as to do wrong. They wrong first of all themselves, and then also their neighbors, since they give themselves bad counsel in what they do and set a wicked example for others. On the day of judgment you will not be able to say, "I did not know the good." Your own scales will be brought forward against you, for they contained enough to discern good from evil. We test the weights of bodies by the way the balance tips. But we discern what is to be chosen in life by the free will of the soul. This is what he called a scale, because it can incline equally to either side. 5. "Do not hope in injustice, and do not long for plunder." Above he said, "Hope in him, all you assembly of peoples." He saw how slow they were to obey, and declared, "But the sons of men are vain." Again he forbids them to hope in injustice. The one who judges that wealth gathered by injustice gives him enough means to be strong and powerful is like a sick man who thinks an abundance of disease is good health. "Do not hope in injustice." It hinders you in everything you do. "And do not long for plunder." He urges us not to desire what belongs to others. "If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it." If you see someone who is exceedingly rich, do not call his life blessed. If money flows around you from many sides and from abundant springs, do not welcome its abundance. "If wealth flows." Marvel at the word: the nature of wealth is to flow. It runs past those who have it more swiftly than a torrent, now to one, now to another [?]

passing by. A river rushing down from a height comes near those standing on the bank, but no sooner has it touched them than it has gone on its way. In the same way, the easy flow of wealth makes its presence very fleeting and slippery, and its nature is to pass from one person to another. Today the field is this man's, tomorrow another's, and soon after someone else's. Look at the houses in the city: how many names they have taken since they were built, called now after one owner, now after another. Gold, too, always slips through the hands of its owner and passes to another, and from him to someone else. You could more easily hold water in your closed hand than keep wealth for yourself permanently. So it is well said, "If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it." Do not let your soul be attached to it. Accept what is useful in it, not loving and admiring it too much as though it were one of the good things, but choosing it for the service it can render as a tool. Then, after all that he has said, he adds a declaration that is no longer in his own words but one he heard from God himself. "For God spoke once," he says, "these two things I heard." Let no one be troubled by this statement as if it were strange, that God spoke once but the Prophet heard two things. It is possible for someone to speak once and yet say many things in that one time. A man may meet someone once and talk with him about many matters, and the one who heard his words can say, "He spoke to me once, but he talked about many things." This is what is said here: God appeared to me once, but he spoke of two things. He did not say, "God spoke one thing, but I heard these two," for then the statement would have seemed to contradict itself. What, then, were the two things he heard? "That power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy": God is mighty in judgment, and the same God is merciful. So do not hope in injustice, do not set your heart on wealth, do not choose vanity, and do not carry around the judgment of your soul in a corrupted state. Knowing that our Master is mighty, fear his strength, and do not despair of his love for mankind. Fear is good for keeping us from doing wrong. And hope of mercy is good for the one who has once slipped into sin, so that he does not abandon himself to despair. "For power belongs to God, and from him is mercy." "For you will repay each according to his works." "For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you." Did you oppress your brother? Expect the same. Did you plunder the goods of those poorer than you, beat the poor, shame them with insults, accuse falsely, tell lies, plot against other men's marriages, swear falsely, move the boundaries set by your fathers, encroach on the property of orphans, crush widows, and prefer present pleasure to the good things of the promises? Expect the [?]

…the repayment [?]. For whatever each one sows, that he will also reap. And if you have done anything good [?], expect many times over the reward for that too. For you will repay each one according to his works. If you remember this declaration throughout your life, you will be able to escape the penalties [?] for sins, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

…with joy [?] I accepted. What these things are he sets out a little later: the pangs of death, the dangers of Hades, the affliction, the pain. All of these seemed dear to him because of his love for God and the hope laid up for those who accept sufferings for the sake of godliness. "For I did not endure these contests against my will," he says, "nor by force and under compulsion. I accepted the hardships with a kind of affection and goodwill, so that I can say: For your sake we are being put to death all day long." These words seem to be equal in force to those of the Apostle, and to be spoken from the same disposition as his: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication. For this is how each of us too can carry through what is hard in the commandments: when he lives as though he were displaying his way of life to God, the spectator of all.

2. Because he inclined his ear to me. He said "inclined" not so that you would form some bodily notion of God, as though he had ears and bent them toward a quiet voice, the way we bring our ears close to people who speak softly so that we can catch what is said with our senses from nearby. No, he said "inclined" to show his own weakness: "Out of his love for humankind he came down to me as I lay on the ground." It is as if a sick man were so weak that he could not even speak clearly, and a kindly physician brought his ear close and learned from near at hand what the patient needed. So he inclined his ear to me. For the divine hearing does not need a voice in order to perceive. It knows how to recognize what is being asked even in the movement of the heart. Or have you not heard that Moses said nothing, but pleaded with the Lord with his unspoken groans, and the Lord heard him and said: Why are you crying out to me? God knows how to hear even the blood of the righteous, which has no tongue and no voice that travels through the air. And the presence of righteous works is a loud voice before God. And in my days I will call upon him. We pray on one day, or spend one hour feeling a little gloomy about our sins, and then we stop worrying, as though we had already done something to match our wickedness. The saint, however, says that he shows a confession measured out over the whole span of his life. "For in my days,"

3. The Lord is merciful and righteous. Everywhere Scripture joins God's righteousness to his compassion, teaching us that God's mercy is not without judgement, and his judgement is not without mercy. When he shows mercy, he measures out his compassion with judgement to those who are worthy. When he judges, he brings judgement with his eye on our weakness, and punishes us with love for humankind rather than with strict repayment in equal measure. And our God shows mercy. Mercy is a feeling for those who have been brought low beyond what they deserve, and it arises in people who are inclined to sympathy. We pity someone who has fallen from great wealth into utter poverty, someone who has been thrown down from the peak of bodily health into extreme sickness, someone who once delighted in the beauty and bloom of his body and has been ruined by the most shameful passions. Since we too were once in glory, living in paradise, but became inglorious and lowly through the fall, our God shows mercy, seeing what we have become in place of what we were. That is why he called Adam back with the voice of mercy, saying: Adam, where are you? He who knows all things was not asking to be informed. He wanted Adam to realize what he had become in place of what he had been. "Where are you?" means "What a fall you have come down to from such a height!"

4. The Lord keeps the little ones; I was brought low, and he saved me. Take it first in the natural sense: human nature could not have survived if very young children and infants were not kept by the Lord. How could the unborn in the womb be nourished, or move about in such cramped spaces, with no room to turn? They live in dark and watery places. They cannot breathe or live a human life, but are carried about in fluid like fish. How could they survive unless they were held fast by God's keeping? And when they drop into this unfamiliar place and are chilled by the air after the warmth of the womb, how could they last even a short while if God did not preserve them? So, The Lord keeps the little ones; I was brought low, and he saved me. Or you may understand the saying this way: "Since I turned and became like a little child, and received the kingdom of heaven like a child, and through innocence brought myself down to the lowliness of children…

5. Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has been good to you. The noble contestant addresses words of encouragement to himself, much as Paul says: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me. The Prophet says the same to himself: "Since you have fully run the long course of this life, return now to your rest, for the Lord has been good to you." For eternal rest is laid up for those who have fought through this present life according to the rules. It is not paid out as a debt owed for their works. It is granted by the grace of our bountiful God to those who have hoped in him. Then, before describing the good things there, he describes his escape from the troubles of the world, and for these he gives thanks to the liberator of souls, who frees him from the varied [?] and relentless slavery of the passions. What are these? For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from slipping. He sketches the rest to come by contrasting it with things here. "Here," he says, "the pangs of death encompassed me; there he delivered my soul from death. Here the eyes pour out tears of affliction; there no tear will any longer cloud the eyes of those who rejoice in contemplating the beauty of God's glory." For God will wipe away every tear from every face. Here the danger of slipping is great; that is why Paul said: Let whoever thinks he stands take care that he does not fall. But there one's footing is firm and life [?] cannot be overturned. There is no longer any danger of being led into sin, for there is neither the rebellion of the flesh nor a woman's partnership in sin. For in the resurrection there is no male and female. There is one single, uniform life for those who dwell in the land of the living, all of them pleasing their Master. This world is itself mortal and a place of the dying. Since the visible order is composite, and everything composite naturally comes apart, those who are in the world, being parts of the world, necessarily [share] the…

…of ages and ways of life a human being [passes through], and at each period of seven years a boundary of its own marks off what has gone before and shows the change clearly. The age of the infant ends in the first seven years, with the loss of the teeth. Next, the time of the boy, now fit for learning, lasts until puberty. The adolescent, once he has reached the twenty-first year and the first down begins to shade his cheeks, disappears without anyone noticing, as the youth passes over into the man. So when you see a man who has left behind the growth that comes with age, who is now steady in his thinking and bears no trace of youth, will you not conclude that what went before has died in him? Again, the old man, reshaped into a different form and a different disposition of soul, is plainly another person from the earlier ones. So human life is by nature made up of many deaths, not only in the change from one age to the next but also in the falls of souls into sin. But where there is no alteration of body or of soul (for there is no turning aside of thought, no change of mind, since no circumstance takes away the steadiness and calm of one's thoughts), that is truly the land of the living, where they are always the same as themselves. It is there above all that the Prophet promises to be well-pleasing to the God of all, since nothing outside will interrupt him in pursuing the true service, equal in honour to that of the angels. "We make it our aim," he says, "whether at home in the body or away from the body, to be pleasing to him." That is the land of the living, where there is no night, no sleep, that imitation of death; where there is no eating, no drinking, those props of our weakness; no sickness, no pains, no medical treatment, no law courts, no trading, no crafts, no money, which is the beginning of evils, the occasion of wars, the root of hatred. It is a land of the living: not of those who die through sin, but of those who live the true life in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
